en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.1 1.

Āhuneyyavagga First Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Paṭhama-āhuneyyasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What five? The one who has attained destruction of the taints; the one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; and the noble disciple who possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. These, bhikkhus, are the five persons worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
(AN 6.1, PTS AN iii 279) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the six?
Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.]
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad; one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
First. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.2 1.
Āhuneyyavagga (The Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings)
The Second Discourse on Those Worthy of Offerings (Dutiya-āhuneyyasutta):
“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of offerings … [as above] … an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
By which six?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu wields the various kinds of psychic power: being one, he becomes many;
being many, he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he passes through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains...
He moves without clinging, just as in the air; he dives in and out of the earth, just as in water;
he walks on water without breaking the surface, just as on earth; he travels cross-legged through the air, just like a winged bird;
and with his hand, he touches and strokes these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic.
He touches and strokes [the earth]; he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
He understands the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing their minds with his own.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," or a mind without lust as "a mind without lust," or a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred"... [and so on].
A mind free from hatred...
a mind with delusion...
or a mind free from delusion...
Whether the mind is contracted … or whether the mind is distracted … or whether the mind is exalted …
...a mind that is not sublime ...
a surpassable mind ...
or an unsurpassable mind ...
Whether the mind is concentrated or unconcentrated,
whether the mind is liberated or not liberated...
Or, he understands an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus, with their aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past abodes.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and reappearing.
He understands beings as they pass away and reappear—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body..."
After the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.

But these worthy beings, who were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, and undertook kamma based on right view—after the breakup of the body, after death... [they have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world].
‘Having died, they have been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
he sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

“With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he abides therein.

It is, monks, when a monk possesses these six qualities that he is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
This is the second [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.3 1.

Āhuneyyavagga Indriyasutta “Monks, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These, monks, are the five faculties.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What six? [The sūtra continues with the six qualities.]”
By means of the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom,
through the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Thus was the third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.4.

1. Āhuneyyavagga: Balasutta (AN 6.4, PTS AN iii 282) "Bhikkhus, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five powers."
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
With which six?
With the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, and through the destruction of the taints.”
Having personally realized through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he enters and dwells therein.

Possessing these six qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus it was said.
The fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.5 1. Āhuneyyavagga First Discourse on the Well-Bred Horse (Paṭhama-ājānīya-sutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these five qualities of a well-bred horse that a well-bred horse possesses because of which he is worthy of a king, an accessory of a king, and considered a factor of kingship.

What five? Here, bhikkhus, a well-bred horse is well-grown, well-proportioned, and well-built; he is swift, patient, and docile. These are the five qualities of a well-bred horse that a well-bred horse possesses because of which he is worthy of a king, an accessory of a king, and considered a factor of kingship. In the same way, bhikkhus, there are these five qualities of a person who is like a well-bred horse that a noble disciple possesses because of which he is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is well-grown, well-proportioned, and well-built; he is swift, patient, and docile. And how, bhikkhus, is a noble disciple well-grown, well-proportioned, and well-built? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has faith; he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a noble disciple is well-grown, well-proportioned, and well-built. And how, bhikkhus, is a noble disciple swift? Here, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple hears a teaching that he has not heard before, he quickly gains confidence in it, quickly gains faith in it, and quickly attains a state of gladness. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a noble disciple is swift. And how, bhikkhus, is a noble disciple patient? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple patiently endures cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sunburn, and creeping things; he patiently endures ill-spoken, unwelcome words and arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and life-threatening. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a noble disciple is patient. And how, bhikkhus, is a noble disciple docile? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is compliant toward his fellow monks; he does not oppose them in matters of Dhamma or Vinaya. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a noble disciple is docile. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities of a person who is like a well-bred horse that a noble disciple possesses because of which he is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

“Bhikkhus, possessing six factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What six? [The text continues with the list of six qualities.]”
"Here, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, patient with tangibles, and it is endowed with beauty.
Possessing these six factors, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu possessing six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. [He is: patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, patient with tangibles, and he is endowed with beauty."
“By what six?
Here, monks, a monk is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, patient with tangibles, and patient with mental phenomena.
Possessing these six qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of offerings … an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.6 1.
Āhuneyyavagga (The Chapter on Those Worthy of Offerings)
The Second Discourse on the Noble Steed (Dutiya-ājānīya-sutta).
“Bhikkhus, possessed of six factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What six? [Text follows]”
By what six?
Here, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, patient with tactile objects, and it is endowed with strength.
Possessing these six factors, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, a royal possession, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the six?
Here, monks, a monk is patient with forms... [and so on] ...he is patient with mental phenomena.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 6.7

1. Āhuneyyavagga Tatiyaājānīyasutta (AN 6.7, PTS AN iii 283) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of thoroughbred persons (*ājānīya*). What four? The person who is like a thoroughbred in appearance; the person who is like a thoroughbred in conduct; the person who is like a thoroughbred in both appearance and conduct; and the person who is like a thoroughbred in the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a thoroughbred in appearance? Here, bhikkhus, a person is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent, seven generations back, unbroken, of well-attested lineage, and endowed with physical beauty. This is called a person like a thoroughbred in appearance. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a thoroughbred in conduct? Here, bhikkhus, a person is well-conducted, possessed of conduct that is guarded, protected, and restrained by the restraint of the Patimokkha. This is called a person like a thoroughbred in conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a thoroughbred in both appearance and conduct? Here, bhikkhus, a person is well-born on both sides... [as above] ...and is also well-conducted, possessed of conduct that is guarded, protected, and restrained by the restraint of the Patimokkha. This is called a person like a thoroughbred in both appearance and conduct. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a thoroughbred in the destruction of the taints? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This is called a person like a thoroughbred in the destruction of the taints. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of thoroughbred persons.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of six factors, a king’s excellent thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.
What are the six?
Here, bhikkhus, a king’s excellent thoroughbred horse is patient with forms, patient with sounds, patient with odors, patient with tastes, patient with tactile objects, and it is endowed with speed.
“Monks, when a noble thoroughbred horse possessed of these six factors is worthy of a king, a royal asset, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king;

even so, monks, a monk possessed of six qualities is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of veneration, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the six? [The text continues with the six qualities].”
"Here, monks, a monk is patient with forms... [as before] ...he is patient with mental phenomena.
Endowed with these six qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts... [as before] ...an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
This was the seventh [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.8 1.
Āhuneyyavagga Anuttariyasutta (The Discourse on the Unsurpassed)
“Bhikkhus, there are these six unsurpassable things. Which six? [The text continues:]”
“Supreme seeing, supreme hearing, supreme gain, supreme training, supreme service, and supreme recollection.
These, monks, are the six supremacies. This is the eighth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.9 1. Āhuneyyavagga Anussatiṭṭhānasutta (The Discourse on the Bases of Recollection) “Bhikkhus, there are these six bases of recollection. What six? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. When a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Tathāgata. When his mind is straight, he attains the four jhānas—states of bliss here and now.

This, bhikkhus, is the first basis of recollection. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. When a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Dhamma. When his mind is straight, he attains the four jhānas—states of bliss here and now. This, bhikkhus, is the second basis of recollection. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. When a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the Saṅgha. When his mind is straight, he attains the four jhānas—states of bliss here and now. This, bhikkhus, is the third basis of recollection. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects his own virtuous behavior as unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unblotched, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple recollects his virtuous behavior, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on virtuous behavior. When his mind is straight, he attains the four jhānas—states of bliss here and now. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth basis of recollection. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects his own generosity thus: ‘It is truly my good fortune and gain that in a generation obsessed by the stain of miserliness, I dwell at home with a mind devoid of the stain of miserliness, freely generous, open-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, delighting in giving and sharing. When a noble disciple recollects his generosity, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on generosity. When his mind is straight, he attains the four jhānas—states of bliss here and now. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth basis of recollection. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects the deities thus: ‘There are devas [ruled by] Four Great Kings, Tāvatiṃsa devas, Yāma devas, Tusita devas, Nimmānarati devas, Paranimmitavasavatti devas, devas who are the retinue of Brahmā, and devas who are the retinue of Mahābrahmā. At the time of my death, may I be reborn in their company! When a noble disciple recollects the deities, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, hatred, or delusion; on that occasion his mind is simply straight, based on the deities. When his mind is straight, he attains the four jhānas—states of bliss here and now. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth basis of recollection. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases of recollection.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these six subjects of recollection. Which six? [The Buddha said: (AN 6.9, PTS AN iii 284) “Bhikkhus, there are these six subjects of recollection.
Which six?”
“Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the deities.
These, monks, are the six bases for recollection. Thus [ends] the ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.10 1. Āhuneyyavagga Mahānāmasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the householder Mahānāma approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many qualities does a noble disciple possess to be worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world?

“A noble disciple, Mahānāma, possesses four qualities to be worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What four? Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He is possessed of unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. Possessing these four qualities, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. When this was said, the householder Mahānāma said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach the Dhamma in brief, so that I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if anyone should develop the four bases for spiritual power—each accompanied by zeal, accompanied by diligence, accompanied by mind, accompanied by investigation—then by developing them for seven years, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return. Since I recall, Ānanda, having developed the four bases for spiritual power—each accompanied by zeal, accompanied by diligence, accompanied by mind, accompanied by investigation—for seven days, by developing them, I have attained final knowledge here and now. If, Ānanda, you should develop the four bases for spiritual power—each accompanied by zeal, accompanied by diligence, accompanied by mind, accompanied by investigation—for seven days, then by developing them, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge here and now, or if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Ānanda became one of the arahants.
(AN 6.10, PTS AN iii 284) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.

Then Mahānāma the Sakyan approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, with what dwelling does that noble disciple who has arrived at the fruit and understood the teaching mostly dwell?
“Mahānāma, that noble disciple who has arrived at the fruit and understood the teaching mostly dwells with this dwelling.
Here, Mahānāma, the noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus:”

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
rather, at that time his mind is directed straight toward the Tathāgata.
Moreover, Mahānāma, a noble disciple with a straightforward mind gains knowledge of the meaning, gains knowledge of the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
This, Mahānāma, is called:

“The noble disciple dwells having attained equanimity amidst a generation that has fallen into partiality; he dwells without malice amidst a generation full of malice; having entered the stream of the Dhamma, he develops recollection of the Buddha.
Furthermore, Mahānāma, the noble disciple recollects the Dhamma:
“The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One—it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be realized individually by the wise.”
At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
rather, at that time his mind is directed straightly toward the Dhamma.
And when the mind of a noble disciple is directed straightly, Mahānāma, he gains inspiration from the meaning, he gains inspiration from the Dhamma, and he gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, Mahānāma, is called:

"The noble disciple dwells having attained equanimity amidst a generation that has fallen into unevenness; he dwells free from affliction amidst a generation that is afflicted; having entered the stream of the Dhamma, he develops mindfulness of the Dhamma."
Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus:
"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically;
the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing appropriately—that is to say, the four [pairs of persons]."
‘The eight pairs of persons, the individuals— this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality,
worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Mahānāma,
at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight toward the Saṅgha.
And when a noble disciple’s mind is directed straight, Mahānāma, he gains inspiration from the meaning, he gains inspiration from the Dhamma, and he gains joy connected with the Dhamma.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil feels happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.
This, Mahānāma, is called:

‘The noble disciple dwells having attained equanimity amidst a generation that has fallen into unevenness; he dwells free from affliction amidst a generation that is afflicted; having entered the stream of the Dhamma, he develops recollection of the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, Mahānāma, the noble disciple recollects his own virtues—virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects his virtue, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
rather, at that time his mind is directed straightly with reference to virtue.
And when a noble disciple’s mind is directed straightly, Mahānāma, he gains inspiration in the meaning, he gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and he gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is glad, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, Mahānāma, is called:

"The noble disciple dwells having attained composure amidst a generation that has gone astray; he dwells free from affliction amidst an afflicted generation; having entered the stream of the Dhamma, he develops the recollection of virtue."
Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects his own generosity:
“It is a gain for me, it is a great fortune for me,

that among people overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess, I dwell at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, accessible to requests, and rejoicing in the distribution of gifts.”
At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects his generosity, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
rather, on that occasion his mind is directed straight toward generosity.
And when his mind is directed straight, Mahānāma, the noble disciple gains inspiration from the meaning, gains inspiration from the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, Mahānāma, is called:

"A noble disciple dwells having attained evenness amidst a generation that has gone astray; he dwells without affliction amidst a generation that is afflicted; having entered the stream of the Dhamma, he develops the recollection of generosity."
Furthermore, Mahānāma, a noble disciple develops recollection of the deities thus:
‘There are the gods of the Four Great Kings; there are the gods of the Thirty-three; there are the Yāma gods; there are the Tusita gods;
there are the gods who delight in creation; there are the gods who wield power over the creations of others; there are the gods of Brahmā’s retinue.’
There are deities even higher than those.
Whatever kind of faith those deities were endowed with who, having passed away from here, were reborn there—that same kind of faith exists in me as well.
Whatever kind of virtue those deities were endowed with who, having passed away from here, were reborn there—that same kind of virtue exists in me as well.
‘Possessed of such learning as those deities possessed, who passed away from here and were reborn there, such learning exists in me too;
possessed of such generosity as those deities possessed, who passed away from here and were reborn there, such generosity exists in me too;
possessed of such wisdom as those deities possessed, who passed away from here and were reborn there, such wisdom exists in me too.’”
At whatever time, Mahānāma, a noble disciple recollects his own faith,
virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, as well as those of those deities, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust,
nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight toward those deities.
When, Mahānāma, the mind of a noble disciple is directed straight, he gains inspiration from the meaning, he gains inspiration from the Dhamma, and he gains joy connected with the Dhamma.

In one who is joyful, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness; and the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
“Mahānāma, this is called:

‘The noble disciple dwells having attained equanimity amidst a generation that has fallen into unevenness; he dwells free from malice amidst a generation full of malice; having entered the stream of the Dhamma, he develops the recollection of the deities.
Mahānāma, that noble disciple who has reached the fruit and understood the teaching dwells frequently in this dwelling.”
The tenth.
The first chapter, on those Worthy of Offerings.
Its summary verse:
The two worthy of offerings, the faculties,
the three powers, the noble breeds,
the unsurpassed, and the recollections.
"Ten things by Mahānāma.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.11, Sāraṇīyavagga.
The First Discourse on the Recollections (Paṭhamasāraṇīyasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these six qualities that are conducive to recollection.
What are the six?
Here, monks, a monk maintains bodily conduct imbued with loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates, both openly and in private; this too is a principle that should be remembered.
Furthermore, monks, a monk maintains verbal conduct imbued with loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates, both openly and in private; this too is a principle that should be remembered.
Furthermore, monks, a monk maintains a mental action of loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners both openly and in private; this too is a principle that should be remembered.

Furthermore, monks, whatever righteous gains a monk has obtained in accordance with the Dhamma—even if it is merely the contents of his alms bowl—he shares such gains unreservedly with virtuous fellow practitioners, enjoying them in common with them.
This too is a quality that calls for recollection.
Furthermore, monks, a monk possesses those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration; such [virtues]...
He dwells in conformity with virtuous behavior with his fellow celibate practitioners, both openly and in private; this too is a principle that leads to recollection.

Furthermore, monks, whatever view is noble, leading out, and leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering—a monk dwells in conformity with such a view with his fellow celibate practitioners.
“Both in public and in private—this too is a principle that calls for recollection.
These, monks, are the six principles that call for recollection. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.12 2. Sāraṇīyavagga Dutiyasāraṇīyasutta (The Second Discourse on Endearing Qualities) “Monks, there are these five endearing qualities that lead to being loved and respected, to being esteemed and venerated, to being a source of delight and non-displeasure, and to the arising of a mind of loving-kindness.

What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first endearing quality… Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view. This is the second endearing quality… Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the third endearing quality… Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu possesses the wisdom that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is the fourth endearing quality… Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu inclines his mind toward the realization of the fruit of arahantship, if it has not yet been realized. This is the fifth endearing quality… These, monks, are the five endearing qualities that lead to being loved and respected, to being esteemed and venerated, to being a source of delight and non-displeasure, and to the arising of a mind of loving-kindness.”

“Bhikkhus, there are these six qualities that are memorable, which create affection, create respect, lead to being gathered together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity. What are the six? [The text continues with the list of six qualities.]”
“Here, monks, a monk maintains bodily action imbued with loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates, both openly and in private.
This, too, is a principle that is memorable, endearing, and respectful; it leads to cohesion, to lack of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk maintains verbal action imbued with loving-kindness toward his fellow celibates…. [and so on].

Aloving mental action is established toward one’s fellow practitioners both openly and in private; this quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring, leading to inclusion, non-contention, harmony, and unity.

Furthermore, monks, whatever righteous gains are righteously obtained—even if only the mere contents of an alms-bowl—a monk shares such gains with virtuous fellow practitioners, enjoying them in common.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to non-contention, to harmony, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk possesses those virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration—such virtues as these...
He dwells in conformity with virtuous behavior with his fellow celibates, both openly and in private;
this too is a principle that is consoling, endearing, and inspiring, leading to inclusion, non-dispute, harmony, and unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk possesses that noble view which leads out, which leads the one who practices it toward liberation.
He dwells with his fellow practitioners of the holy life, both openly and in private, having attained conformity of view through such a right view for the complete destruction of suffering.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and respectful; it leads to inclusion, to non-contention, to harmony, and to unity.
"Monks, these six qualities are memorable, endearing, and respectful; they lead to inclusion, to non-contention, to harmony, and to unity."
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.13 2.
Sāraṇīyavagga (The Chapter on Recollections)
The Discourse on the Elements Leading to Escape (Nissāraṇīyasutta). “Monks,
there are these six elements leading to escape.”
What six?
Here, monks, a monk might say:
"The liberation of mind through loving-kindness has indeed been developed by me, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken."
‘And yet ill will still persists, obsessing my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, friend! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.

It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen that when the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, ill will should still persist, obsessing the mind.’”
"Yet it is impossible that ill will would persist, taking possession of his mind;
for this, friends, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness.
Then, monks, a monk might say this:
‘Indeed, my liberation of mind through compassion has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken;
yet nevertheless, violence still persists, seizing hold of my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, Venerable One! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One would not speak thus.’

"It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen, that when the liberation of mind through compassion has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, harm could still take possession of one's mind—such a thing is not possible.
For this, friend, is the escape from harm: namely, the liberation of mind through compassion."
"Furthermore, monks, a monk might say this:
‘Indeed, I have developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a foundation of, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy;
yet still, discontent persists, seizing hold of my mind.’"
Thus you should say to him: “Do not say so, friend. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.

Friend, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that when the liberation of the mind through sympathetic joy has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, discontent could still take possession of the mind—such a thing cannot happen.”
"For this, friends, is the escape from aversion: namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy.
But here, monks, a monk might say:

"The liberation of mind through equanimity has indeed been developed by me, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken; it has been practiced extensively."
‘And yet, passion still persists, having taken possession of my mind.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not speak thus, venerable sir; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, nor would the Blessed One ever say such a thing.

It is impossible, friend, it is out of the question that when the liberation of the mind through equanimity has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, passion should still persist, having taken possession of the mind.’”
"And yet, it is impossible that passion should persist by taking possession of his mind;
for this, friends, is the escape from passion, namely, the liberation of the mind through equanimity.
Then, monks, a monk might say this:
‘Indeed, my mind-liberation has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken as signless;
yet nevertheless, my consciousness still follows after signs.
To him it should be said: ‘Do not say so, Venerable Sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus.’

"It is impossible, friend, it is out of the question, that for one who has developed, cultivated, made a vehicle of, made a basis of, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken the signless liberation of mind,
their consciousness should still follow after signs— such a case is not possible. For this, friend,
is the escape from all signs, namely, the signless liberation of mind."
But here, monks, a bhikkhu might say:
"The thought 'I am' has indeed vanished from me, and I do not perceive 'this I am';
yet still, the arrow of doubt and perplexity remains obsessing my mind."
He should be told: "Do not say so, friend. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not speak thus.

It is impossible, friend, it cannot happen, that in one who has eliminated the thought 'I am' and does not regard 'this I am,' the arrow of doubt and perplexity should still persist, taking possession of the mind—such a thing is not possible."
“Indeed, friends, this is the escape from the arrow of doubt and perplexity, namely, the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am’.
“These, monks, are the six elements leading to deliverance. Thus was the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.14 2. Sāraṇīyavagga Bhaddakasutta “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons who are excellent. What five? The person who is excellent by birth; the person who is excellent by wealth; the person who is excellent by learning; the person who is excellent by virtue; and the person who is excellent by realization. And how, monks, is one a person excellent by birth?

Here, monks, someone is born into a high family—whether a khattiya clan, a brahmin clan, or a householder clan—one that is rich, with great wealth and property, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and granaries, abundant wealth and grain. This, monks, is called a person excellent by birth. And how, monks, is one a person excellent by wealth? Here, monks, someone has great wealth, many possessions, abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and granaries, abundant wealth and grain. This, monks, is called a person excellent by wealth. And how, monks, is one a person excellent by learning? Here, monks, someone has learned much, remembered much, retained what he has learned; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the holy life in its purity and fullness—such teachings as these he has learned much of, remembered, mastered verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. This, monks, is called a person excellent by learning. And how, monks, is one a person excellent by virtue? Here, monks, someone is endowed with virtuous behavior, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha; being consummate in proper conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts. This, monks, is called a person excellent by virtue. And how, monks, is one a person excellent by realization? Here, monks, someone has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This, monks, is called a person excellent by realization. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons who are excellent.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus."
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, in whatever way a bhikkhu makes his dwelling, in that way, as he makes his dwelling, there is no auspicious death for him, no auspicious passing away.”
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu conduct himself in such a way that, as he so conducts himself, his death is not auspicious, nor is his passing away auspicious?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu delights in work, takes delight in work, is devoted to delighting in work;
he delights in talk, takes delight in talk, is devoted to delighting in talk; he delights in sleep, takes delight in sleep, is devoted to delighting in sleep.
He delights in company, takes pleasure in company, and is devoted to delighting in company; he delights in socializing, takes pleasure in socializing, and is devoted to delighting in socializing;
he delights in conceptual proliferation, takes pleasure in conceptual proliferation, and is devoted to delighting in conceptual proliferation.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu conducts himself such that, while so conducting himself, his death is not auspicious and his passing away is not auspicious.
"Friends, this is called a bhikkhu who delights in personal existence and does not abandon personal existence for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.
In whatever way, friends, a bhikkhu conducts his life such that while conducting his life in that way, he meets a noble death and passes away nobly."
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu conduct himself in such a way that, as he so conducts himself, his death is auspicious and his passing away is auspicious?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu does not delight in work, does not take pleasure in work, and is not devoted to delighting in work;

he does not delight in talk, does not take pleasure in talk, and is not devoted to delighting in talk; he does not delight in sleep, does not take pleasure in sleep, and is not devoted to delighting in sleep.
Devoted [to seclusion], he does not delight in company, does not take pleasure in company, and is not devoted to the delight in company;
he does not delight in socializing, does not take pleasure in socializing, and is not devoted to the delight in socializing;
he does not delight in conceptual proliferation, does not take pleasure in conceptual proliferation, and is not devoted to the delight in conceptual proliferation.
In this way, friends, a bhikkhu conducts himself in such a manner that, as he so conducts himself, his death is auspicious and his passing away is auspicious.
This, friends, is called:
“A bhikkhu who delights in Nibbāna abandons identity for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.”
The fool who is devoted to conceptual proliferation and delights in conceptual proliferation has missed out on Nibbāna.
The unsurpassed security from bondage. And he who,
having abandoned conceptual proliferation,
delights in the state free from proliferation;
He attained Nibbāna,
the unsurpassed security from bondage. Thus ends the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.15 2. Sāraṇīyavagga Anutappiya-sutta (The One to Be Regretted) “Monks, there is one person who, when deceased, passes away, is to be regretted by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. Who is that one? It is the person who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This is the one person who, when deceased, passes away, is to be regretted by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. Monks, there is one person who, when deceased, passes away, is not to be regretted by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. Who is that one? It is the person who abstains from destroying life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This is the one person who, when deceased, passes away, is not to be regretted by the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, by this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: "In such and such a way, friends,
a bhikkhu conducts his life so that as he conducts it, his passing away is without regret."
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu conduct himself in such a way that his passing away while so conducting himself is regrettable?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu delights in work, takes delight in work, is devoted to delighting in work; he delights in talk...
he delights in sleep... [and so on].
He delights in company...
he delights in socializing...
he delights in conceptual proliferation, takes pleasure in conceptual proliferation, and is devoted to delighting in conceptual proliferation.
In this way, friend, a bhikkhu conducts himself in such a manner that, as he so conducts himself, his passing away is not to be regretted.
This, friend, is called a bhikkhu who delights in personal existence and does not abandon personal existence for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.
In such and such a way, friends, does a bhikkhu conduct his life so that as he conducts it, his passing away is without regret.
And how, friends, does a bhikkhu conduct his life so that as he conducts it, his passing away is without regret?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu does not delight in work, does not take pleasure in work, and is not devoted to delighting in work; he does not delight in talk... [and so on].
He does not delight in sleep… he does not delight in socializing… he does not delight in company…
He does not delight in conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), he does not rejoice in conceptual proliferation, nor is he devoted to delighting in conceptual proliferation.
It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu conducts his life so that, as he conducts his life, his passing away is without regret.
This, friends, is called:
“The bhikkhu who delights in Nibbāna abandons identity for the sake of making a complete end of suffering.
He who is devoted to conceptual proliferation,
who delights in proliferation, is a beast.
He fails to attain Nibbāna,
the unsurpassed security from bondage— he who,
having abandoned conceptual proliferation (papañca),...
Delighting in the state beyond conceptual proliferation,
he attained Nibbāna,
the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.16 2.
Sāraṇīyavagga (The Chapter on Endearing Qualities)
The Discourse to Nakula’s Father (Nakulapitusutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park.
Now at that time, the householder Nakulapita was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then the housewife Nakulamātā said this to the householder Nakulapita:
“Do not, householder, pass away while full of longing.”
Householder, death while full of longing is suffering;
death while full of longing is censured by the Blessed One.
It may be, householder, that you think thus:
‘After my passing, Nakulamātā the housewife will not be able to support the children or maintain the household.
But, householder, you should not view it in that way.
Householder, I am skilled at spinning cotton and braiding hair.
"I am able, householder, to support your children and maintain the household life after your passing.
Therefore, householder, do not die with longing.
For a death with longing, householder, is painful."
And the Blessed One has censured dying with worldly attachments.
Now, householder, it may occur to you:
"After my passing, Nakulamātā the housewife will go to another family."
"But it should not be viewed in this way, householder.
You yourself, householder, know and I also know that for sixteen years we have practiced the celibate life as householders.
Therefore, householder, do not die with longing."
Householder, death while still possessed of longing is painful;
death while possessed of longing is censured by the Blessed One.
It may be, householder, that you think thus:
‘After my passing, Nakulamātā, the housewife, will not wish to see the Blessed One, nor will she wish to see the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
But, householder, you should not view it in that way.
For after your passing, householder, I shall wish to see the Blessed One even more than that, and I shall wish to see the Saṅgha of bhikkhus even more than that.”
Therefore, householder, do not pass away with longing.
For a householder, to pass away with longing is painful;
passing away with longing is censured by the Blessed One.
It may be, householder, that you think:
"After my passing, Nakulamātā the housewife will not be one who fulfills her duties regarding virtuous conduct.
But, householder, this should not be viewed in such a way.
"To the extent that there are female lay disciples of that Blessed One who are clothed in white and are perfect in their virtuous conduct, I am one among them.

But if you have any doubt or uncertainty, go to that Blessed One—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—who is staying among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park, and ask him.
Therefore, householder, do not pass away with lingering attachment."
Householder, death while full of longing is painful;
death while full of longing is censured by the Blessed One.
It may be, householder, that you think thus:
‘The housewife Nakulamātā does not possess internal tranquility of mind.
But, householder, you should not view it in that way.
To whatever extent there are female lay disciples of that Blessed One dressed in white who possess internal tranquility of mind, I am one among them.

But for anyone who has doubt or uncertainty, let them approach that Blessed One—the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—who is staying among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park, and ask him.
Therefore, householder, do not pass away with longing.
For householder, passing away with longing is painful.
And the Blessed One has censured death while still having worldly concerns.
Now, householder, it may occur to you:

"The housewife Nakulamātā has not reached a foothold, has not reached a firm foundation, has not reached consolation, has not crossed over doubt, is not free from perplexity, has not attained self-confidence, and does not dwell in the Teacher’s instruction independent of others within this Dhamma and Vinaya. [But that is not so.]
But it should not be viewed in this way, householder.
For as many white-robed female lay disciples of that Blessed One as have entered this Dhamma and Vinaya,
having reached a firm footing, having reached a secure foothold, having attained consolation, having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, and having attained self-confidence—
They dwell in the Teacher’s dispensation independent of others; I am one among them.

But whoever has any doubt or uncertainty, let him approach that Blessed One—the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One—who is staying among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park, and ask him.
Therefore, householder, do not pass away with longing.
“Householder, death while full of longing is painful;
death while full of longing has been censured by the Blessed One.
Then, as the householder Nakulapita was being exhorted with this advice by the housewife Nakulamātā, that affliction of his subsided on the spot.
And the householder Nakulapita recovered from that illness;
indeed, that illness was completely abandoned by the householder Nakulapita.
Then, not long after recovering from his sickness, the householder Nakulapita, leaning on a staff, rose from his bed.
He approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As Nakulapitā the householder was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“It is a gain for you, householder! It is well gained by you, householder!”
Nakulamātā, the housewife, is compassionate toward you, desiring your welfare, and is your instructor and adviser.
Householder, among all my female lay disciples who are clothed in white and who fulfill their moral precepts, Nakulamātā the housewife is one of them.
Householder, among all my female lay disciples who are clothed in white and who have attained internal tranquility of mind, Nakulamātā the housewife is one of them.
"To whatever extent, householder, there are female lay disciples of mine, dressed in white, who have gained a foothold, gained a firm footing,
and attained consolation in this Dhamma and Discipline— having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having attained self-confidence,
and dwelling in the Teacher’s instruction without depending on others— Nakulamātā the housewife is one among them."
“It is a gain for you, householder!
It is well gained by you, householder, that Nakulamātā the housewife—who is compassionate, desirous of your welfare, and a teacher and instructor—is yours.
The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.17 2. Sāraṇīyavagga Soppasutta – On Sleeping “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in sleeping during the day. What five? One sleeps at an improper time; one’s sleep is heavy; one’s digestion is disturbed; one becomes indolent; and one’s mind does not become concentrated when one wishes. These, bhikkhus, are the five dangers in sleeping during the day. There are, bhikkhus, these five benefits in staying awake at night. What five? One sleeps at a proper time; one’s sleep is light; one’s digestion is well-balanced; one does not become indolent; and one’s mind becomes concentrated when one wishes. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits in staying awake at night.”
(AN 6.17, PTS AN iii 297) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also… The Venerable Mahākassapa also… [did likewise].
The Venerable Mahākaccāna also...
the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika also...
the Venerable Mahācunda also...
The Venerable Mahākappina also...
the Venerable Anuruddha also...
the Venerable Revata also...
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, approached the assembly hall; having arrived, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Then the Blessed One, having spent much of the night sitting, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Not long after the Blessed One had departed, those two venerable ones also rose from their seats and went to their respective dwellings.
But those monks there who were new, recently ordained, and had only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya, slept on while snoring until sunrise.
With his purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One saw those monks sleeping while snoring until sunrise.
Having seen them, he went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Where, bhikkhus, is Sāriputta?
Where is Mahāmoggallāna?”
Where is Mahākassapa?
Where is Mahākaccāna?
Where is Mahākoṭṭhika?
Where is Mahācunda?
Where is Mahākappina?
Where is Anuruddha?
“Where is Revata?
Where is Ānanda?
Where, monks, have those elder disciples gone?”
“But, Bhante, as soon as the Blessed One had departed, those venerable ones rose from their seats and went to their respective dwellings.
“Because of that, monks, you elder bhikkhus did not come; you slept until sunrise, snoring.
What do you think, monks?”
“Have you ever seen or heard that a consecrated kṣatriya king,

while living for his entire life exercising sovereignty and remaining devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsing, is dear and pleasing to the people of the countryside?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Excellent, bhikkhus!
Even I, bhikkhus, have neither seen nor heard this:

that an anointed khattiya king, while living his life ruling the kingdom, remains devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of sloth, yet is still dear and agreeable to the people of the countryside.”
"What do you think, bhikkhus, have you ever seen or heard this: ‘A provincial governor...
[and so on as in the full passage]?"
a paternal kinsman … a commander of the army … a village headman …

“Would a guild-leader, while dwelling devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness as much as he desires, and while exercising his authority as guild-leader for as long as he lives, be dear and pleasing to the guild?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Good, monks.”
“Monks, I too have neither seen nor heard this:

that a guild-president, while living devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of sloth as much as he desires, and while exercising the office of guild-president for as long as life lasts, remains dear and pleasing to the guild.
What do you think, monks?”
Have you ever seen or heard of a recluse or a brahmin who, devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of drowsing as much as he desires;
who does not guard the doors of his sense faculties; who is immoderate in eating; who is not devoted to wakefulness; and who lacks insight into wholesome states?
“Is it possible for one who is not devoted to the practice of developing the qualities conducive to enlightenment during the first and last watches of the night to personally realize,
through direct knowledge, and dwell having attained in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which are free from taints through the destruction of the taints?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.
I too have neither seen nor heard this, bhikkhus:”
‘Whether a recluse or a brahmin, one who is devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of drowsiness to their heart’s content;
who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties; who is immoderate in eating; who is not devoted to wakefulness; who lacks insight;
and who, during the first and last watches of the night, is not devoted to the cultivation of wholesome states and the qualities conducive to enlightenment—’
‘Having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints,
I shall dwell having attained it.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall guard the doors of the sense faculties, be moderate in eating, be devoted to wakefulness,
be possessors of insight into wholesome states, and during the first and last watches of the night, we shall dwell devoted to the practice of developing the qualities conducive to enlightenment.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.”
The Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.18 2.
Sāraṇīyavagga (The Chapter on Recollections)
The Discourse on the Fisherman (Macchabandhasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
While traveling along the highway, the Blessed One saw, in a certain place, a fisherman selling fish after having repeatedly slaughtered them.
Having seen him, he stepped down from the road and sat down on a seat prepared at the foot of a tree.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, do you see that fisherman there selling fish after having killed them one by one?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
“Have you ever seen or heard of a fisherman who,
having repeatedly killed fish and sold them, by that deed and that livelihood, became one who travels by elephant,
or travels by horse, or travels by chariot, or travels by vehicle, or enjoys wealth, or dwells in a great mass of riches?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.
I too have neither seen nor heard this, bhikkhus:”
‘A fisherman, a fisher, killing fish again and again, sells them;
by that deed and by that livelihood, he travels by elephant, or travels by horse, or travels by chariot, or travels by vehicle, or enjoys wealth, or dwells in great abundance of riches.
For what reason?
For he, monks, looks with an evil mind upon those fish brought forward for execution; therefore, he does not travel by elephant,
nor by horse, nor by chariot, nor by vehicle, nor does he enjoy wealth, nor does he dwell in a great mass of possessions.
"What do you think, monks?
Have you ever seen or heard that a cow-slaughterer,
having repeatedly slaughtered cows and selling them, traveled by elephant because of that deed and that livelihood?"
“Or one who travels by horse, or travels by chariot, or travels by carriage, or enjoys sensual pleasures, or dwells with a great mass of wealth?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Good, bhikkhus.”
“Monks, I too have neither seen nor heard this:

that a cow-slaughterer, having repeatedly slaughtered cows and selling them, by means of that action and that livelihood, would travel by elephant, travel by horse, travel by chariot, or travel by vehicle; or enjoy wealth, or dwell over a vast mass of riches. And why is that?”
For he, monks, looks on with an evil mind at those oxen that have been brought forward for slaughter;
therefore, he is neither a rider of elephants, nor a rider of horses, nor a rider of chariots, nor a rider of vehicles, nor an enjoyer of wealth,
nor does he dwell in possession of a great mass of riches.
"What do you think, monks?
Have you ever seen or heard of this: that a butcher of sheep... [and so forth]?"
“...a pig-breeder ...
a fowler ...

a hunter who, having repeatedly slaughtered deer, sells them—if by that deed and that livelihood he travels by elephant, or travels by horse, or travels by chariot, or travels by carriage, or enjoys wealth, or dwells in great abundance of riches?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Good, bhikkhus.
By me too, bhikkhus, this has neither been seen nor heard:”

‘A hunter, having repeatedly slaughtered game, sells it; by that deed and by that livelihood, he travels by elephant, or travels by horse, or travels by chariot, or travels by vehicle, or enjoys wealth, or dwells possessing a great mass of riches.
For what reason?
Because, monks, when those animals are brought to the slaughter as victims, he looks on with an evil mind; therefore he—
He does not travel by elephant, nor by horse, nor by chariot, nor by vehicle; he does not enjoy sensual pleasures, nor does he dwell amidst a great mass of wealth.
For even when a living being belonging to the animal realm has been brought to the slaughter for execution, that person looks on with an evil mind.
He will not be one who travels by elephant, nor by horse, nor by chariot, nor by carriage;
he will not be an enjoyer of pleasures, nor will he dwell in a great mass of wealth.
What need is there to mention him who, having become a human being, looks with an evil mind upon one condemned to death who has been brought to the place of execution?
"For that, monks, leads to his harm and suffering for a long time.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Thus ends the eighth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.19 2. Sāraṇīyavagga First Discourse on Mindfulness of Death “Monks, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the stream, who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, who is firmly established and destined for full enlightenment.

What are these four? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, monks, he is one who has reached the stream, who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, who is firmly established and destined for full enlightenment.”
(AN 6.19, PTS AN iii 303) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick Hall.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.
Develop mindfulness of death, bhikkhus.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I indeed cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But in what way, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“In this case, venerable sir, it occurs to me thus:”
“‘Oh, may I live for a day and night, that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching;
indeed, much would have been accomplished by me!’—it is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”
"‘Oh, may I live for a day so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would be accomplished by me!
It is in this way, venerable sir, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”
"‘Oh, may I live for just that long—the interval it takes to eat a single alms-meal—so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me!
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”
"‘Oh, may I live for just as long as it takes to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me!
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, it occurs to me thus:”
‘Oh, may I live for just as long as it takes to chew and swallow a single mouthful of food, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me!
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
Then another bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I too cultivate mindfulness of death.
“But how, monk, do you cultivate mindfulness of death?
“Here, venerable sir, this occurs to me:”

“‘Oh, may I live for just that interval—whether it be the time between an inhalation and an exhalation, or an exhalation and an inhalation—to attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; indeed, much would have been accomplished by me!
It is in this way, Bhante, that I develop mindfulness of death.
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed those bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, there is the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘O, may I live for a day and night so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me.

And there is the bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus: [‘May I live for a day,’ or ‘for a half-day,’ or ‘for as long as it takes to eat a meal,’ or ‘for as long as it takes to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls,’ or ‘for as long as it takes to chew and swallow one mouthful,’ or ‘may I live just as long as it takes to breathe out after breathing in, or to breathe in after breathing out,’ so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me].”
‘Oh, may I live for a day so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me.
And as for the monk, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘Oh, may I live for the interval of time it takes to eat a single alms-meal so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me.’”
“And yet, bhikkhus, there is the bhikkhu who develops mindfulness of death thus:
‘O, may I live for as long as it takes to chew and swallow four or five mouthfuls, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would be accomplished by me.
These, bhikkhus, are called bhikkhus who dwell negligently and develop mindfulness of death sluggishly for the destruction of the taints.”
And as for the monk, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus:
"O, may I live just long enough to chew and swallow a single mouthful of food, so that I might attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; much indeed would have been accomplished by me.
And as for the monk, bhikkhus, who develops mindfulness of death thus: [in this way, he develops it].

"O, may I live for just that interval—between breathing in after breathing out, or breathing out after breathing in—to attend to the Blessed One’s teaching; then indeed much would have been accomplished by me.
These, monks, are called the monks who dwell heedfully, developing keen mindfulness of death for the destruction of the taints.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall dwell heedfully; we shall develop the mindfulness of death keenly for the destruction of the taints.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves. Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.20 2. Sāraṇīyavagga The Second Discourse on Mindfulness of Death “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that are conducive to mindfulness of death. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not intent on his own welfare, nor on the welfare of others, nor on the welfare of both;

he does not train for the sake of attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, or realizing the unrealized by means of wholesome qualities that have been fully understood, well-penetrated, mastered, and well-undertaken.
