This is the first thing conducive to mindfulness of death. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not intent on his own welfare... [as before] ...by means of wholesome qualities that have been fully understood, well-penetrated, mastered, and well-undertaken. This is the second thing conducive to mindfulness of death. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not intent on his own welfare... [as before] ...by means of wholesome qualities that have been fully understood, well-penetrated, mastered, and well-undertaken. This is the third thing conducive to mindfulness of death. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not intent on his own welfare... [as before] ...by means of wholesome qualities that have been fully understood, well-penetrated, mastered, and well-undertaken. This is the fourth thing conducive to mindfulness of death. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not intent on his own welfare, nor on the welfare of others, nor on the welfare of both; he does not train for the sake of attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, or realizing the unrealized by means of wholesome qualities that have been fully understood, well-penetrated, mastered, and well-undertaken, and yet he dwells with a mind that is often accompanied by remorse. This is the fifth thing conducive to mindfulness of death. These, bhikkhus, are the five things that are conducive to mindfulness of death.”
(AN 6.20, PTS AN iii 306) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick Hall.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, mindfulness of death, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the Deathless and culminates in the Deathless.
And how, monks, is mindfulness of death developed and cultivated so that it is of great fruit and great benefit, plunging into the Deathless and culminating in the Deathless?
Here, monks, when the day has passed and the night has arrived, a monk reflects thus:”
‘There are indeed many conditions for my death—
a snake might bite me, or a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me;
by that I would meet my end, and that would be an obstacle for me.’
‘I might stumble and fall, or the food I have eaten might cause illness, or my bile might be disturbed, or my phlegm might be disturbed, or my piercing winds might be disturbed;
because of that, my death might come about, and that would be an obstacle for me.
Therefore, monks, that monk should reflect thus:
‘Are there indeed within me evil, unwholesome states that have not been abandoned, which might become an obstacle for me as I am passing away during the night?
Monks, if, upon reflection, a monk knows thus:
‘There are within me evil, unwholesome states that have not been abandoned, which might become an obstacle for me as I am passing away during the night,’ [he should strive to abandon them].”
"Therefore, monks, for the sake of abandoning those very same evil, unwholesome states, that monk must apply superior desire,
effort, exertion, perseverance, undaunted mindfulness, and clear comprehension—
just as one whose clothes are on fire, or whose head is on fire, would act toward that very clothing or that very head."
He should exercise superior desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension for their extinguishing;
even so, monks, should that bhikkhu [deal] with those very same evil, unwholesome states.
For the sake of abandoning [them], there must be intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension. But if, monks, while examining himself, a monk knows thus:
‘There are no evil, unwholesome states that have not been abandoned by me which might become an obstacle for me as I am passing away during the night,’ with this,
monks, that bhikkhu should dwell in joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states. Furthermore, monks,
when the night has passed and the day has dawned, a bhikkhu reflects thus:
‘There are indeed many conditions for my death:
a snake might bite me, a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me;
by that I would meet my end, and that would be an obstacle for me.’
‘I might stumble and fall into a precipice, or the food I have eaten might cause illness, or my bile might be disturbed, or my phlegm might be disturbed, or my wind-humors might be disturbed;
because of that, my death would come about, and that would be an obstacle for me.
Therefore, monks, that monk should reflect thus:
‘Are there indeed evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that might become an obstacle for me were I to die during the day?
Monks, if, upon reviewing, a monk knows thus:
‘There are evil, unwholesome states unabandoned in me that might become an obstacle for me were I to die during the day,’ [he should strive to abandon them].”
Therefore, monks, for the sake of abandoning those very same evil, unwholesome states, that bhikkhu must exert intense desire,
effort, perseverance, fortitude, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension. Just as, monks,
one whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would act toward that very garment or that very head—
He should exercise superior desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension for their extinguishing;
even so, monks, should that bhikkhu [proceed] toward those very same evil, unwholesome states.
For the sake of abandoning [them], there must be intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, undauntedness, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension. But if, monks, while examining himself, a monk knows thus:
‘There are no evil, unwholesome states that have not been abandoned by me which might become an obstacle for me were I to die this day,’ with these words,
monks, that bhikkhu should dwell in joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.
It is when mindfulness of death is thus developed and cultivated, monks, that it is of great fruit and great benefit, plunging into the Deathless, culminating in the Deathless.”
The tenth.
The second chapter, on the Recollections.
Its summary (uddāna):
Two [types of] remembrances, one to be cast out,
the auspicious, and that which is not to be regretted;
the mongoose, sleep, and the fish.
"There are two [types of] mindfulness of death.
— Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.21, Chapter 3: The Section on the Unsurpassed.
The Sāmakasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at the village of Sāmagāma by the lotus pond.
Then, when the night had advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire lotus pond, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there are three things that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu.
Which three?
Delight in work, delight in talk, and delight in sleep.”
“Venerable sir, these three things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said.
The Teacher approved.
Then that deity, thinking, "The Teacher has consented to me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, during this night, as the night was far spent, a certain deity of surpassing beauty approached the entire extent of [this assembly]..."
Having illuminated the lotus pond, he approached me; having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to me:
“Venerable sir, there are these three qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu.”
‘Which three?
Delight in work, delight in talk, and delight in sleep—
these, venerable sir, are the three qualities that lead to the decline of a bhikkhu.’”
"This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, she paid homage to me, circumambulated me with her right side toward me, and vanished right there.
It is their misfortune, monks, it is their ill-gotten lot, that even deities know you are declining in wholesome qualities."
“Monks, I will teach you three further qualities that lead to decline.
Listen to them and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, are the three qualities that lead to decline?
Delight in company, being difficult to correct, and having evil friends.”
“Monks, these indeed are the three factors of decline.
Whatever monks, monks, have declined in wholesome qualities in the past, all of them declined in wholesome qualities because of these very six factors.
And whatever monks, monks, will decline in wholesome qualities in the future, all of them will decline in wholesome qualities because of these very six factors.”
“Bhikkhus, whoever at present is declining from wholesome states, all of them decline from wholesome states because of these very six things.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.22

3. Anuttariya Chapter: The Discourse on Non-Decay (Aparihāniyasutta) (AN 6.22, PTS AN iii 310) “Monks, there are these seven factors of non-decline. What seven? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. “He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for use when ill. “He dwells possessing virtuous behavior that is restrained by the Pātimokkha, which is unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unblotched, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and leading to concentration. “He dwells possessing right view, which is straight, leading out, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering. “He is one who gains internal serenity of mind, and does not neglect the higher mind. “He gains the wisdom that arises from hearing, and does not neglect the higher wisdom. “These, monks, are the seven factors of non-decline.”
“Monks, I will teach you six qualities that prevent decline; listen to that….
And what, monks, are the six qualities that prevent decline?
Not delighting in work, not delighting in talk, not delighting in sleep, not delighting in company, being easy to speak to, and having virtuous friends.”
“Monks, these are the six qualities that prevent decline.
For whatever monks, in the past, did not decline in wholesome qualities, all of them did so because of these very six qualities.
And whatever monks, in the future, will not decline in wholesome qualities, all of them will do so because of these very six qualities.”
“Bhikkhus, whoever at present does not decline in wholesome qualities, all of them do not decline in wholesome qualities because of these very six things.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.23
3. Anuttariya Chapter:
The Discourse on Fear (Bhayasutta) (AN 6.23, PTS AN iii 310)
“‘Fear,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures;
‘suffering,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures;
‘disease,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.”
“‘A tumor,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures;
‘a snare,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures;
‘a mire,’ monks, is a designation for sensual pleasures.”
And why, monks, is “fear” a designation for sensual pleasures?

One who is stained by lust for sensual pleasures, bound by desire and lust, is not released from fears pertaining to this present life, nor is he released from fears pertaining to future lives; therefore, “fear” is a designation for sensual pleasures.
And why, monks, is “suffering” [a designation for sensual pleasures]? ... (as above) ...
It is a disease...
it is a boil...
it is a dart...
“Mud” is a designation for sensual pleasures.

For one who is stained by lust for sensual pleasures, monks, and bound by desire and lust, one is not liberated from the mud of this present life, nor is one liberated from the mud of future lives; therefore, “mud” is a designation for sensual pleasures.
Fear, suffering, disease, and a boil—[these are also designations for them].”
Attachment and the mire—
both these are called sensual pleasures,
wherein the ordinary person is stuck.
Seeing danger in clinging,
which gives rise to birth and death,
they are liberated through non-clinging.
In the destruction of birth and death,
they have attained security and are happy,
having realized Nibbāna in this very life.
“Having transcended all enmity and fear,
they have overcome all suffering. Thus ends the third [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.24 3. Anuttariyavagga Himavantasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five unsurpassed things. What five? The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, and the unsurpassed service. And what, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed sight? It is the sight of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This is called the unsurpassed sight. And what, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed hearing? It is the hearing of the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This is called the unsurpassed hearing. And what, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed gain? It is the gain of the noble birth. This is called the unsurpassed gain. And what, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed training? It is the training in the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom taught by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This is called the unsurpassed training. And what, bhikkhus, is the unsurpassed service? It is the service rendered to those who are worthy of offerings, such as the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, or their disciples. This is called the unsurpassed service. These, bhikkhus, are the five unsurpassed things.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu could split the Himalayas, the king of mountains; what need is there to speak of splitting this wretched ignorance? What are the six? [The sutta continues with the list.]”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is skilled in the attainment of concentration, skilled in the maintenance of concentration,
skilled in the emergence from concentration, skilled in the fitness of concentration, skilled in the range of concentration,
and skilled in the directing of concentration.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities could shatter the Himalayas, the king of mountains; what need is there to mention this wretched ignorance?
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.25
3. The Chapter on the Incomparable:
The Discourse on the Bases of Recollection (Anussatiṭṭhānasutta) (AN 6.25, PTS AN iii 312)
“Bhikkhus, there are these six bases for recollection.
What are the six?
Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus:”
‘Such indeed is the Blessed One … the Teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
On whatever occasion, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata,
on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, and not obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight ahead; it has gone forth, been released, and emerged from greed.
"Greed," monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
It is by making this an object of focus, monks, that some beings here become purified.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma thus:
“The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One … to be personally realized by the wise.
Monks, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight ahead; it has gone forth, been released, and emerged from greed.
"Greed," monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
It is by taking this as an object, monks, that some beings here are purified in this way.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha thus:
“The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well... [as above] ...it is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Monks, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight ahead; it has gone forth, been released, and emerged from greed.
“Greed,” monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
It is by taking this as an object, monks, that some beings here are purified.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects his own virtues—unbroken, ... [as before] ... leading to concentration.
Monks, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects virtue, on that occasion his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
on that occasion his mind is simply upright, having emerged, been released, and risen above greed.
“‘Vomit,’ monks, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
It is by taking this as an object, monks, that some beings here are purified.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects his own generosity:”
“It is indeed a gain for me! It is truly well-gained by me...
[he reflects] ...that he is devoted to making requests and delights in giving and sharing.
In this way, some beings here are purified.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple recollects the deities:
"There are the Cātumahārājika deities; there are the Tāvatiṃsa deities; there are the Yāma deities; there are the Tusita deities."
There are gods who delight in creation, there are gods who wield power over the creations of others, there are gods of the Brahma-body,
and there are gods even higher than those.
Endowed with such faith as those deities possessed when they passed away from here and were reborn there, that same kind of faith exists in me as well.
By means of such virtue… learning… generosity…
‘Those deities were endowed with wisdom; having passed away from here, they have been reborn there. Such wisdom as theirs exists in me as well.
Monks, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects his own faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, as well as those of those deities, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust.
The mind is not obsessed by lust, the mind is not obsessed by hatred, and the mind is not obsessed by delusion;
at that time his mind is straight, having emerged, been released, and withdrawn from greed.
“Greed,” monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"Monks, making this too their object of focus, in this way some beings here are purified.
These, monks, are the six bases for recollection.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.26 3. Anuttariyavagga Mahākaccānasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna. The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this: “Friends, there are these six unsurpassed things. What six?

The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection. And what, friends, is the unsurpassed sight? Here, friends, a noble disciple sees the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. This, friends, is called the unsurpassed sight. And what, friends, is the unsurpassed hearing? Here, friends, a noble disciple hears the Dhamma not heard before, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he experiences the holy life itself, both in its particulars and in its entirety, surpassingly pure. This, friends, is called the unsurpassed hearing. And what, friends, is the unsurpassed gain? Here, friends, a noble disciple gains the gain that is unsurpassed, namely, the gain of faith, the gain of virtuous behavior, the gain of learning, the gain of generosity, and the gain of wisdom. This, friends, is called the unsurpassed gain. And what, friends, is the unsurpassed training? Here, friends, a noble disciple trains in the unsurpassed training of higher virtue, the unsurpassed training of higher mind, and the unsurpassed training of higher wisdom. This, friends, is called the unsurpassed training. And what, friends, is the unsurpassed service? Here, friends, a noble disciple serves the Teacher or a disciple of the Teacher with the unsurpassed service of providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This, friends, is called the unsurpassed service. And what, friends, is the unsurpassed recollection? Here, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. As he recollects the Tathāgata, his mind becomes concentrated within, and he attains the unsurpassed happiness and joy born of seclusion. This, friends, is called the unsurpassed recollection. These, friends, are the six unsurpassed things. When the Venerable Mahākaccāna had spoken, the Venerable Sāriputta said to him: “It is wonderful, friend Kaccāna, it is marvelous, friend Kaccāna! How well this has been stated by you, friend Kaccāna: ‘There are these six unsurpassed things…’” Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta, it is marvelous, friend Sāriputta! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Mahākaccāna: ‘There are these six unsurpassed things…’” When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken, the Venerable Sāriputta said to him: “It is wonderful, friend Ānanda, it is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How well this has been stated by the Venerable Mahākaccāna: ‘There are these six unsurpassed things…’” This is what the Venerable Mahākaccāna said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Venerable Mahākaccāna’s words. This is the sixth discourse in the Third Chapter on the Unsurpassed Things in the Book of Sixes.
There, the Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus!"
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:
“It is wonderful, friends!
It is wonderful, friends!
To such an extent has this attainment of an opening within confinement been discovered by that Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One,
the Perfectly Self-Awakened One— for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, and for the disappearance of pain and grief.
For the attainment of the method and for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, these six bases of recollection.
What are the six?
Here, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus:
‘Such indeed is the Blessed One … the Teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
At whatever time, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
at that time his mind is simply straight, having emerged from, been released from, and risen above worldly greed.
“‘Carrion,’ friends, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Now, that noble disciple dwells with a mind entirely equal to space—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
It is by taking this as an object, friends, that some beings here become pure in nature.”
Furthermore, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma thus:
"The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One... to be personally realized by the wise.
Friends, at the time when a noble disciple recollects the Dhamma, his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight ahead; it has gone forth, been released, and emerged from greed.
"Greed," friends, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
That noble disciple, friends, dwells with a mind entirely equal to space—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
"Friends, having taken this as an object, some beings here become pure by nature.
Furthermore, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha:
'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well... [as before] ...the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.'"
"Friends, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects the Saṅgha, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
at that time his mind is simply upright, having emerged, been released, and risen above craving.
'Craving,' friends, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure."
"Friends, that noble disciple dwells with a mind entirely equal to space—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
This too, friends, is an object by taking which some beings here become pure in nature.
Furthermore, friends, the noble disciple recollects his own virtues, unbroken... [and so on] ...conducive to concentration."
At whatever time, friends, a noble disciple recollects his own virtue, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is it obsessed by hatred, nor is it obsessed by delusion;
at that time his mind is simply straight, having emerged from, been released from, and risen above craving.
"Craving," friends, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
"Friends, that noble disciple dwells with a mind entirely equal to space—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

This too, friends, is an object by taking which some beings here become pure in nature. Furthermore, friends, the noble disciple recollects his own generosity: "I have given this gift; I have shared these things. This too, friends, is an object by taking which some beings here become pure in nature."
“It is a gain for me indeed, it is a great fortune for me indeed...
that I am devoted to the practice of requesting [gifts], delighting in giving and sharing.
At whatever time, friends, a noble disciple recollects his own generosity, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion.
At that time, his mind is directed straight ahead; it has gone forth, been released, and emerged from greed.
"Greed," friends, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
That noble disciple, friends, dwells with a mind entirely equal to space—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
"Furthermore, friends, by taking this as an object, some beings here become possessed of the nature of purification.
Moreover, friends, a noble disciple recollects the deities:
'There are the gods of the Four Great Kings; there are the gods... [and so on] up to those even higher than these.'"
"Those deities who were endowed with such faith as they possessed when they passed away from here and were reborn there—such faith exists in me as well.
Such virtue... such learning..."
‘Those deities were endowed with generosity… and wisdom; having passed away from here, they have been reborn there. Such wisdom as theirs exists in me too.
Friend, when a noble disciple [reflects] upon his own faith, virtue, learning, and so forth, as well as those of those deities…
When he recollects generosity and wisdom, at that time his mind is not obsessed by lust,
nor is his mind obsessed by hatred, nor is his mind obsessed by delusion;
at that time his mind is straight, having emerged, been released, and risen above greed.
“‘Ravenous greed,’ friends, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Now, that noble disciple dwells with a mind entirely equal to space—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
It is by taking this as an object, friends, that some beings here become pure in nature.”
It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends!

To what an extent this attainment of an opening within confinement has been discovered by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, and for the disappearance of pain and grief.
"For the attainment of the method, for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, these six bases of recollection.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.27

3. The Chapter on the Incomparable (Anuttariya-vagga) The First Discourse on the Occasion (Paṭhama-samaya-sutta) (AN 6.27, PTS AN iii 317) “Monks, there are these five incomparable things. What five? The incomparable vision, the incomparable hearing, the incomparable gain, the incomparable training, and the incomparable service. These, monks, are the five incomparable things.”
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhante, how many occasions are there for approaching a bhikkhu who is esteemed by the mind?
"Bhikkhu, there are these six occasions for approaching a bhikkhu who is esteemed by the mind."
Which six? Here, bhikkhu,
at whatever time a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, overwhelmed by sensual lust,
and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sensual lust— at that time, he is one who should be cultivated by the mind.
Having approached that bhikkhu, he should speak to him thus:
“Friend, I dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual lust and overcome by sensual lust; and I do not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual lust.
It would be good if the Venerable One would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual lust.”
To him, the esteemed monk teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual lust.
This, bhikkhu, is the first occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, on another occasion, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will...
When one dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will and dominated by ill will, and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen ill will,
at that time one should approach a monk who is esteemed by the wise and say this:
"Friend, I dwell with a mind obsessed by ill will and dominated by ill will, and I do not understand as it really is the escape from arisen ill will."
“It would be well indeed if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of ill will.
Then the monk who is a mentor teaches him the Dhamma for the abandoning of ill will.
This, bhikkhu, is the second occasion for approaching to see a monk who is a mentor.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor,
overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sloth and torpor—
at that time, having approached a bhikkhu who is esteemed by the mind, he should speak to him thus:
"Friend, I dwell with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overcome by sloth and torpor, and I do not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sloth and torpor.
It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of sloth and torpor.
Then that monk, who is worthy of esteem, teaches him the Dhamma for the abandoning of sloth and torpor.
This, bhikkhu, is the third occasion for approaching to see a bhikkhu who is worthy of esteem.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, on another occasion when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed and overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse,
and he does not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse.
At that time, one should approach a monk who is esteemed by his fellows and say to him:
“Friend, I am dwelling with a mind obsessed and overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse; I do not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen restlessness and remorse.
It would be good if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.”
To him, the venerable monk teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of restlessness and remorse.
This, monk, is the fourth occasion for approaching to see a venerable monk.
Furthermore, monk, when a monk dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt...

At that time, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt and overcome by doubt, and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt, one should approach a monk who is esteemed by the wise and say this:
"Friend, I dwell with a mind obsessed by doubt and overcome by doubt; I do not understand as it really is the escape from arisen doubt."
“It would be well indeed if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of doubt.
Then that monk who is worthy of esteem teaches him the Dhamma for the abandoning of doubt.
This, bhikkhu, is the fifth occasion for approaching to see a monk who is worthy of esteem.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu does not understand that sign by means of which, when attending to it,
the immediate destruction of the taints occurs, on that occasion he should approach a bhikkhu who is a mentor and say this:
“Friend, I do not understand that sign by means of which, when attending to it, the immediate destruction of the taints occurs.
It would be well if the Venerable One would teach me the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.
Then the esteemed monk taught him the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.
“Monk, this is the sixth occasion for approaching to see a monk who is a mind-developer.
These, monk, are the six occasions for approaching to see a monk who is a mind-developer. This was the seventh [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.28 3. Anuttariyavagga Dutiyasamayasutta (The Second Discourse on the Occasion) “Monks, there are these six unsurpassed things. What six? The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection.

And what, monks, is the unsurpassed sight? Here, monks, a noble disciple sees the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata; having seen him, he gains faith. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed sight. And what, monks, is the unsurpassed hearing? Here, monks, a noble disciple hears the Dhamma not heard before, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which reveals the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. Having heard it, he gains faith. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed hearing. And what, monks, is the unsurpassed gain? Here, monks, a noble disciple gains the gain that is the arising of the wholesome roots that have not yet arisen. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed gain. And what, monks, is the unsurpassed training? Here, monks, a noble disciple trains himself in the training of the higher mind, which leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to nibbāna. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed training. And what, monks, is the unsurpassed service? Here, monks, a noble disciple serves those who are worthy of offerings, those who are fields of merit for the world. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed service. And what, monks, is the unsurpassed recollection? Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. Recollecting the Tathāgata, his mind becomes concentrated, his defilements are purified, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage. This, monks, is called the unsurpassed recollection. These, monks, are the six unsurpassed things.”
(AN 6.28, PTS AN iii 320) On one occasion,
a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then, after their meal, on returning from their alms round, while those elder bhikkhus were sitting gathered together in the pavilion, this discussion arose among them:
“Friends, at what time is it appropriate to go to see a monk who is cherished by the mind?
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to those elder bhikkhus:
“Friends, at the time when a cherished monk has returned from his almsround after his meal and is washing his feet...”
"Having washed his feet, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him;
this is the time to approach the monk who is esteemed by the mind for the sake of seeing him.
When this was said, a certain monk said this to that monk:
“Indeed, friend, that is not the time to approach for the sake of seeing a monk who is esteemed by the mind.
Rather, friend, it is at the time when the esteemed monk has returned from his almsround after his meal,
has washed his feet, and is sitting with his legs crossed, holding his body erect, and having established mindfulness before him.”
Having attended to him, at that time his exhaustion from walking about has not subsided, and his exhaustion from eating has also not subsided.
Therefore, that is not the right time to approach for the sake of seeing a monk who is esteemed by the mind.
"Friends, at whatever time a monk who is esteemed by his mind has risen from seclusion in the evening and is sitting in the shade of the dwelling,
having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness before him—
that is the time to approach that esteemed monk for an audience."
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to that bhikkhu:
"Friend, it is not the right time to approach a bhikkhu who is worthy of esteem in order to see him.
Friend, at the time when a bhikkhu worthy of esteem has emerged from seclusion in the evening and is sitting in the shade of his dwelling..."
He sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him;
whatever sign of concentration he has attended to during the day, that very same one manifests for him at that time.
Therefore, this is not the right occasion for approaching to see a monk who is worthy of esteem.
"Friends, at whatever time a monk who is esteemed by his mind has risen at the dawn of night and is seated with his legs crossed,
his body held erect, and mindfulness established before him—
that is the time to approach that esteemed monk for an audience."
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to that bhikkhu:
"Friend, it is not the right time to go to see a bhikkhu who is worthy of esteem.
Friend, it is at the time when a bhikkhu worthy of esteem has risen at the dawn of night and is sitting..."
"He sits with his legs crossed, holding his body erect, having established mindfulness before him;
at that time, his body is full of vigor and fit to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas.
Therefore, this is not the right time to approach a monk who is esteemed by the mind for the purpose of seeing him."
When this was said, the Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed the elder bhikkhus:
"Friends, I have heard and received this directly from the Blessed One:
'Bhikkhus, there are these six occasions for approaching a bhikkhu who is esteemed by mind to see him.'"
Which six? Here, bhikkhu,
at whatever time a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, overcome by sensual lust,
and does not understand as it really is the escape from arisen sensual lust— at that time, he is one who should be cultivated by mind.
Having approached that bhikkhu, he should speak to him thus:
“Friend, I dwell with a mind obsessed by sensual lust and overwhelmed by sensual lust; and I do not understand, as it really is, the escape from arisen sensual lust.
It would be good if the Venerable One would teach me the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual lust.”

To him, the esteemed monk teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of sensual lust. This, bhikkhu, is the first occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will … [as before] … this, bhikkhu, is the second occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness … [as before] … this, bhikkhu, is the third occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse … [as before] … this, bhikkhu, is the fourth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt … [as before] … this, bhikkhu, is the fifth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind that has not abandoned the five hindrances—those imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom—and has not calmed his body, which is agitated and uncalmed, this, bhikkhu, is the sixth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells with a mind that has abandoned the five hindrances and has calmed his body, which was previously agitated and uncalmed, this, bhikkhu, is the seventh occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and breaks that concentration, this, bhikkhu, is the eighth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person does not come and break that concentration, this, bhikkhu, is the ninth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he is unable to explain it, this, bhikkhu, is the tenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he is able to explain it, this, bhikkhu, is the eleventh occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person gains confidence in what he says, this, bhikkhu, is the twelfth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person does not gain confidence in what he says, this, bhikkhu, is the thirteenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! and gains confidence in what he says, this, bhikkhu, is the fourteenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! but does not gain confidence in what he says, this, bhikkhu, is the fifteenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! and gains confidence in what he says, and subsequently acts upon it, this, bhikkhu, is the sixteenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! but does not gain confidence in what he says, and does not act upon it, this, bhikkhu, is the seventeenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! and gains confidence in what he says, and acts upon it, and as a result, that person attains the destruction of the taints, this, bhikkhu, is the eighteenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! but does not gain confidence in what he says, and does not act upon it, yet as a result, that person attains the destruction of the taints, this, bhikkhu, is the nineteenth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! and gains confidence in what he says, and acts upon it, and as a result, that person attains final knowledge, this, bhikkhu, is the twentieth occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! but does not gain confidence in what he says, and does not act upon it, yet as a result, that person attains final knowledge, this, bhikkhu, is the twenty-first occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! and gains confidence in what he says, and acts upon it, and as a result, that person becomes one who has entered the stream, this, bhikkhu, is the twenty-second occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Furthermore, bhikkhu, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu dwells having attained a certain state of concentration, and while he is in that state, some other person comes and asks about the meaning of that concentration, and he explains it, and that person thinks: "It is wonderful, it is marvelous! How the Venerable One has attained such a state of concentration and can explain its meaning so well! but does not gain confidence in what he says, and does not act upon it, yet as a result, that person becomes one who has entered the stream, this, bhikkhu, is the twenty-third occasion for approaching to see the esteemed monk. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and
He dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor… he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse… he dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt.

If, by relying on a certain sign and attending to that sign, the immediate destruction of the taints occurs, yet one does not know or see that sign, at that time one should approach a monk who is worthy of esteem and say this:
“Friend, I do not know or see the sign by relying on which and attending to which the immediate destruction of the taints occurs.
It would be well if the venerable one would teach me the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.”
To him, the esteemed monk teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints.
This, bhikkhu, is the sixth occasion for approaching to see an esteemed monk.
"I have heard this from the Blessed One’s own presence, friend; I have received it directly from his presence:"
“Monk, these are the six occasions for approaching a monk who is esteemed by mind to see him.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.29
3. Anuttariya Chapter:
Udāyī Sutta (AN 6.29, PTS AN iii 322)
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyī:
“Udāyī, how many bases for recollection are there?
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī remained silent.
A second time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyī:
“Udāyī, how many bases for recollection are there?
A second time, the Venerable Udāyī remained silent.
A third time the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyī:
“Udāyī, how many bases for recollection are there?
A third time the Venerable Udāyī remained silent.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
"Friend Udāyī, the Teacher calls for you.
"I shall hear from the Blessed One, friend Ānanda."
"Here, Bhante, a bhikkhu recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
This, Bhante, is a basis for recollection.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“I knew, Ānanda,
that this foolish man Udāyī does not dwell devoted to higher mind.
How many, Ānanda, are the bases for recollection?”
“Bhante, there are five bases for recollection. Which five?
Here, Bhante, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the third jhāna.”
“Venerable sir, this basis for recollection, when developed and cultivated in this way, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
Furthermore, venerable sir, a bhikkhu attends to the perception of light; he resolves upon the perception of day: as by day, so at night; as at night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind open and unenveloped, he develops a mind imbued with luminosity.”
“Venerable sir, this basis for recollection, when developed in this way and cultivated extensively, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, venerable sir, a bhikkhu contemplates this very body—up from the soles of the feet and down from the hair of the head, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys;”
"The heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; the intestines, mesentery, gorge, feces;
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil-of-the-joints, and urine.
Venerable sir, this basis for recollection, when developed in this way and cultivated extensively in this way, leads to the abandoning of sensual lust.

Furthermore, Bhante, just as if a bhikkhu were to see a body discarded in a charnel ground— one dead for one day, or two days, or three days— swollen, discolored, and festering, he applies this to his own body:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate."
Or again, as if one were to see a corpse cast away in a charnel ground, being devoured by crows, being devoured by hawks,
being devoured by vultures, being devoured by dogs, being devoured by jackals,
or being devoured by various kinds of worms.
He applies this very body to that [state], thinking:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this.
Or, as if he were to see a corpse discarded in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood still adhering, bound together by sinews... [and so on].
A skeleton, stripped of flesh and smeared with blood, bound together by sinews;
... a skeleton, devoid of flesh and blood, bound together by sinews;
bones separated from their attachments, scattered in all directions and intermediate points—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone.
With one [hand] the shin bone, with another the thigh bone, with another the hip bone, with another the rib bone,
with another the vertebra, with another the shoulder bone, with another the neck bone, with another the jaw bone,
with another the tooth bone, and with another the skull; bones white, resembling the color of a conch shell.
He sees bones heaped together, bones more than three years old, rotten and crumbled to dust.
He applies this very same body to that:
"This body, too, is of such a nature, of such a character, and not exempt from this fate."
"Venerable sir, this basis for recollection, when developed and cultivated in this way, leads to the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.
Furthermore, venerable sir, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as above] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Venerable sir, this basis for recollection, when developed and cultivated in this way, leads to the penetration of the various elements."
“Venerable sir, these are the five subjects of recollection.
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
Therefore, Ānanda, you should also remember this as the sixth subject of recollection.”
"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu moves forward mindfully, moves backward mindfully, stands mindfully, sits mindfully, lies down mindfully, and undertakes his work mindfully.
This, Ānanda, is the basis for recollection that, when developed and cultivated in this way, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.30 3.
Anuttariyavagga Anuttariyasutta (The Discourse on the Unsurpassed)
“Bhikkhus, there are these six unsurpassable things. Which six? [The text continues with the list.]”
The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection.
And what, monks, is the unsurpassed sight?
Here, monks, someone goes to see the elephant-treasure, or to see the horse-treasure... [and so forth].
One goes to see a jewel, or one goes to see various high and low things, or one goes to see an ascetic or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly.
This seeing exists, monks; I say it is not non-existent.
But this view, monks, is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.
But whoever, monks, goes to see the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, having established faith, established affection,
being resolutely intent and full of confidence— this, monks, is the unsurpassed way of seeing for the purification of beings,
for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, and for the realization of the True Dhamma.
For the attainment and realization of Nibbāna, he goes to see either the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata—
one who is established in faith, established in love, having reached a single-pointed conclusion, and full of confidence. This, monks,
is called the unsurpassed excellence of seeing.
Thus is the unsurpassed sight.
And how does the unsurpassed hearing come about?
Here, monks, someone goes to hear the sound of a drum, or goes to hear the sound of a lute.
One goes to hear the sound of singing, or one goes to hear various things high and low, or one goes to hear the Dhamma from a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly.
This hearing exists, monks; I say this is not non-existent.
And yet, monks, this kind of hearing is inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna.
But whoever, monks, goes to hear the Dhamma from a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata—
one whose faith is settled, whose love is settled, who has gone to the conclusion and is fully confident— this, monks, is the unsurpassed excellence among hearings for the purification of beings,
for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, and for the disappearance of pain and grief.
For the attainment of the method and for the realization of Nibbāna, he goes to hear the Dhamma from a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata—
firm in faith, firm in love, having gone to the one-sided conclusion, and full of confidence. This, monks,
is called the unsurpassed excellence of hearing the Dhamma.
Thus there is the unsurpassed sight and the unsurpassed hearing.
And how is there the unsurpassed gain?
Here, monks, a certain person gains the gain of a son, gains the gain of a wife, and gains the gain of wealth.
He gains gain, or he gains gain that is high and low; or he acquires faith in recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and practice wrongly.
There is such gain, monks; I say it is not non-existent.
But this gain, monks, is inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
it does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna.
However, monks, when one acquires faith in the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, being firmly established in that faith—
Having established affection, being resolutely intent, and full of confidence— this, monks, is the unsurpassed thing for the purification of beings,
for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way,
and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, faith in the Tathāgata or in a disciple of the Tathāgata.
He acquires it, possessing settled faith, settled affection, having reached a state of certainty, and being fully confident.
This, monks, is called the unsurpassed gain.
Thus: the unsurpassed vision, the unsurpassed hearing, and the unsurpassed gain.
And what is the unsurpassed training? Here, monks,
a certain person trains in elephant-riding, trains in horsemanship, trains in chariot-fighting,
trains in archery, trains in swordsmanship, or trains in various other arts, or he trains under a recluse.
or from a brahmin who holds wrong view and practices wrongly—one trains in that.
There is this training, monks; I do not say it does not exist.
But this training, monks, is inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial.
It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna.
But whoever, monks, trains in higher virtue and also in higher mind within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata...
He trains in the higher mind and he trains in the higher wisdom—firm in faith, firm in love, having reached a definitive conclusion, and full of confidence.

This, monks, is the unsurpassed training for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say:
In the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, one trains in higher virtue, trains in higher mind, and trains in higher wisdom;
one is established in faith, established in love, having gone to the conclusion, and fully confident.
This, monks, is called the unsurpassed training.
Thus there is the unsurpassed vision, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, and the unsurpassed training.
And how does the unsurpassed service come about?
Here, monks, someone serves a kshatriya, serves a brahmin, or serves a householder.
One serves them, or one serves variously, or one serves a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly.
There is such service, monks; I say it is not non-existent.
But this service, monks, is inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; it does not lead to disenchantment … [as before] … nor to Nibbāna.

However, monks, when one serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata with established faith, established love, having gone to the conclusion, and being fully convinced—this, monks, is the unsurpassed service for beings.
For the sake of purification, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way,
and for the realization of Nibbāna— namely, that one serves the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata,
established in faith, established in love, having gone to the conclusion, and being fully confident.
This, monks, is called the unsurpassed service.
Thus there is the unsurpassed seeing, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, and the unsurpassed service.
And how does the unsurpassed recollection come about?
In this case, monks, a certain person recollects the acquisition of a son, recollects the acquisition of a wife, recollects the acquisition of wealth,
or recollects various kinds of acquisitions; or he recollects a recluse or a brahmin who holds wrong views and practices wrongly.
"Bhikkhus, this recollection exists; I say it is not non-existent.
Yet, bhikkhus, this recollection is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;
it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, nor to Nibbāna."
It leads to Nibbāna. And whoever, monks,
recollects the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, being established in faith, established in love, having gone to the one-sided conclusion,
and being full of confidence— this, monks, is the unsurpassed among the objects of recollection for beings.
For the sake of purification, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way,

and for the realization of Nibbāna— namely, that one who possesses established faith, established love, who has gone to the conclusion and is fully confident, recollects either the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata.
This, monks, is called the unsurpassed recollection.
These, monks, are the six unsurpassed things.
Those who have obtained the unsurpassed vision—
And the unsurpassed hearing;
having attained the unsurpassed gain,
they delight in the unsurpassed training.
Attentive in service,
they cultivate recollection connected with seclusion.
The secure path leading to the Deathless.
Rejoicing in heedfulness,
prudent and restrained by virtue;
They indeed arrive in due time,
where suffering ceases. Thus ends the tenth [sutta].
The third chapter: On the Incomparables.
Its summary verse:
Sāmaka and Aparihāniya.
Bhaya [recited] the Himavanta;
Kaccāna, two Samayas;
and Udāyī, "The Unsurpassed."

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.31 4. Devatāvagga Sekhasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five trainees. What five? The one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship; and the one who is practicing for the realization of the unsurpassed security from bondage. These, bhikkhus, are the five trainees.”
“Bhikkhus, these six things lead to the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What six? [The text continues with the list.]”
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, lack of restraint over the sense faculties,
and lack of moderation in eating— these six things, monks, lead to the decline of a monk in training. These six things, monks, lead to the non-decline of a monk in training.
“What six?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, and moderation in eating.
These, monks, are the six qualities that lead to the non-decline of a monk in training.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.32 4.
Devatāvagga (The Chapter on Devas)
The First Discourse on Non-Deterioration (Paṭhama-aparihāna-sutta). Then,
when the night had advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached.
Having illuminated the area, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, these six qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu."
“What six? Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for heedfulness,
and reverence for hospitality— these, venerable sir, are the six qualities that lead to a bhikkhu’s non-decline.”
Thus spoke that deity.
The Teacher approved.
Then that deity, thinking, "The Teacher has approved of me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to her right, and vanished right there.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, during this night, as the night was drawing to a close, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, having illuminated the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached me;
having approached, she paid homage to me and stood to one side.”
He stood to one side. Standing there, monks, that deity said this to me:
"Venerable sir, these six qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
Which six?"

“Veneration for the Teacher, veneration for the Dhamma, veneration for the Saṅgha, veneration for the training, veneration for heedfulness, and veneration for hospitality— these six qualities, bhante, lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said, bhikkhus.
Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished on the spot.
Reverent toward the Teacher, reverent toward the Dhamma,
and possessing intense reverence for the Saṅgha;
A bhikkhu who values heedfulness and respects hospitality is incapable of decline.
“...in the very vicinity of Nibbāna.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.33

4. Devatāvagga The Second Discourse on Non-Deterioration (Dutiya-aparihāna-sutta) At Sāvatthī. Then a certain deity, having approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him and stood to one side. Standing there, that deity addressed the Blessed One with a verse: “Bhikkhu, what is it that does not deteriorate? What is it that does not grow old? What is it that does not die? What is it that does not pass away? “Faith, friend, does not deteriorate; wisdom does not grow old; the Dhamma does not die; and Nibbāna does not pass away. “Bhikkhu, what is it that brings happiness? What is it that brings delight? What is it that is most excellent among things that have arisen? What is it that is supreme among all conditioned phenomena? “Truth, friend, brings happiness; Dhamma brings delight; the Sangha is most excellent among things that have arisen; and concentration is supreme among all conditioned phenomena. “Bhikkhu, what is it that is difficult to cross? What is it that is difficult to fill? What is it that is difficult to pull out? What is it that is difficult to fill up? “The ocean, friend, is difficult to cross; the belly is difficult to fill; the wind is difficult to pull out; and the world is difficult to fill up. “Bhikkhu, what is it that is difficult to guard? What is it that is difficult to satisfy? What is it that is difficult to fill? What is it that is difficult to appease? “A woman, friend, is difficult to guard; fire is difficult to satisfy; the ocean is difficult to fill; and the world is difficult to appease. “Bhikkhu, what is it that is difficult to see? What is it that is difficult to understand? What is it that is difficult to reach? What is it that is difficult to master? “Nirvāṇa, friend, is difficult to see; the Dhamma is difficult to understand; the realm of the Buddhas is difficult to reach; and self-mastery is difficult to master. “Bhikkhu, what is it that is most excellent among bipeds? What is it that is most excellent among quadrupeds? What is it that is most excellent among those who have wings? What is it that is most excellent among those who have teeth? “The one who has vision is most excellent among bipeds; the horse is most excellent among quadrupeds; the garuḍa is most excellent among those who have wings; and the elephant is most excellent among those who have teeth. “Bhikkhu, what is it that is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma? What is it that is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma? What is it that is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma? What is it that is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma? “Faith is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma; wisdom is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma; the Sangha is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma; and the Dhamma is most excellent among those who live by the Dhamma. When this was said, that deity said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, bhante! Magnificent, bhante! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
“Monks, this very night, when the night was far spent, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, having illuminated the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached me.
Having approached and paid homage to me, she stood to one side.
Standing to one side, monks, that deity said this to me:”
“Bhante, there are these six qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
What are the six?
Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for moral shame, and reverence for moral dread.”
“Venerable sir, these six qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, she paid homage to me, kept me on her right, and vanished right there.
Revering the Teacher, revering the Dhamma,
and possessing intense reverence for the Saṅgha;
endowed with moral shame and fear of wrongdoing.
Possessing deference and respect,
he is incapable of decline and is indeed close to Nibbāna.
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.34 4.
Devatāvagga (The Chapter on Devas)
The Mahāmoggallāna Sutta (AN 6.34).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then, while the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"Of which deities is there such knowledge as this:
'Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal'?"
Now at that time, a bhikkhu named Tissa, having recently passed away, had been reborn in a certain Brahma-world.
There too they knew of him thus:
"Brahmā Tissa is of great psychic power and great majesty."
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—disappeared from Jeta’s Grove and reappeared in that Brahma world.
The Brahmā Tissa saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Come, dear Moggallāna! Welcome, dear Moggallāna!

“Tissa, among which gods does such knowledge arise as this: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal’?

“Sir Moggallāna, among the gods of the Four Great Kings, such knowledge arises: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal. “Tissa, does such knowledge arise for all the gods of the Four Great Kings, or not?”

“Not all the gods of the Four Great Kings, dear Moggallāna, possess this knowledge: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal.

Those gods of the Four Great Kings, dear Moggallāna, who are not endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha, not endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, not endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and [not endowed] with the qualities pleasing to the Noble Ones...”

Those who are not endowed with virtuous conduct do not possess such knowledge regarding those devas as: "Stream-enterers are indeed of a nature not subject to falling away, fixed in destiny, and having enlightenment as their final goal.
But, dear Moggallāna, those Cātumahārājika devas who are endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha [do possess it].
“Those who are endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha, and endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones,
have this knowledge: ‘We are stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.’”

“Tissa, does this knowledge— ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to states of deprivation, they are fixed in destiny and have enlightenment as their final goal’— belong only to the gods of the Four Great Kings,
or does it also belong to the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, and the Tusita gods?”

“Do even the gods who delight in creation… and the gods who wield power over the creations of others possess this knowledge: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal’?

“Indeed, dear Moggallāna, even the gods who wield power over the creations of others possess this knowledge: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal.’”

“Tissa, do all the gods who wield power over the creations of others possess this knowledge: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal’?

“No indeed, worthy Moggallāna, not all the gods who wield power over the creations of others possess this knowledge: ‘Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, they are fixed in destiny, and have enlightenment as their final goal.
For those gods who wield power over the creations of others, worthy Moggallāna, who are not endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha...”
Those who are not endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, not endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha,
and not endowed with the virtues dear to the Noble Ones, do not have this knowledge regarding those gods: “These are stream-enterers, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds,

But those, dear Moggallāna, among the Paranimmitavasavatti devas who are endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha,
verified confidence in the Dhamma, and verified confidence in the Saṅgha,
and who are endowed with the virtues beloved by the noble ones— they possess this knowledge: "Those called stream-enterers are no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms."
“...they are destined for enlightenment.
Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having rejoiced and approved of the words of the Brahmā Tissa,

4. Devatāvagga Vijjābhāgiyasutta (AN 6.35, PTS AN iii 334) “Monks, there are these four factors conducive to true knowledge (*vijjābhāgiya*). What four? Right view is a factor conducive to true knowledge; right intention is a factor conducive to true knowledge; right speech is a factor conducive to true knowledge; and right concentration is a factor conducive to true knowledge. These, monks, are the four factors conducive to true knowledge.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these six things that partake of true knowledge.
Which six?

The perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.”
“Monks, these six things are conducive to true knowledge.

“Bhikkhus, there are these six roots of dispute.

“Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu who is prone to anger and resentment dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher,

"Monks, that bhikkhu who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Teacher, who dwells disrespectful and undeferential toward the Dhamma,

and such a dispute is for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, and for the ruin of many people."
This leads to harm and suffering for gods and humans.

Monks, if you do not perceive such a root of dispute within yourselves or among others, you should practice there, monks, so that that very evil root of dispute does not flow forth in the future.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute. In this way, there is the future non-arising of this evil root of dispute.

In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute; in this way, there is the future non-arising of this evil root of dispute.
