Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.37 4. Devatāvagga Chaḷaṅgadānasutta (The Discourse on the Sixfold Gift) “Monks, there are these six kinds of gifts. What six? The gift of one who is angry, not at peace, with a mind full of ill will; the gift of one who is cruel, not at peace, with a mind full of cruelty; the gift of one who is stingy, not at peace, with a mind full of stinginess; the gift of one who gives out of fear; the gift of one who gives for the sake of reciprocal benefit; and the gift of one who gives with a mind full of faith, at peace, with a mind free from ill will, free from cruelty, and free from stinginess. These, monks, are the six kinds of gifts.”
(AN 6.37, PTS AN iii 336) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the female lay follower Veḷukaṇḍakī Nandamātā established a sacrificial offering endowed with six factors for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One saw the female lay follower Veḷukaṇḍakī,
Nanda’s mother, establishing a gift endowed with six factors for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Having seen this, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, this laywoman Veḷukaṇḍakī Nandamātā establishes an offering endowed with six factors before the Saṅgha of monks headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
And how, monks, is an offering endowed with six factors?
Here, monks, there are three factors on the part of the donor and three factors on the part of the recipients.
What are the three factors of the giver?
Here, monks, before giving, the giver is joyful; while giving, he clarifies his mind; after giving, he is elated.
These are the three factors of the giver.
What are the three factors of the recipients?

Here, monks, the recipients are either free from lust or are practicing for the removal of lust; they are either free from hatred or are practicing for the removal of hatred; they are either free from delusion or are practicing for the removal of delusion.
These are the three factors of the recipients.
Thus there are three factors for the donor and three factors for the recipients.
In this way, monks, an offering is endowed with six factors.
For an offering endowed with these six factors, monks, it is not easy to grasp the measure of its merit:
‘Such an outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness—leading to heaven, having a happy result, conducive to heaven;
it leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant’—this, indeed, is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
Just as, monks, it is not easy to take the measure of the water in the great ocean:
“‘So many handfuls of water,’ or ‘so many hundreds of handfuls of water,’ or ‘so many thousands of handfuls of water,’ or ‘so many hundreds of thousands of handfuls of water.
Rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable mass of great water.
In the same way, monks, it is not easy to grasp the measure of the merit of a gift endowed with these six factors.”

‘So great an influx of merit, an influx of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness—leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven—that leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy’;
rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
“Before the act of giving, one is joyful;”
One should clarify the mind while giving;
having given, one becomes glad at heart—
this is the perfection of sacrifice.
Those who are free from lust, free from hatred,
free from delusion, and free from taints—
such a field is perfect for sacrifice.
The self-restrained practitioners of the holy life,
having themselves rinsed their mouths and having given [water] with their own hands;
This sacrifice brings great fruit both for oneself and for others.
Having sacrificed thus, the wise one—
With a faithful and liberated mind,
the wise person is reborn in a world of happiness free from harm.
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.38 4.

“Bhikkhus, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma.
What three?
Greed is a cause for the origination of kamma; hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma; delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma.”
“Monks, non-greed does not arise from greed;
rather, monks, greed itself arises from greed.
Monks, non-hatred does not arise from hatred;”
Then, monks, from hatred indeed arises hatred.
Monks, from delusion does not arise non-delusion;
rather, monks, from delusion arises only delusion.
“Monks, it is not through action born of greed, action born of hatred, or action born of delusion that gods are known, nor humans, nor any other happy destinations whatsoever.

Rather, monks, it is through action born of greed, action born of hatred, and action born of delusion that hell is known, the animal realm is known, the sphere of hungry ghosts is known, and any other miserable destinations whatsoever are known.
These, monks, are the three origins for the arising of kamma.”
“Monks, there are these three causes for the origination of kamma.
Which three?
Non-greed is a cause for the origination of kamma; non-hatred is a cause for the origination of kamma; non-delusion is a cause for the origination of kamma.”
“Monks, from non-greed, greed does not arise;
rather, monks, from non-greed, only non-greed arises.
Monks, from non-hatred, hatred does not arise;”
Then, monks, from non-hatred, non-hatred itself arises.
Monks, delusion does not arise from non-delusion;
rather, monks, from non-delusion, non-delusion itself arises.

“Monks, by means of action born of non-greed, action born of non-hatred, and action born of non-delusion, hell is not made known; the animal realm is not made known; the sphere of hungry ghosts is not made known; nor indeed are any other states of woe made known.

Rather, monks, by means of action born of non-greed, action born of non-hatred, and action born of non-delusion, gods are made known; humans are made known; nor indeed are any other happy destinies made known.
These, monks, are the three causes for the origination of kamma.”

The Kimila Sutta (AN 6.40, PTS AN iii 339):
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā in the Nicula Grove.

Then the Venerable Kimila approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Kimila said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not endure for long?”
“Here, Kimila, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher;
they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Saṅgha;
they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the training; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward heedfulness.”
“They dwell without respect and without deference toward hospitality.
This, Kimila, is the cause, this is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not endure for long.
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, the true Dhamma endures for long?”
“Here, Kimila, when the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen followers, and laywomen followers dwell with reverence and deference toward the Teacher;
they dwell with reverence and deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell with reverence and deference toward the Saṅgha;
they dwell with reverence and deference toward the training; they dwell with reverence and deference toward heedfulness.”
They dwell with respect and reverence toward one another.
This, Kimila, is the cause, this is the reason why, after a Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the True Dhamma endures for a long time. Thus ends the tenth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.41 4. Devatāvagga Dārukkhandhasutta (The Discourse on the Log) “Monks, suppose a man were to throw a log of wood into a great body of water. It would be carried along by the current, from east to west, from west to east, from south to north, and from north to south. It would be washed up against reeds, rushes, and thickets; it would be caught in whirlpools; it would be struck by a large fish and split in two;

it would be seized by a crocodile; it would sink into a whirlpool; and it would be seized by a sea monster. “Now, monks, what do you think? Would that log of wood ever reach a state of security, a state free from danger, or would it eventually come to rest? “It is impossible, venerable sir, for that log of wood to reach a state of security, a state free from danger, or to come to rest. Rather, venerable sir, that log of wood will eventually end up in the ocean. “In the same way, monks, when a noble disciple possesses four things, it is impossible for him not to reach the state of security, the state free from danger, the state of final nibbāna. What are these four? “Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. “When a noble disciple possesses these four things, monks, it is impossible for him not to reach the state of security, the state free from danger, the state of final nibbāna.”
(AN 6.41, PTS AN iii 340) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Then, in the morning, the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and while descending from Vulture Peak Mountain together with a large company of bhikkhus, he saw a great log of wood in a certain place.
Having seen it, he addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, do you see that great log of wood?"
“Yes, friend.
“If a bhikkhu with psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind so desired, friend, he could resolve that this block of wood be earth. Why is that?
[Because] it is by resolution that it becomes so.”

"Friend, there is the earth element in that log of wood, depending upon which a bhikkhu possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind might resolve upon that log as being earth itself.
If he so desires, friend, a bhikkhu possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind might resolve upon that log as being water itself...
or as being fire itself..."
One should resolve upon it as air;
one should resolve upon it as beautiful;
one should resolve upon it as unattractive.
"And for what reason?

Because, friends, there exists in that log of wood the element of the unattractive; depending upon this, a bhikkhu possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind might resolve upon that log of wood as being simply unattractive.
(The eleventh.)

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.42 4. Devatāvagga Nāgitasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the young deva Nāgita approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a bhikkhu possess to be dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks? “A bhikkhu, Nāgita, possesses five things that are dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. What five? (1) Here, Nāgita, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first thing a bhikkhu possesses that is dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. (2) He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated mentally, and penetrated well through view. This is the second thing a bhikkhu possesses that is dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. (3) He is a speaker on the Dhamma, one who utters the Dhamma at the right time, concerning the right matter, and in accordance with the goal. This is the third thing a bhikkhu possesses that is dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. (4) He is one who gives advice and provides instruction. This is the fourth thing a bhikkhu possesses that is dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. (5) He is one who lives in harmony with his fellow monks, causing no dispute among those who live in harmony, and who delights in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks in accordance with concord.

This is the fifth thing a bhikkhu possesses that is dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. A bhikkhu, Nāgita, possesses these five things that are dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. When this was said, the young deva Nāgita said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Then the young deva Nāgita, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and vanished right there. Not long after the young deva Nāgita had departed, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Who was it, venerable sir, who just now approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and spoke thus? “That was the young deva Nāgita, Ānanda,” the Blessed One replied. “And he spoke thus to me. “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How the Venerable Nāgita has been inspired by the Blessed One with such a talk on the Dhamma! For if the Venerable Nāgita were to speak such a talk on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus, they would listen to him with eager ears, and they would remember what they have heard. “It is because he has been inspired by me, Ānanda, that the Venerable Nāgita has spoken thus. And it is because he has been inspired by me, Ānanda, that the Venerable Nāgita has spoken thus. “This is another quality, Ānanda, that the Venerable Nāgita possesses: he is one who gains internal serenity of mind, but does not gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. Now, Ānanda, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? (1) Here, Ānanda, a certain person gains internal serenity of mind, but does not gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. (2) Another person gains the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena, but does not gain internal serenity of mind. (3) Still another gains neither internal serenity of mind nor the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. (4) And still another gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. The person who gains internal serenity of mind but does not gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena is called a ‘one-sided’ person. So too is the person who gains the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena but does not gain internal serenity of mind. The person who gains neither internal serenity of mind nor the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena is called a ‘lame’ person. But the person who gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena is called a ‘well-rounded’ person. Now, Ānanda, the person who gains internal serenity of mind but does not gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena should, with reference to himself, direct his mind toward the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. When he directs his mind toward the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena, he becomes one who gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. This is his true goal, this is his true excellence. The person who gains the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena but does not gain internal serenity of mind should, with reference to himself, direct his mind toward internal serenity of mind. When he directs his mind toward internal serenity of mind, he becomes one who gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. This is his true goal, this is his true excellence. But the person who gains neither internal serenity of mind nor the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena should put forth extraordinary desire, effort, zeal, enthusiasm, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension to obtain both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. Why is that? So that he may become one who gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. This is his true goal, this is his true excellence. The person who gains both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena should dwell in dependence upon both of these things. Why is that? Because when one dwells in dependence upon both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena, one is called a ‘well-rounded’ person. And it is because of this that the Venerable Nāgita has been inspired by me to speak thus. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir! those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee, one who has not yet attained his heart’s ideal, one who dwells aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage. What five? (1) Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (2) He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated mentally, and penetrated well through view.

(3) He gains internal serenity of mind, and he does not neglect the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena. (4) He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick. (5) He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. These, bhikkhus, are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee, one who has not yet attained his heart’s ideal, one who dwells aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage. (AN 6.42, PTS AN iii 341) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Icchānaṅgala.
There the Blessed One was staying at Icchānaṅgala, in the grove of Icchānaṅgala.
The brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying at Icchānaṅgala in the grove of Icchānaṅgala."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama’s fame has spread abroad:
“Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct...
[as above] ...a Buddha, a Blessed One. It is good to see such arahants.
Then, when that night had passed, the brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala took abundant hard and soft food and approached the grove of Icchānaṅgala; having arrived, they stood outside the gateway,
making a loud noise and a great clamor.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nāgita was the Blessed One’s attendant.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Nāgita:
“Nāgita, who are those making such loud noises, such great clamor? They sound like fishermen over a haul of fish.”

“Venerable sir, these brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala have brought abundant hard food and soft food and are standing outside the gateway, having brought them specifically for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“Nāgita, let there be no meeting with fame, and let there be no fame from me.
For whoever, Nāgita, does not abandon this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening—”
“May he be one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, that bliss of renunciation, that bliss of seclusion, that bliss of peace,
that bliss of enlightenment, which I obtain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble;
may he accept that dross-like pleasure, that slothful pleasure, that pleasure of gain, honor, and fame.”
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now consent; let the Sugata now consent.
Venerable sir, it is now the time for the Blessed One’s consent.
Whichever way the Blessed One now goes, venerable sir, the brahmins and householders, both those of the towns and the countryside, will surely incline in that very direction.”
"Just as, venerable sir, when it rains in thick drops, the waters flow along whatever downward slope there is;
even so, venerable sir, wherever the Blessed One goes now, the brahmins, householders, town-dwellers, and country-folk will incline in that very direction. And why is that?
[Because of the excellence of his teaching]."
"For it is thus, Bhante, with regard to the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.
"Nāgita, let there be no meeting of me with fame, and let there be no fame for me.
For whoever, Nāgita, does not [cling] to this happiness of renunciation, this happiness of seclusion, this happiness of peace, this happiness of awakening—"
One who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble that bliss of renunciation, that bliss of seclusion, that bliss of peace, and that bliss of enlightenment—
such a one might accept that filthy pleasure, that slothful pleasure, the pleasure of gain, honor, and fame.
“Here, Nāgita, I see a bhikkhu dwelling near a village who is sitting in concentration.
Then, Nāgita, this occurs to me:
‘Now, either a monastery attendant or a novice will disturb this venerable one from that concentration.’”
Therefore, Nāgita, I am not pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the vicinity of a village.
But here, Nāgita, I see a forest-dwelling bhikkhu sitting dozing away in the forest.
Then, Nāgita, this occurs to me:
‘Now this venerable one, having dispelled this drowsiness and fatigue, will attend to the perception of the forest itself as a single unity.
Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
But here, Nāgita, I see a forest-dwelling bhikkhu sitting in the forest who is not concentrated.
“Nāgita, it occurs to me:
‘Now this venerable one will concentrate his unconcentrated mind, or he will protect his concentrated mind.
Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.”
Furthermore, Nāgita, here I see a forest-dwelling bhikkhu sitting in the forest, concentrated.
Then, Nāgita, this occurs to me:
‘Now this venerable one will either liberate an unliberated mind, or he will maintain a liberated mind.’”
Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
But here, Nāgita, I see a bhikkhu living near a village who is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Craving for gain, honor, and fame, he neglects seclusion and neglects remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves.
Having descended to a village, town, or capital city, he makes his dwelling there.
Therefore, Nāgita, I am not pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the vicinity of a village.
But here, Nāgita, I see a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller and a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
"Therefore, having set aside gain, honor, and fame, he does not neglect seclusion; he does not neglect remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
For that reason, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu’s dwelling in the forest.
Because, Nāgita, when I am traveling along a highway at a time when I see no one ahead or behind, on that occasion, Nāgita, I have comfort even for the purpose of relieving myself."

The Discourse on the Nāgas (Nāgasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after his meal, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to the Eastern Monastery, Migāra’s Mother’s Palace, for our midday rest.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Eastern Park, the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Pubbakoṭṭhaka to bathe our limbs.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to Pubbakoṭṭhaka to bathe his limbs.
Having bathed his limbs at the eastern gatehouse and emerged, he stood there wearing a single robe, drying his limbs.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala’s elephant named Seta was emerging from the eastern gatehouse to the accompaniment of great instrumental music and singing.
And when people saw him, they said this:

“Truly, sirs, the king’s elephant is handsome; truly, sirs, the king’s elephant is beautiful to behold; truly, sirs, the king’s elephant is pleasing; truly, sirs, the king’s elephant is well-proportioned.
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One:
“Is it only when people see a large, vast elephant that they say this: ‘Truly, sirs, the king’s elephant is handsome...’?”

“Is it only when people see a true *nāga* that they say, ‘A *nāga*, indeed! A *nāga*, indeed!’? Or do people also say, ‘A *nāga*, indeed! A *nāga*, indeed! when they see someone else who has acquired a body that is great and vast?
“Udāyi, when people see even an elephant that has acquired a body that is great and vast, they say, ‘A *nāga*, indeed!
A *nāga*, indeed!’”
“Even a horse, Udāyi, that is large and massive...
even a bull, Udāyi, that is large and massive...
even a serpent, Udāyi, that is large and massive... [and so on].
“Furthermore, Udāyi, when people see a great, vast tree... or a person endowed with a great, vast body, they say:
‘A nāga indeed, sirs! A nāga!’”

"Moreover, Udāyi, whoever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, does no harm by body, speech, or mind—I call him a 'nāga'.
"It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One!"

Moreover, Udāyi, whoever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, does no harm by way of body, speech, or mind—I call him a “Nāga.
And, Bhante, I rejoice in these well-spoken verses uttered by the Blessed One:
“The Fully Awakened One, having become human...”
One who has tamed themselves, is composed,
walking upon the path of the Brahmas,
and delights in the tranquility of the mind.
Whom humans revere,
the one who has gone beyond all phenomena—
even the gods revere him.
Thus have I heard from the Arahant:
he who has transcended all fetters and come from the forest to the state beyond sorrow (nibbāna).
Delighting in renunciation of sensual pleasures,
liberated like gold from a rock—
this Naga, Sabbe Accaru, is such a one.
And Himavā among the mountain ranges;
among all those named "Nāga," he is the supreme one whose name is true.
I shall proclaim the Naga to you,
for he commits no evil;
gentleness and non-violence—
Those two are the feet of the Nāga;
asceticism and the holy life are his other two feet.
The great elephant has faith as its trunk,
equanimity as its white tusks,
mindfulness as its neck, and wisdom as its head.
Investigation is the contemplation of the Dhamma;
the heat of the sun is the censure of the Dhamma;
and seclusion is its tail.
Thus meditating, delighting in inhalation and exhalation,
well-composed within,
the Naga goes along in concentration.
The Naga stands concentrated;
the Naga lies down concentrated,
and even when seated, he is concentrated.
The elephant is restrained in every way;
this is the perfection of the elephant.
He eats what is blameless.
He does not consume things that are blameworthy;
having obtained food and clothing,
he avoids hoarding them.
Having cut every fetter, both subtle and gross, and all bonds;
wheresoever he goes, [he is unattached].
He goes forth without longing.
Just as a white lotus born in the water grows within it;
It is not smeared by water,
being pure-scented and delightful;
even so is one well-born in the world.
The Buddha dwells in the world;
he is not defiled by the world,
just as a lotus is not defiled by water.
Like a great fire blazing,
it is extinguished without fuel; when the formations have been stilled, [the mind is at peace].
"He is called 'extinguished' (nibbuto).
This simile, taught by the wise, is for the purpose of making the meaning understood.
The great elephants will understand the elephant taught by the Elephant;
he who is free from passion and free from hatred.
Free from delusion and without taints,
the Naga, casting off the body,
will attain final nibbāna, free from taints.
First.

Migasālā Sutta (AN 6.44).
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the laywoman Migasālā. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the female lay follower Migasālā approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached, she paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, the female lay follower Migasālā said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"How indeed, Bhante Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One so that it can be understood, wherein both the one who lives the holy life and the one who does not live the holy life will have an identical destination in the future life?"
"Venerable sir, my father Purāṇa was a celibate, living apart and abstaining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of village life.
When he passed away, the Blessed One declared: ‘This being is a once-returner; having returned once more to this world, he will make an end of suffering.
My paternal grandfather, Isidatta, venerable sir, was not a celibate, but was content with his own wife."
“He too has passed away, and the Blessed One has declared that he has attained the state of a once-returner and has been reborn in the Tusita realm.

How, venerable Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be understood, when both the one who leads the holy life and the one who does not lead the holy life will have exactly the same destination in the future?
“It is indeed so, sister, as the Blessed One has declared.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received almsfood at the residence of the female lay follower Migasālā, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, having returned from the almsround after his meal, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I approached the residence of the female lay follower Migasālā; having arrived, I sat down on the prepared seat.

Then, Bhante, the female lay follower Migasālā approached me; having arrived, she paid homage to me and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Bhante, the female lay follower Migasālā said this to me:”

"How indeed, venerable Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One so difficult to understand, that both one who lives the holy life and one who does not live the holy life will have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?
My father, venerable sir, Purāṇa, lived the holy life; he was a practitioner of remote conduct, abstaining from sexual intercourse and the village way.
When he passed away, the Blessed One declared: 'He has attained the state of a once-returner and has been reborn in the Tusita host.'"
"Venerable sir, my father Isidatta was not a celibate practitioner; he was content with his own wife.
Yet, after he passed away, the Blessed One declared that he had attained the fruit of a once-returner and was reborn in the Tusita realm.

How, venerable Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One to be understood, when both a celibate practitioner and one who is not a celibate practitioner will have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?"
When this was said, Bhante, I said to the female lay follower Migasālā:
"Indeed, sister, it has been declared thus by the Blessed One.

"But who, Ānanda, is this female lay follower Migasālā—she who is foolish, incompetent, a mere woman with a woman’s wit—and who are those who possess the knowledge of discerning the higher and lower qualities of persons?"
“Ānanda, there are these six persons found existing in the world.
Which six?
Here, Ānanda, a certain person is gentle and pleasant to dwell with; his fellow practitioners in the holy life rejoice in living together with him.”
He has not acted upon what he has heard, he has not mastered it through great learning, he has not penetrated it with right view, and he does not attain even temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to decline rather than to distinction; he is one who goes only to decline, not to distinction.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is gentle and pleasant to live with, and his fellow celibates delight in dwelling together with him in solitude.
For him, it has been accomplished through hearing; it has been accomplished through great learning; it has been penetrated through right view; and he attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline; he is one who goes toward distinction, not one who goes toward decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who measure things by measure make their assessments:
‘The qualities of this one are exactly the same as those of the other; why then is one inferior and the other superior?
For that, Ānanda, leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for the person who is gentle and pleasant to dwell with, his fellow practitioners in the holy life rejoice in living together with him in solitude.
For him, it has been accomplished through hearing, it has been accomplished through great learning, it has been penetrated through right view,
and he attains temporary liberation.
This person, Ānanda, is more excellent and more refined than the former person.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, this person is carried away by the stream of the Dhamma;
who else but the Tathāgata could know that in the interval?
Therefore, Ānanda, do not be one who measures persons;
do not take the measure of persons.
For one who takes the measure of persons, Ānanda, is harmed.
Either I, Ānanda, would measure people out, or someone like me.
But here, Ānanda, in a certain person anger and conceit have been overcome, yet from time to time states of greed arise in him.
He has neither heard [the Dhamma], nor mastered it through great learning, nor penetrated it with vision; he does not even attain temporary liberation.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to decline and not to distinction; he is one who goes only to decline, not to distinction.
But here, Ānanda, for a certain person, anger and conceit have been overcome, yet from time to time states of greed arise in him.
He has, however, acted upon what was heard... [and so on].
It does not lead to decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who measure things by measure...
[as before] ...or whoever is like me.
But here, Ānanda, in a certain person anger and conceit have been overcome, yet from time to time formations of speech arise within him.
He has not even heard [the teaching]... [as before] ...and he does not attain even temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes toward decline rather than distinction; he is one who goes only toward decline, not toward distinction.
But here, Ānanda, for a certain person, anger and conceit have been overcome, and from time to time verbal formations arise in him.
He has accomplished his task through hearing, he has accomplished it through great learning, and he has penetrated it through right view; he also attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline; he is one who goes toward distinction, not one who goes toward decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who judge by measure judge thus:
‘These same qualities belong to this one; these same qualities belong to that other. Why then is one inferior and the other superior?
For that, Ānanda, leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.
In this regard, Ānanda, for a person in whom anger and conceit have been overcome, from time to time verbal formations arise;
for such a person, it has been accomplished through hearing, it has been accomplished through great learning, it has been penetrated by means of right view,
and they attain temporary liberation.
This person, Ānanda, is more excellent and more sublime than that former person.
Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the stream of Dhamma carries this person across.
Who else but the Tathāgata could know that?
Therefore, Ānanda, do not be one who measures persons;
do not take the measure of persons.
One incurs harm, Ānanda, by taking a measure of individuals.
Either I, Ānanda, might take a measure of individuals, or one who is like me.
And what, Ānanda, is Migasālā the female lay follower? She is foolish, incompetent, a mere woman with a woman’s wit; and what is the knowledge of the higher and lower qualities of persons for men?
"These, Ānanda, are the six persons found existing in the world.
If, Ānanda, Isidatta had been endowed with such virtue as Purāṇa was endowed with, then Purāṇa would not have known even the destination of Isidatta here.
And if, Ānanda, Purāṇa had been endowed with such wisdom as Isidatta was endowed with, then Isidatta would not have known even the destination of Purāṇa here."
“Thus, Ānanda, these two persons are both deficient in one factor.
The second [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.45

5. Dhammika Chapter Iṇasutta (The Discourse on Debt) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a debt; the person who is like a deposit; the person who is like a field; and the person who is like a treasury. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a debt? Here, bhikkhus, a person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is like a debt. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a deposit? Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is like a deposit. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a field? Here, bhikkhus, a person destroys life... [and so on] ...indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. Yet they give gifts to those who do not destroy life... [and so on] ...who do not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is like a field. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a treasury? Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life... [and so on] ...does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. And they do not give gifts to those who do not destroy life... [and so on] ...who do not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is like a treasury. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, is poverty suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”— “And when one who is poor, destitute, and without means incurs debt, is indebtedness also suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.

“Furthermore, monks, when one who is poor, destitute, and without means takes a loan and agrees to pay interest—monks, is that interest also suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Furthermore, monks, when a poor man, destitute and lacking possessions, having agreed to pay interest, does not give the interest when it is due, they even summon him to account.
Monks, being summoned to account is also a suffering in this world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures.
“It is so, Bhante.”
“Bhikkhus, when one who is poor, destitute, and without possessions does not give even when being urged, and they pursue him;
for in this world, bhikkhus, the pursuit of one who enjoys sensual pleasures is painful.
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, when one who is poor, destitute, and lacking possessions does not give while wandering about, they even bind him.
Bhikkhus, bondage is suffering in this world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures.
“It is so, Bhante.”
“Thus, monks, poverty is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures; contracting debt is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures;
interest is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures; being summoned for debt is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures;
being pursued by creditors is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures; and imprisonment is suffering in the world for one who enjoys sensual pleasures.”
In the same way, monks, whoever lacks faith in wholesome states,
lacks moral shame in wholesome states, lacks moral dread in wholesome states, lacks energy in wholesome states,
and lacks wisdom in wholesome states—
This, monks, is called one who is poor, destitute, and indigent in the discipline of the Noble One.
Such a person, monks— being poor, destitute, and indigent— is without faith regarding wholesome states,
without a sense of shame regarding wholesome states, without moral dread regarding wholesome states, and without energy regarding wholesome states.
When there is no wisdom regarding wholesome states, one engages in misconduct by way of body, misconduct by way of speech,
and misconduct by way of mind.
This, I say, is his taking up of debt.
Thus, for the sake of concealing that misconduct of body, he forms an evil wish.
He wishes, “May they not know me”; he intends, “May they not know me”; he speaks the words, “May they not know me”;
he exerts himself with the body, “May they not know me. For the sake of concealing that misconduct of speech... [and so forth].
Because of concealing that mental misconduct... [and thinking] "May they not know me," he exerts himself with the body.
This, I say, is his growth.
Then, his virtuous fellow-celibates speak to him thus:
‘This venerable one is of such conduct and such behavior.
This, I say, is for the purpose of reproving him.
Then, when he has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, evil unwholesome thoughts accompanied by remorse assail him.
This, I say, is the consequence of following such a course.
For that person, monks, who is poor, destitute, and lacking in possessions, having practiced misconduct by body, having practiced misconduct by speech,
and having practiced misconduct by mind, after the breakup of the body, after death, is bound in the bonds of hell.
Or the bond of the animal realm.
Monks, I do not see any other single bond so cruel, so harsh,
and so obstructive to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage as this bond of hell or the bond of the animal realm.
Poverty is suffering in the world,
and it is called taking on debt;
the poor man, having taken on debt, [suffers].
While enjoying it, he is distressed;
then they pursue him, and he falls into bondage.
For this bond is suffering:
the longing for the acquisition of sensual pleasures.
Even so, in the discipline of the Noble Ones—
He in whom faith is not found—
shameless, lacking fear of wrongdoing,
and devoted to evil deeds.
Having committed misconduct of body,
and misconduct of speech,
and having committed misconduct of mind,
‘May they not know me,’ he desires;
thus he creeps along with body,
speech, and mind.
Increasing his evil karma again and again in various places,
that foolish man of evil deeds—
Knowing his own misdeed,
the poor man, having incurred debt,
suffers while consuming [the food].
Then mental intentions, painful to the mind, follow after him,
whether in the village or in the forest.
He who, being of evil deeds and dull-witted, knowingly commits a misdeed for himself, suffers remorse born thereof.
Having gone to one of the other [realms],
or even being bound in hell—
this indeed is the painful bondage.
From which the wise man is liberated:
by giving away wealth acquired through righteous means, he gladdens his heart.
The seeker of a home who possesses faith gains a victory in both worlds:
for the sake of his welfare and benefit in this present life, and...
And for the sake of happiness in the future life;
thus, for householders,
through such giving, merit increases.
In the same way, for one whose faith is firmly established in the noble discipline,
who possesses a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing—
Possessing wisdom and restrained by virtue—
this one, indeed, is called "one who lives happily" in the discipline of the Noble Ones.
Having attained spiritual happiness,
he abides in equanimity;
having abandoned the five hindrances, he remains steadfast.
Always energetic,
having attained the jhānas,
he is unified, wise, and mindful.
Having thus known this as it truly is,
for the destruction of all fetters,
and by not clinging in every respect,
The mind is rightly liberated.
For one who is rightly liberated,
if there is knowledge for such a person:
‘My liberation is unshakable,’ through the destruction of the fetters of existence—
this indeed is the supreme knowledge.
This is the unsurpassed happiness;
this is the sorrowless, stainless, secure state—
this is the supreme freedom from debt.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.46 5.
Dhammika Vagga (The Chapter on the Righteous)
The Mahācunda Sutta (AN 6.46, PTS AN iii 355):
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetis at Sayañjāti.
There the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus!"
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahācunda.
The Venerable Mahācunda said this:
“In this case, friends, bhikkhus devoted to the Dhamma disparage bhikkhus who are meditators:”

"But these [others] meditate, thinking, 'We are meditators, we are meditators'; they meditate, they brood, they contemplate, they reflect. What do they meditate upon? What do they meditate with? How do they meditate?

In this regard, the monks who are devoted to the Dhamma have no confidence in them, nor do the monks who are meditators have confidence in them; and they do not practice for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the many, including gods and humans."
Furthermore, friends, here a meditating bhikkhu disparages bhikkhus who are practitioners of the Dharma, saying:

"But these [others] are practitioners of the Dharma, practitioners of the Dharma! They are actually agitated, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose-tongued, muddle-minded, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, and with unrestrained faculties.
What practitioners of the Dharma are they? What practitioners of the Dharma are they? How can they be practitioners of the Dharma?"

In that case, the meditating monks do not have confidence, nor do the Dhamma-practicing monks have confidence; they do not practice for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the many, including gods and humans.
But here, friends, the Dhamma-practicing monks speak in praise only of the Dhamma-practicing monks, and they do not speak in praise of the meditating monks.

In that case, the monks who are practitioners of the Dharma do not have confidence, nor do the meditative monks have confidence; they do not practice for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the many, including gods and humans.
But here, friends, the meditative monks speak in praise only of the meditative monks, and do not speak in praise of the monks who are practitioners of the Dharma.

In that case, the meditating bhikkhus do not have confidence, nor do the Dhamma-practicing bhikkhus have confidence; they do not practice for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the multitude of gods and humans.
Therefore, friends, you should train yourselves thus:
"Being Dhamma-practitioners, we shall speak in praise of the meditating bhikkhus."
"In this way, friends, you should train yourselves.
And why is that? Because such persons, friends, are wonderful and rare in the world—those who dwell having touched the deathless element with their own bodies."
Therefore, friends, you should train yourselves thus:
"Being meditators ourselves, we shall speak in praise of those bhikkhus who are devoted to the Dhamma.
In this way, friends, you should train yourselves.
And why is that? Because, friends, those persons who, having penetrated with wisdom a profound point of meaning, see it clearly, are wonderful and rare in the world.
The fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.47 5. Dhammika Vagga First Discourse on the Immediately Visible “Monks, there are these five immediately visible qualities that lead to the decline of a lay follower. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower is addicted to strong drink, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence; he frequents the company of women; he frequents the company of men; he frequents the company of eunuchs; and he does not attend upon those who are worthy of offerings. These, monks, are the five immediately visible qualities that lead to the decline of a lay follower. Monks, there are these five immediately visible qualities that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower. What five? Here, monks, a lay follower is not addicted to strong drink, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence; he does not frequent the company of women; he does not frequent the company of men; he does not frequent the company of eunuchs; and he attends upon those who are worthy of offerings. These, monks, are the five immediately visible qualities that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower.”
(AN 6.47, PTS AN iii 356) Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘the directly visible Dhamma, the directly visible Dhamma.
To what extent, venerable sir, is the Dhamma directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise?
“In that case, Sīvaka, I shall question you in turn regarding this matter. Answer as you see fit.”
“What do you think, Sīvaka, when greed is present within you, do you know, ‘Greed is present within me’; and when greed is not present within you, do you know, ‘Greed is not present within me’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Sīvaka, when you understand that greed which is present within you as ‘There is greed within me,’ and when you understand that greed which is absent within you as ‘There is no greed within me’—
even this, Sīvaka, is a Dhamma visible here and now… What do you think, Sīvaka?”
Or, when hatred is present within oneself … or when delusion is present within oneself … or when states of greed are present within oneself … [and so forth].

“Do you know, when the quality of hatred is present within you, ‘The quality of hatred is present within me,’ and when the quality of hatred is not present within you, ‘The quality of hatred is not present within me’? … Do you know, when the quality of delusion is present within you, ‘The quality of delusion is present within me,’ and when the quality of delusion is not present within you, ‘The quality of delusion is not present within me’?
“Yes, venerable sir.”

“Sīvaka, when you understand that the quality of delusion exists within you when it is present, saying, ‘The quality of delusion is in me,’ and when you understand that the quality of delusion does not exist within you when it is absent, saying, ‘The quality of delusion is not in me’—in this way, Sīvaka, the Dhamma is directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! … [as before] …
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.48
5. Dhammika Chapter Second Discourse on the Evident (Dutiyasandiṭṭhikasutta) (AN 6.48, PTS AN iii 357)
Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, it is said: ‘The Dhamma is directly visible, the Dhamma is directly visible.’"
“To what extent, Master Gotama, is a Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise?
“In that case, brahmin, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.
What do you think, brahmin?”
“When there is lust within you, do you know: ‘There is lust within me’? And when there is no lust within you, do you know:
‘There is no lust within me’? “Yes, sir. “In that you know, Brahmin, when there is lust within you: ‘There is lust within me,’ and when there is no lust within you: ‘There is no lust within me’—”
In this way too, brahmin, the Dhamma is directly visible...
What do you think, brahmin,
when there is hatred within oneself...?
Or, when delusion is present within oneself … or when bodily corruption is present within oneself … or when verbal corruption is present within oneself … [and so forth].

“When there is mental corruption within you, do you know, ‘There is mental corruption within me’; and when there is no mental corruption within you, do you know, ‘There is no mental corruption within me’?”—
“Yes, sir.”— “In that you, brahmin, when there is mental corruption within you, know, ‘There is mental corruption within me’...”
“If you understand that there is no mental corruption within yourself, you know: ‘There is no mental corruption within me.
It is in this way, brahmin, that the Dhamma is directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! … [as above] …”
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.49

5. Dhammika Chapter: The Discourse on Security (Khema Sutta) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of security. What four? Security from human beings, security from non-human beings, security from the elements, and security from all states of being. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of security. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, is there security from human beings? “Here, bhikkhu, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He does not harbor thoughts of enmity toward others, nor does he harbor thoughts of ill will. Thus, bhikkhu, there is security from human beings. “And how, bhikkhu, is there security from non-human beings? Here, bhikkhu, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He does not harbor thoughts of enmity toward others, nor does he harbor thoughts of ill will. Thus, bhikkhu, there is security from non-human beings. “And how, bhikkhu, is there security from the elements? On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Khema and the Venerable Sumana were dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Blind Men’s Grove.
Then the Venerable Khema and the Venerable Sumana approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Khema said this to the Blessed One:

“Bhante, regarding a bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—it does not occur to him:
‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior.’”
The Venerable Khema spoke thus.
The Teacher approved.
Then the Venerable Khema, thinking, "The Teacher has approved of me," rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then, not long after the Venerable Khema had departed, the Venerable Sumana said this to the Blessed One:

“Bhante, regarding that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right knowledge—it does not occur to him:
‘I am better,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior.’”
The Venerable Sumanas said this.
The Teacher approved.
Then the Venerable Sumanas, thinking, "The Teacher has approved of me," rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, not long after the Venerable Khema and the Venerable Sumana had departed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"It is in this way, bhikkhus, that clansmen declare final knowledge.
The meaning has been stated, yet the self has not been brought forward."
"And yet, here some foolish men seem to give an answer while laughing;
they later fall into distress.
[They do so] neither for those who are superior nor for those who are inferior."
They do not fall back into the cycle of existence;
birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived,
and they wander free from the fetters.
The Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.50 5.
Dhammika Vagga (The Chapter on Dhammika)
“Bhikkhus, when there is no restraint of the sense faculties,
for one who has failed in the restraint of the sense faculties, virtue lacks its proximate cause.
When virtue is absent, for one deficient in virtue, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When right concentration is absent, for one deficient in right concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they truly are lacks its proximate cause.
When knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is absent, for one deficient in knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, disenchantment and dispassion lack their proximate cause.
When disenchantment and dispassion are absent, for one deficient in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause.

Just as, monks, a tree deficient in branches and foliage does not reach fulfillment in its shoots, nor in its bark, nor in its sapwood, nor in its heartwood; so too, when disenchantment and dispassion are absent, for one deficient in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause.
In the same way, monks, when there is no restraint of the sense faculties, for one who has failed in the restraint of the sense faculties, virtue lacks its proximate cause... [and so on] ...
up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.

When there is restraint of the sense faculties, monks, for one who is accomplished in the restraint of the sense faculties, virtue possesses its proximate cause; [and so on] ... up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
When virtue is present, for one endowed with virtue, right concentration is possessed of its proximate cause.
When right concentration is present, for one endowed with right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is possessed of its proximate cause.

When the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is present, for one endowed with the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, disenchantment and dispassion are possessed of their proximate cause.
When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation possesses its proximate cause.

Just as, bhikkhus, when a tree is endowed with branches and foliage, its shoots reach full development, its bark reaches full development, its inner bark reaches full development, and its heartwood also reaches full development;
even so, bhikkhus, when there is restraint of the sense faculties, for one endowed with restraint of the sense faculties, virtuous conduct possesses its proximate cause... [and so on].
“...the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The eighth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.51

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"To what extent, friend Sāriputta, does a bhikkhu hear a Dhamma not heard before, and [retain] that which has been heard?"
“Do phenomena not pass away, and do those phenomena that were previously touched by his mind recur to him,
such that he recognizes what was previously unrecognized?
“Venerable Ānanda is indeed learned.”
"Let it occur to the Venerable Ānanda himself.
"Then listen, friend Sāriputta, and pay close attention; I shall speak," he said.
"Yes, friend," the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda said this: “In this case, friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma— the discourses (sutta),

mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), ‘Thus it was said’ (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical expositions (vedalla).”
Thus, he teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as it was heard and mastered;
he recites the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as it was heard and mastered;

he performs the recitation of the Dhamma in detail exactly as it was heard and mastered; and he reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma exactly as it was heard and mastered.

In whatever residence elder bhikkhus dwell—those who are learned, who have mastered the tradition, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā—one enters the rains retreat in that residence.
From time to time, one approaches them and inquires and questions them:
"Venerable sirs, what is this? What is the meaning of this?"
They reveal to that venerable one what has not yet been revealed, they clarify what has not yet been made clear, and they dispel his doubt regarding various matters that give rise to uncertainty.
It is in this way, friend Sāriputta, that a bhikkhu hears a Dhamma he has not heard before,
his previously heard teachings do not fade away, and those teachings with which he was formerly acquainted through the mind continue to manifest.
"And one cognizes what has not yet been cognized.
"It is wonderful, friend; it is marvelous, friend! How well this has been spoken by the Venerable Ānanda.
And we shall remember the Venerable Ānanda as being endowed with these six qualities."

For the Venerable Ānanda has mastered the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers.

5. Dhammika Chapter:
Discourse on the Warrior-Noble (Khattiyasutta) (AN 6.52, PTS AN iii 362)
Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, what is the underlying purpose of the khattiyas, what is their range of activity, what is their foundation, what is their fixation, and what is their culmination?"
“Khattiyas, brahmin, have wealth as their aim, investigation by wisdom as their range, power as their foundation, attachment to the earth as their fixation, and sovereignty as their culmination.
“But what, Master Gotama, is the aim of brahmins, what is their range, what is their foundation, what is their fixation, and what is their culmination?
“Brahmins, brahmin, have wealth as their aim, investigation by wisdom as their range, the mantras as their foundation, sacrifice as their fixation, and the Brahma-world as their culmination.”
“But, Master Gotama, what is the aim of householders, what is their range of activity, what is their foundation, what is their fixation, and what is their culmination?
“Householders, brahmin, have wealth as their aim, wisdom as their range of activity, craft as their foundation, business as their fixation, and the completion of their business as their culmination.
“But, Master Gotama, what is the aim of women, what is their range of activity, what is their foundation, what is their fixation, and what is their culmination?”
“A woman, brahmin, has the man as her aim; she dwells on ornaments; she is intent upon children; she is settled on the absence of rivals; and her culmination is sovereignty.
“But what, Master Gotama, is the aim of thieves, what is their dwelling on, what is their intent, what is their settlement, and what is their culmination?
“Thieves, brahmin, have seizing as their aim; they dwell on hiding places; they are intent upon weapons; they are settled on darkness; and their culmination is non-seeing.”
“But, Master Gotama, what is the aim of the recluses, what is their range of activity, what is their foundation, what is their fixation, and what is their culmination?

“Recluses, brahmin, have patience and gentleness as their aim; wisdom as their range of activity; virtue as their foundation; the state of nothingness as their fixation; and Nibbāna as their culmination.
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!”
The venerable Gotama knows the intention, the mental preoccupation, the resolve, the adherence, and the conclusion of the khattiyas.

The venerable Gotama knows [the intention, the mental preoccupation, the resolve, the adherence, and the conclusion] of the brahmins... of the householders... of women... of thieves... and of the ascetics.
“Master Gotama knows the intention, the mental preoccupation, the resolve, the adherence, and the conclusion.
Excellent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”

The Discourse on Heedfulness (Appamādasutta).
Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, is there perhaps a single quality that, when developed and cultivated, stands securing both kinds of benefit—the benefit pertaining to the present life and the benefit pertaining to the future life?"

“There is, brahmin, one thing that, when developed and cultivated, stands having fully attained both kinds of welfare: the welfare pertaining to the present life and the welfare pertaining to future lives.

“But what, Master Gotama, is that one thing which, when developed and cultivated, stands having fully attained both kinds of welfare: the welfare pertaining to the present life and the welfare pertaining to future lives?”

“Diligence, brahmin, is a single quality that, when developed and cultivated, stands having mastered both kinds of benefit: the benefit pertaining to the present life and the benefit pertaining to the future life.

Just as, brahmin, whatever footprints of forest animals there may be, they all fit within the footprint of an elephant; the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among them by virtue of its size.

"In the same way, brahmin, the single quality of heedfulness, when developed and cultivated, stands having fully attained both kinds of welfare: the welfare pertaining to the present life and the welfare pertaining to future lives.
Just as, brahmin, whatever rafters there are in a peaked-roof house, they all lead to the peak, incline toward the peak, converge at the peak, and the peak is declared to be their chief;
even so, brahmin, [heedfulness]..."
"Just as, brahmin, a reed-cutter, having cut a reed, takes it by the tip and shakes it out, winnows it, and cleanses it;
even so, brahmin, [is it with one who has abandoned the five lower fetters]...
Just as, brahmin, when the stalk of a cluster of mangoes is cut, whatever mangoes were attached to that stalk all fall down following it."
"In the same way, brahmin...
Just as, brahmin, whatever minor kings there may be, they all become followers of the wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and that wheel-turning monarch is declared to be their chief;
even so, brahmin... [and so on]."
"Just as, brahmin, whatever light there is from the stars, all that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance;

the moon’s radiance is declared the foremost among them—even so, brahmin, the single quality of heedfulness, when developed and cultivated, stands having attained both kinds of welfare: the welfare pertaining to the present life and the welfare pertaining to future lives."

“This, brahmin, is one quality that, when developed and cultivated, stands having fully attained both purposes: the purpose pertaining to the present life and the purpose pertaining to the future life.
“Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
