The Dhammika Sutta (AN 6.54).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, the Venerable Dhammika was a resident in his native land, in all seven monasteries throughout that native land.
There, the Venerable Dhammika would revile, abuse, harass, pierce, and provoke visiting monks with his speech.
And those visiting monks, being reviled, abused, harassed, pierced, and provoked by the Venerable Dhammika with his speech, departed; they did not stay, but abandoned their residence.
Then it occurred to the lay followers from that native region:
“We have indeed attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
yet still, visiting bhikkhus depart, do not settle down, and abandon their residence.”
“What indeed is the cause, what is the reason, why visiting monks depart, do not settle down, and abandon their lodgings?
Then it occurred to the lay followers of that native region:
“This venerable Dhammika reviles, insults, harms, pierces, and provokes visiting monks with his speech.”
And those visiting monks, being reviled, censured, harassed, tormented, and provoked by the Venerable Dhammika with his speech, departed; they did not remain and abandoned the residence.
“What if we were to expel the Venerable Dhammika?
Then the lay followers from the native region approached the Venerable Dhammika; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Dhammika:
“Venerable sir, let the Venerable Dhammika depart from this residence;
enough of your staying here.
Thereupon, the Venerable Dhammika went from that residence to another residence.
There, the Venerable Dhammika would indeed abuse, revile, harass, pierce, and provoke with harsh words those visiting monks.
And those visiting monks, being abused, reviled, harassed, pierced, and provoked with harsh words by the Venerable Dhammika, would depart; they did not remain and abandoned the residence.
Then it occurred to the lay followers of that native region:
“Bhikkhus, we have attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Yet, nevertheless, visiting bhikkhus depart; they do not settle down; they abandon the residence.
What is the cause, what is the reason, why visiting bhikkhus depart, do not settle down, and abandon the residence?”
Then it occurred to the lay followers from that native region:
“This venerable Dhammika insults, reviles, harms, pierces, and provokes with his speech visiting monks.
Because they are being insulted, reviled, harmed, pierced, and provoked with speech by the venerable Dhammika, those visiting monks depart; they do not remain and they abandon the residence.”
“Perhaps we should now cause the Venerable Dhammika to leave.
Then the lay followers from his native district approached the Venerable Dhammika; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Dhammika:
“Venerable sir, let the Venerable Dhammika depart from this residence as well.”
“Enough of your staying here.
Then the Venerable Dhammika went from that residence to another residence.
There too, the Venerable Dhammika would revile, abuse, injure, pierce, and provoke visiting monks with his speech.
And those visiting monks, being reviled, censured, harassed, tormented, and provoked by the Venerable Dhammika with his speech, departed; they did not remain and abandoned the residence.
Then it occurred to the local lay followers:
"We have been attending upon the Saṅgha of monks with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick."
"Yet still, visiting monks depart, do not settle down, and abandon the residence.
What is the cause, what is the reason why visiting monks depart, do not settle down, and abandon the residence?
Then it occurred to the local lay followers: "This venerable Dhammika insults visiting monks... [and so on]."
“Now, let us cause the Venerable Dhammika to depart entirely from his native land along with seven monasteries.
Then the lay followers of his native land approached the Venerable Dhammika; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Dhammika:
“Venerable sir, may the Venerable Dhammika depart entirely from his native land along with seven monasteries.”
Then it occurred to the Venerable Dhammika:
“I have been ordained by the lay followers of my native land, and I have completely left behind all seven monasteries in my native land.
Where indeed shall I go now?”
Then it occurred to the Venerable Dhammika:
“What if I were to go to where the Blessed One is?
Thereupon, the Venerable Dhammika took his bowl and robe and set out for Rājagaha.
Gradually, he approached Rājagaha, Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, and where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Dhammika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Well now, from where have you come, brahmin Dhammika?”
“I have been ordained, venerable sir, by the lay followers of my native land from all seven monasteries in that region.
“Enough, Dhammika brahmin; what is the use of this? Since they have expelled you from here and there, you have come to me after being expelled from those very places.
Once upon a time, Dhammika brahmin, sea-faring merchants would take a bird capable of seeing the shore and plunge their ship into the ocean.”
From a boat that cannot see the shore, they release a bird capable of seeing the shore.

It goes toward the eastern direction, it goes toward the western direction, it goes toward the northern direction, it goes toward the southern direction, it goes upward, and it goes to the intermediate directions.
If it sees a shore on any side, it is indeed like one who has reached the Tathāgata.
"But if he does not see the shore all around him, he returns to that very same boat.
In the same way, Brahmin Dhammika, you who were expelled from here and there have come back into my very presence.
Once upon a time, Brahmin Dhammika, King Koravya had a royal banyan tree named Suppatiṭṭha, which had five branches, cool shade, and was delightful."
Moreover, Brahmin Dhammika, the King Nigrodha Suppatiṭṭha had a circumference of twelve yojanas and its root-branches extended for five yojanas.
Furthermore, Brahmin Dhammika, the fruits of that King Nigrodha Suppatiṭṭha were so large they were like water-jars.
Thus its fruits became sweet,
just like pure, unadulterated honey. And,
brahmin Dhammika, King Suppatiṭṭha used to enjoy the fruit from one trunk of that royal banyan tree.
Together with the women’s quarters, the army consumes one portion; the townspeople and countryfolk consume one portion;
the ascetics and brahmins consume one portion; and the wild animals consume one portion.
Furthermore, Brahmin Dhammika, no one guards the fruits of the royal banyan tree Suppatiṭṭha, nor do they ever harm one another for the sake of its fruits.
Then, Dhammika, a certain man, having eaten as much fruit as he desired from the well-established royal banyan tree, broke off a branch and departed.
Then, Dhammika, the deity dwelling in the well-established royal banyan tree thought this:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
"How wicked is this man, that he should eat as much fruit as he desires from the well-established King Nigrodha,
break off a branch, and depart! What if the well-established King Nigrodha were not to give fruit in the future?"
Then, Dhammika, the Nigrodha king Suppatiṭṭha did not yield fruit for the future.
Then, Dhammika, King Koravya approached Sakka, the lord of the devas; having approached, he said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas:
“Pray, dear sir, you should know that the Nigrodha king Suppatiṭṭha does not yield fruit.”
Then, Dhammika, Sakka, lord of the devas, performed such a feat of psychic power that a violent wind and rainstorm came and toppled the well-rooted royal banyan tree, uprooting it.
Then, Dhammika, the deity dwelling in the royal banyan tree Suppatiṭṭha stood to one side, pained, dejected, with a tearful face, weeping.

Then, brahmin Dhammika, Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the deity dwelling in the Suppatiṭṭha royal banyan tree. Having approached, he said this to the deity dwelling in the Suppatiṭṭha royal banyan tree:
“Why, deity, do you stand to one side, pained, dejected, with tears on your face, weeping?
“Because, dear sir, a violent wind and rain came upon me and overturned my abode, uprooting it.”
“‘Devatā, when you were established in the nature of a tree, did a violent wind and rain come and overturn your dwelling and uproot you?
‘But how, dear sir, is a tree established in the nature of a tree?

‘In this case, devatā, those who need roots take the tree’s roots; those who need bark take the bark; those who need leaves take the leaves; those who need flowers take the flowers; and those who need fruit take the fruit.’”
"And that deity should not feel displeasure or dissatisfaction because of it.
Thus, O deity, does a tree abide in the nature of a tree.
"Indeed, dear sir, while I was not yet abiding in the nature of a tree, a violent wind and rain came and overturned my dwelling, uprooting it."
“If you, deity, would abide by the nature of a tree, your dwelling might become as it was before.
“I shall abide, dear sir, by the nature of a tree; let my dwelling be as it was before.
Then, Brahmin Dhammika, Sakka, lord of the devas, performed such a feat of supernormal power.
"Just as a violent wind and rainstorm might come and uproot a well-established royal banyan tree, leaving its roots bare;
even so, Brahmin Dhammika, did those lay followers from your native land cause one established in the duty of a recluse to be expelled from all seven monasteries in that native land?
"But how, Bhante, is a recluse established in the duty of a recluse?"
“Here, brahmin Dhammika, a monastic does not revile one who reviles him, does not respond with anger to one who is angry, and does not argue back with one who argues.
It is in this way, brahmin Dhammika, that a monastic stands firm in the duty of a monastic.
“But, Bhante, those lay followers from my native land have completely expelled me from all seven monasteries in my native land because I am not standing firm in the duty of a monastic.”
“Once upon a time, Brahmin Dhammika, there was a teacher named Sunetta, a founder of a spiritual order who was free from passion for sensual pleasures.
Brahmin Dhammika, that teacher Sunetta had many hundreds of disciples.
Teacher Sunetta taught the Dhamma to his disciples for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world.”
But those, Brahmin Dhammika, whose minds did not become serene while Sunetta the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā world,
at the breaking up of the body after death, were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination,
the lower world, hell.

“Furthermore, Dhammika, those who gained confidence in the mind while Sunetta the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā world, at the breaking-up of the body after death, were reborn in a happy destination,
a heavenly world. Once in the past, Dhammika, there was a teacher named Mūgapakkha … [and so on] … there was a teacher named Aranemi.”
… There was a teacher named Kuddālaka … there was a teacher named Hatthipāla … there was a teacher named Jotipāla,
a founder of a sect who was free from passion for sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, Brahmin Dhammika, the Teacher Jotipāla had many hundreds of disciples.
The Teacher Jotipāla taught the Dhamma to his disciples for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world.
And those, Brahmin Dhammika, who [followed] the Teacher Jotipāla’s teaching for the sake of companionship with the Brahmā-world...

But those who, while Jotipāla was teaching the Dhamma for companionship with the Brahmā world, did not clear their minds of doubt, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. However, Brāhmaṇa Dhammika,

those who cleared their minds while Jotipāla the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma for companionship with the Brahmā world, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
“What do you think, Brahmin Dhammika,

if someone with a corrupted mind were to revile and abuse these six teachers, founders of sects who are free from passion for sensual pleasures and are accompanied by retinues of many hundreds along with their assemblies of disciples, would he produce much demerit?
“Yes, venerable sir.”

“Brahmin Dhammika, whoever with a corrupt mind should revile and abuse these six teachers who are founders of sects, free from lust for sensual pleasures, and surrounded by retinues of many hundreds along with their assemblies of disciples, would produce much demerit.
But whoever with a corrupt mind reviles and abuses a single person accomplished in view produces even more demerit than that.
Why is that? Because...”
“Brahmin Dhammika, I do not speak of such forbearance toward those outside this teaching as I do toward my fellow celibates.
Therefore, Brahmin Dhammika, you should train yourself thus:
‘Our minds shall not be corrupted toward our fellow celibates.’”
"In this way, Brahmin Dhammika, you should train yourself.
Thus spoke Sunetta, Mūgapakkha,
and the Brahmin Aranemi.
The Teacher was Kuddālaka,
and the young brahmin was Hatthipāla;
Jotipāla was Govinda.
There was Sattapurohita;
in the past, there were six illustrious teachers who were non-violent.
Free from the stench of raw flesh, devoted to compassion,
having transcended the fetter of sensual desire,
and having dispelled lust for sense-pleasures—
I was one who had attained the Brahma-world.
There were many hundreds of disciples belonging to them.
Free from the stench of raw flesh, devoted to compassion,
having transcended the fetter of sensual desire,
and having dispelled lust for sense-pleasures—
I was one who had attained the Brahma-world.
These seers who were outsiders were free from passion and concentrated in mind.
The person who, with a corrupt intention, reviles another,
produces much demerit.
Such a person creates demerit.
But he who [gives] to a single bhikkhu endowed with right view,
a disciple of the Buddha—
The person who, with a corrupt intention, reviles another—
this [result] is far greater than that.
A person produces demerit by approaching one who is of virtuous character and who has abandoned the standpoints of false views.
This is called the seventh person of the Noble Saṅgha:
one who is not yet free from passion for sensual pleasures.
For whom the five faculties are dull—
the faculty of faith, mindfulness, energy,
serenity, and insight.
Having assailed such a bhikkhu,
one is first harmed oneself; having harmed oneself, one is then harmed by others.
But later he harms others.
But for one who guards himself,
the external is guarded as well.
Therefore, a wise person should always protect themselves; being unharmed, they remain steadfast forever.
Thus ends the twelfth [verse].

Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, the Venerable Soṇa was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Cool Grove.
Then, while the Venerable Soṇa was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“Of those disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with energy aroused, I am one of them.
Yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Now there is wealth in my family, and it is possible both to enjoy that wealth and to perform meritorious deeds.
What if I were to abandon the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?”
Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the Venerable Soṇa—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from Vulture Peak Mountain and reappeared in the Cool Grove before the Venerable Soṇa.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The Venerable Soṇa, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side.
As the Venerable Soṇa was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Did it not occur to you, Soṇa, while you were alone in seclusion, this reflection in your mind:
‘Of those disciples of the Blessed One who dwell with energy aroused, I am one of them.
Yet my mind is not liberated from the taints through non-clinging. Now there is wealth in my family, and it is possible both to enjoy that wealth and to perform meritorious deeds.’”
“What do you think, Soṇa, would it not be better for me to renounce the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?”—
“Yes, Bhante.”—
“What do you think, Soṇa?”

“Were you skilled formerly, when you were a householder, in the tuning of the strings of the lute?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”—“What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were too tight, was your lute at that time resonant or serviceable?”—“No, venerable sir.”—“What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were too loose, was your lute at that time resonant or serviceable?”—“No, venerable sir.”—“What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute were neither too tight nor too loose, but tuned to be even, was your lute at that time resonant and serviceable?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”—“In the same way, Soṇa, if your energy is over-exerted, that is called ‘tension’ in the Noble Dhamma and Discipline; if your energy is slack, that is called ‘laxity. But when energy is neither over-exerted nor slack, but poised in evenness, that is called ‘the middle way’ in the Noble Dhamma and Discipline.”—“It is wonderful, venerable sir! Then, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after Soṇa the Wanderer had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there is this wanderer named Soṇa who is wise, intelligent, and discerning. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Soṇa replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Soṇa with this instruction—just as a strong man might...
Just as one might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm, even so, having vanished from the Cool Grove,
he reappeared on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then, after some time,
the Venerable Soṇa resolved upon energy and tranquility, penetrated the balance of the faculties, and grasped the sign therein.

realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness; having attained it, he dwelt therein.

Then, when the Venerable Soṇa had attained arahantship, this thought occurred to him:
“What if I were now to approach the Blessed One; having approached, I would declare final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One.

Then the Venerable Soṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Soṇa said this to the Blessed One:

“Bhante, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is intent upon six things:

he is intent upon renunciation, he is intent upon seclusion, he is intent upon non-affliction, he is intent upon the destruction of craving, he is intent upon the destruction of clinging, and he is intent upon non-delusion.
Now, Bhante, it may be that some venerable one here might think thus:”
‘Surely this venerable one, relying on mere faith alone, is intent upon renunciation.
But, Bhante, it should not be viewed in that way.
Bhante, this bhikkhu is one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done, and who perceives nothing further for himself to do.
Through the destruction of what has been accumulated, he is intent on renunciation because of being free from lust through the destruction of lust;
he is intent on renunciation because of being free from hatred through the destruction of hatred; he is intent on renunciation because of being free from delusion through the destruction of delusion.
It may be, venerable sir, that some venerable one here might think thus:
‘Surely this venerable one, desiring gain, honor, and praise, is intent on seclusion.
But, Bhante, it should not be viewed in that way.
For a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life and accomplished what was to be done, does not perceive anything further to be done for himself.
Through the destruction of lust, by being free from lust, he is intent on seclusion;
through the destruction of hatred, by being free from hatred, he is intent on seclusion; through the destruction of delusion, by being free from delusion, he is intent on seclusion.
It may be, venerable sir, that some venerable one here might think thus:
‘Surely this venerable one, returning to the core of attachment to rules and observances, is intent on non-affliction.
But, Bhante, it should not be viewed in that way.
For a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life and accomplished what was to be done, does not perceive anything further to be done for himself.
Through the destruction of what has been accumulated, by being free from lust due to the destruction of lust, he is intent upon non-affliction;
by being free from hatred due to the destruction of hatred, he is intent upon non-affliction; by being free from delusion due to the destruction of delusion, he is intent upon non-affliction.

Through the destruction of lust, by being free from lust, through the destruction of craving, he is intent upon the destruction of craving; through the destruction of hatred, by being free from hatred, through the destruction of craving, he is intent upon the destruction of craving; through the destruction of delusion, by being free from delusion, through the destruction of craving, he is intent upon the destruction of craving.

Through the destruction of lust and being free from lust, he is intent upon the destruction of clinging; through the destruction of hatred and being free from hatred, he is intent upon the destruction of clinging; through the destruction of delusion and being free from delusion, he is intent upon the destruction of clinging.

Through the destruction of lust and being free from lust, he is intent upon non-delusion; through the destruction of hatred and being free from hatred, he is intent upon non-delusion; through the destruction of delusion and being free from delusion, he is intent upon non-delusion.
"Venerable sir, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of his vision, they do not overwhelm his mind.
His mind remains unmixed, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its vanishing.
Even if powerful sounds cognizable by the ear..."
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body...
When mental phenomena come into the range of his mind, they do not overwhelm his consciousness.
His consciousness remains unmixed, stable, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.
Just as if, venerable sir, there were a solid rock, without cracks, without holes, a single mass.
Then, even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would not cause it to shake, nor cause it to tremble, nor cause it to quiver;

and even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the western direction… even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the northern direction… even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the southern direction, it would not cause it to shake, nor cause it to tremble, nor cause it to quiver.
"In the same way, Bhante, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of his vision, they do not overwhelm his mind.
His mind remains unmixed, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.
Even if powerful sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on for the other sense objects]."
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body...
When mental phenomena cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, they do not overwhelm his consciousness.
His consciousness remains unmixed, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its passing away.
For one who is intent upon renunciation...
And solitude of mind;
for one intent on non-affliction and the destruction of clinging.
For one who is intent on the destruction of craving and possesses an undeluded mind,
having seen the arising of the sense-bases,
The mind is rightly liberated.
For that bhikkhu whose mind is rightly liberated and tranquil, [there is no further state].
For him there is no further accumulation;
nothing more remains to be done.
Like a solid mass of rock, he stands firm.
It is not stirred by the wind;
even so are all forms, tastes, sounds,
smells, and tactile objects.
Desirable things and undesirable things do not shake one who is such-like;
his mind is steady and fully liberated.
"And we shall observe her. First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.56

6. Mahāvagga Phaggunasutta (AN 6.56, PTS AN iii 379) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Phagguna approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Phagguna, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks to treat him with contempt. What five? Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu is unlearned, has bad friends, is lazy, is unmindful, and lacks wisdom. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks to treat him with contempt. But when a bhikkhu is possessed of five other qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks not to treat him with contempt. What five? Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu is learned, has good friends, is energetic, is mindful, and possesses wisdom. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, it is fitting for his fellow monks not to treat him with contempt. When this was said, the Venerable Phagguna said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how should a bhikkhu who is unlearned dwell so as to become learned? “Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu who is unlearned should dwell thus: ‘I shall be respectful toward the Teacher; I shall be respectful toward the Dhamma; I shall be respectful toward the Saṅgha; I shall be respectful toward the training; I shall be respectful toward concentration. It is in this way, Phagguna, that a bhikkhu who is unlearned should dwell so as to become learned. “And how, Phagguna, does a bhikkhu who has bad friends become one who has good friends? Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu who has bad friends should dwell thus: ‘I shall be respectful toward my preceptors; I shall be respectful toward my teachers; I shall be respectful toward those senior bhikkhus who are my elders; I shall be respectful toward those bhikkhus of middle standing who are my seniors; I shall be respectful toward those junior bhikkhus who are my juniors. It is in this way, Phagguna, that a bhikkhu who has bad friends becomes one who has good friends. “And how, Phagguna, does a bhikkhu who is lazy become energetic? Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu who is lazy should dwell thus: ‘I shall be energetic in abandoning unwholesome states and arousing wholesome states; I shall be steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the duty of cultivating wholesome states. It is in this way, Phagguna, that a bhikkhu who is lazy becomes energetic. “And how, Phagguna, does a bhikkhu who is unmindful become mindful? Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu who is unmindful should dwell thus: ‘I shall be mindful and clearly comprehending while walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or keeping silent. It is in this way, Phagguna, that a bhikkhu who is unmindful becomes mindful. “And how, Phagguna, does a bhikkhu who lacks wisdom become wise? Here, Phagguna, a bhikkhu who lacks wisdom should dwell thus: ‘I shall be intent on hearing the Dhamma; I shall attend carefully to the Dhamma that has been heard; I shall examine the meaning of the Dhamma that has been attended to; I shall practice in accordance with the Dhamma whose meaning has been examined. It is in this way, Phagguna, that a bhikkhu who lacks wisdom becomes wise. When this was said, the Venerable Phagguna said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! The Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways, as though he were turning upright what had been overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. We go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. Let us receive the going forth under the Blessed One; let us receive the full admission. Then the Venerable Phagguna received the going forth under the Blessed One; he received the full admission. And soon, not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Phagguna, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Phagguna became one of the arahants.
Now at that time, the Venerable Phagguna was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Phagguna is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill."
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would approach the Venerable Phagguna out of compassion.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then, having emerged from seclusion in the evening, the Blessed One approached the Venerable Phagguna.
The Venerable Phagguna saw the Blessed One coming from afar.
Upon seeing him, he sat up on his couch.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Phagguna:
“Enough, Phagguna; do not lie down on the couch.
Here are seats prepared by others; there I shall sit.
The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared for him.
Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Phagguna:
“I hope it is bearable for you, Phagguna; I hope you are getting by. I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase.
“Venerable sir, it is not bearable for me; I am not getting by. My painful feelings are severe; they are increasing and not subsiding, and their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.”
"Venerable sir, just as if a strong man were to strike one on the head with a sharp spike, even so, venerable sir, violent winds pierce my head.
It is not bearable for me, venerable sir, it is not sustainable. My intense painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
Venerable sir, just as if a strong man were to bind a firm leather strap around one's head as a head-wrap, even so, venerable sir, there is an extreme headache in my head."
"It is not endurable for me, venerable sir; it is not sustainable. My painful feelings are intense; they increase and do not subside; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
Just as if, venerable sir, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice were to cut open a cow’s belly with a sharp carving knife, even so, venerable sir, violent winds cut through my belly."
“Venerable sir, it is not bearable for me, nor am I able to endure it. My painful feelings are intense; they increase and do not subside; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
Just as if, venerable sir, two strong men were to seize a weaker man by both arms and roast him over a pit of glowing embers, so too, venerable sir, there is an exceeding burning in my body.”
“Venerable sir, it is not endurable for me, nor can I maintain myself. My painful feelings are intense; they increase and do not subside; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Phagguna with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Phagguna passed away.
At that time, at the moment of death, his faculties became serene.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Phagguna has passed away not long after the Blessed One had departed."
"And at that time, at the moment of death, his faculties became serene.
"How could it be otherwise, Ānanda? How could the faculties of the bhikkhu Phagguna not have become serene?
For the mind of the bhikkhu Phagguna had not been liberated from the five lower fetters, Ānanda."
Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, his mind was liberated from the five lower fetters.
"Ānanda, there are these six benefits in listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and in examining its meaning at the proper time.
What are the six?"
In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mind is not yet liberated from the five lower fetters.
At that time, at the moment of death, he obtains a vision of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata teaches him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, his mind is liberated from the five lower fetters.
This, Ānanda, is the first benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.
Furthermore, Ānanda, there is the case where a bhikkhu’s mind has not yet been liberated from the five lower fetters.
Thus, at that time of death, one may not indeed obtain a vision of the Tathāgata, but one does obtain a vision of a disciple of the Tathāgata.

That disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, one’s mind is liberated from the five lower fetters.
This, Ānanda, is the second benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mind may not yet be liberated from the five lower fetters.
At that time, at the moment of death, he does not obtain a vision of the Tathāgata, nor does he obtain a vision of a disciple of the Tathāgata.
Moreover, one reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered.
As one thus reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered, the mind is liberated from the five lower fetters.
This, Ānanda, is the third benefit of examining the meaning at the proper time.
In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from the five lower fetters, yet his mind is not yet liberated from the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
At that time, at the moment of death, he obtains a vision of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata teaches him the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and so on... and reveals the holy life.
Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, his mind is liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
This, Ānanda, is the fourth benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mind may be liberated from the five lower fetters, yet his mind is not yet liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
Thus, at that time of death, one does not indeed obtain the sight of the Tathāgata; however, one obtains the sight of a disciple of the Tathāgata.
That disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma—good in the beginning... [and so on] ...he proclaims the holy life that is utterly pure.
Having heard that teaching of the Dhamma, one’s mind is liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions.
This, Ānanda, is the fifth benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu’s mind may be liberated from the five lower fetters, yet his mind is not liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhi*).
At that time of death, he does not obtain a vision of the Tathāgata, nor does he obtain a vision of a disciple of the Tathāgata.
Moreover, one reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered.

As one thus reflects upon, examines, and contemplates with the mind the Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered, the mind is liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the acquisitions (*upadhisaṅkhaya*).
This, Ānanda, is the sixth benefit of examining the meaning at the proper time.
“Ānanda, these are the six benefits of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and investigating its meaning at the proper time.
The second [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.57

6. Mahāvagga Chaḷabhijātisutta (The Discourse on the Six Classes of Beings) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these six classes of beings. What six? “Beings who are born from eggs; beings who are born from wombs; beings who are born from moisture; beings who are spontaneously born; beings who subsist on solid food; and beings who subsist on the food of contact. These, bhikkhus, are the six classes of beings.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, Pūraṇa Kassapa has proclaimed six classes of birth:”

The black class has been described; the blue class has been described; the red class has been described; the yellow class has been described; the white class has been described; and the supremely white class has been described.
In this regard, venerable sir, this is what the black class was described by Pūraṇa Kassapa:
sheep-butchers, pig-butchers, fowlers, deer-hunters, hunters, fishermen, thieves, executioners, prison wardens, and whatever others have cruel occupations.
"In this regard, venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa has designated the blue class as those monks who live on thorns, or whoever else holds the doctrine of action and the doctrine of performance.
In this regard, venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa has designated the red class as the Nigaṇṭhas clad in a single garment.
In this regard, venerable sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa has designated the yellow class as white-robed householders who are disciples of the naked ascetics."
"In this regard, venerable sir, the white class has been described by Pūraṇa Kassapa as the Ājīvakas and Ājīvakinīs.
In this regard, venerable sir, the supreme white class has been described by Pūraṇa Kassapa as Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla.
It is these six classes, venerable sir, that have been described by Pūraṇa Kassapa."
“But, Ānanda, does the whole world authorize Pūraṇa Kassapa to proclaim these six classes of birth?
“No, venerable sir.
It would be just as if a poor man, destitute and penniless, were to have a pit dug against his will and told: ‘Good man, you must eat this flesh and pay the price for it.’”

“In the same way, Ānanda, Pūraṇa Kassapa has proclaimed these six classes of rebirth without the consent of these recluses and brahmins, as would a fool, an incompetent person, one who does not know the field, and one who is unskilled.
But I, Ānanda, proclaim the six classes of rebirth.
Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, Ānanda, are the six classes of birth?”
In this case, Ānanda, someone belonging to the dark class of beings gives birth to a dark state.
But in this case, Ānanda, someone belonging to the dark class of beings gives birth to a bright state.
And in this case, Ānanda, someone belonging to the dark class of beings gives birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright.
But here, Ānanda, some person belonging to the bright class gives birth to a dark state.
But here, Ānanda, some person belonging to the bright class gives birth to a bright state.
But here, Ānanda, some person belonging to the bright class gives birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright.
And how, Ānanda, does one who belongs to a dark birth give birth to a dark state?
Here, Ānanda, a certain person is reborn into a low family— a family of outcasts, or hunters, or bamboo-workers,
or cartwrights, or waste-removers— one that is poor, with little food and drink, where livelihood is difficult, and where...
Food and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty.
Moreover, he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, and afflicted by many diseases; he may be one-eyed, or have a crooked limb, or be lame, or paralyzed on one side;
and he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps.
Thus he engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that one who belongs to the dark class gives birth to a dark state.
And how, Ānanda, does one who belongs to a dark birth-class give birth to a bright phenomenon?
Here, Ānanda, someone is reborn into a low family—a family of caṇḍālas, or [so forth]...
lacking bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
Thus he practices good conduct by body, he practices good conduct by speech, and he practices good conduct by mind.

Having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
In this way, Ānanda, being of dark birth, one gives birth to a bright state.
And how, Ānanda, does one who belongs to a dark birth give birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright?
Here, Ānanda, someone is reborn into a low family—a family of outcasts, or...
[and so on]—and he is ugly, unsightly, and deformed.
Thus, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron-colored robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he abandons the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—
and with his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, he develops the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, becoming free from darkness.
One of dark birth gives birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright. Thus, Ānanda, one who is of dark birth gives birth to Nibbāna, which is neither dark nor bright.
And how, Ānanda, does one who is of bright birth give birth to a dark state?
In this case, Ānanda, a certain person is reborn into a high family— a prominent khattiya family, a prominent brahmin family,
or a prominent householder family— one that is wealthy, with great riches and vast enjoyments, possessing abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and utensils,

and abundant wealth and grain. And he is handsome, pleasing to behold, attractive, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, and a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
Thus he engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that one who belongs to the fair class gives birth to a dark state.
And how, Ānanda, does one who belongs to a bright birth give birth to a bright state?
Here, Ānanda, someone is reborn into a high family—a great khattiya clan...
[and so on] ...abounding in beds, dwellings, and lighting.
Thus he practices good conduct by body, he practices good conduct by speech, and he practices good conduct by mind.

Having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that one who belongs to the bright class gives birth to a bright state.
And how, Ānanda, does one who belongs to a bright birth give birth to the deathless Nibbāna,
which is neither dark nor bright? Here, Ānanda, someone is reborn into a high family— a wealthy khattiya clan, or a wealthy brahmin clan,
or a wealthy householder clan— one that is rich, with great wealth and vast possessions, abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and equipment, and abundant money and grain.

He is handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; he is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned saffron robes, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, he abandons the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom.
With a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are,
one is born into the deathless, the neither-dark-nor-bright Nibbāna. It is in this way, Ānanda, that one who is of bright birth is born into the neither-dark-nor-bright Nibbāna.
"These, Ānanda, are the six classes of birth.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.58

6. Mahāvagga Āsavasutta (AN 6.58, PTS AN iii 387) “Bhikkhus, there are these three taints. What three? The taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the three taints.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What six?
Here, bhikkhus, those taints that are to be abandoned by restraint are abandoned by him through restraint.
Those taints that are to be abandoned by avoidance have been abandoned by avoidance;
those taints that are to be abandoned by endurance have been abandoned by endurance;
those taints that are to be abandoned by evasion have been abandoned by evasion.
Those taints that are to be abandoned by removal have been abandoned by removal;
those taints that are to be abandoned by development have been abandoned by development.
And what, bhikkhus, are the taints that are to be abandoned by restraint, which have been abandoned by restraint?
In this case, monks, a monk dwells reflecting wisely, restrained by the restraint of the faculty of the eye.
For those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise in one who dwells unrestrained in the faculty of the eye do not arise in one who dwells restrained in the faculty of the eye.
Reflecting wisely on the faculty of the ear … the faculty of the nose … the faculty of the tongue … [and so forth].
He dwells restrained by the restraint of the body-faculty ... and the mind-faculty.

For, monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise in one who dwells unrestrained in the restraint of the mind-faculty do not come to be for one who dwells restrained in the restraint of the mind-faculty.
“Monks, these are called the taints that are to be abandoned by restraint, which have been abandoned by restraint.
And what, monks, are the taints that are to be abandoned by careful use, which have been abandoned by careful use?
Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely, uses his robe:”

‘Only for the removal of hunger and thirst, for the warding off of cold and heat, for the warding off of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and only for the purpose of covering the private parts.
Reflecting wisely, he uses almsfood:
‘Neither for amusement, nor for intoxication, nor for smartening, nor for adornment, but only for the maintenance of this body.’
"For the sake of maintaining life, for the cessation of affliction, and for support of the holy life, thinking:
'Thus I shall eliminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
Thus, he uses his lodging after wise reflection.

“Only for the sake of warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; only for the purpose of removing the distress of the climate and delighting in seclusion.
He uses the requisite of medicine and provisions for the sick after wise reflection:
“Only for the sake of warding off arisen afflictive feelings, and for the sake of supreme health.”
"Monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise for one who does not partake [of certain things] do not exist for one who partakes of them.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by partaking, which are abandoned by partaking.
And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by enduring, which are abandoned by enduring?"
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies,
mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; he is patient with abusive and unwelcome modes of speech,
and with arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, and unpleasant.
He is by nature one who endures those things that take away life.
For those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise from not enduring them, bhikkhus, do not exist for him when he endures them.
These, bhikkhus, are called the taints to be abandoned by endurance, which have been abandoned by endurance.
"And what, bhikkhus, are the taints that are to be abandoned by avoidance,
which are abandoned through avoidance? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, avoids a fierce elephant,
avoids a fierce horse, avoids a fierce ox, avoids a fierce dog, [and avoids] a snake, a stump, and a thicket of thorns."
A wise fellow practitioner of the holy life might suspect one who sits in an improper seat,
wanders in an improper resort, or associates with evil friends, of being established in evil states; he,
having reflected thoroughly upon that improper seat, that improper resort, and those evil friends, avoids them.
"Monks, those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise for one who does not avoid [certain things] do not exist for one who avoids them.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by avoidance, which are abandoned through avoidance.
And what, monks, are the taints to be abandoned by dispelling, which are abandoned through dispelling?"

Here, monks, a monk, reflecting thoroughly, does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent. He reflects thoroughly and does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will... an arisen thought of cruelty... [he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent].
Whenever evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
For those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise for one who does not dispel them do not exist for one who dispels them.
These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by dispelling, which have been abandoned through dispelling.
"And what, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by development, which are abandoned by development?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, reflecting wisely, develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment;
reflecting wisely, he develops the investigation-of-dharmas enlightenment factor..."
He develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility …
He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation,

and results in relinquishment. For those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise in one who does not develop them, these taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist in one who develops them in this way.
“Monks, these are called the taints that are to be abandoned by cultivation, which have been abandoned through cultivation.

Possessing these six qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus was the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.59 6. Mahāvagga Dārukammikasutta At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, suppose a carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice were to look at the mark on a piece of wood while it was still held in his hand, and he would see it as clearly as if it were right before his eyes. So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, whatever kind of form—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—he sees all forms as they really are with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, whatever kind of sound... whatever kind of odor... whatever kind of taste... whatever kind of tactile object... whatever kind of mental phenomenon—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—he sees all mental phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a bronze bowl that had been polished, cleaned, and burnished, and it were placed on a stand. When someone looks at their own reflection in it, they would see it as it really is. So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, whatever kind of form... whatever kind of mental phenomenon—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—he sees all mental phenomena as they really are with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, he does not grasp at anything in the world; not grasping, he is not agitated; being unagitated, he personally attains nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nādika in the Brick Hall.

Then the householder Dārukammika approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Dārukammika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, is alms given in your family?
“Alms, venerable sir, are given in my family.”

"But it is to those monks who are forest-dwellers, alms-collectors, wearers of rag-robes, who are either Arahants or have entered the path to Arahantship— that such a gift is given by me, venerable sir, to such monks. "Householder,
this is difficult for you to know, being a layman enjoying sensual pleasures, living with a bed crowded with children,
using Kāsī sandalwood, wearing garlands, scents, and unguents, and possessing gold and silver."
"By judging thus: 'These are arahants' or 'these have attained the path to arahantship.

But if, householder, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose in speech, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and with unrestrained faculties, then for that reason he is to be censured."

If, householder, a bhikkhu who dwells in the forest is not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not talkative, not loose in speech, but is established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and has his sense faculties well-restrained—then he is praiseworthy in that respect.
And if, householder, a bhikkhu who dwells in a village is restless... [and so on].
Thus, in that respect, he is to be blamed.
But if, householder, a bhikkhu dwelling in a village is not restless...
[and so on] ...in that respect, he is to be praised.
If, householder, a bhikkhu who is an almsfood eater is restless...
[as before] ...he is thus to be criticized for that reason.
If, householder, a bhikkhu who is an almsfood eater is not restless... [as before] ...he is thus to be praised for that reason.
In this way, he is praiseworthy for that factor.
But if, householder, a monk who lives on invitations is restless...
[and so forth] ...in this way, he is blameworthy for that factor.
If, householder, a bhikkhu who lives on invitations is not restless...
[as before] ...in that respect he is praiseworthy.
If, householder, a bhikkhu who wears rag-robes is restless... [as before] ...in that respect he is blameworthy.
Thus, he is to be criticized for that factor.
But if, householder, a monk who wears rag-robes is not restless...
[and so on] ...thus he is to be praised for that factor.

“Householder, even if a bhikkhu wears the robe of a householder, if he is restless, arrogant, fickle, talkative, loose in speech, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind,

and with unrestrained faculties, then for that reason he is to be censured. Householder, even if a bhikkhu wears the robe of a householder, if he is not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not talkative, not loose in speech, established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, concentrated, one-pointed in mind, and with restrained faculties, [then for that reason he is to be praised].”
Thus he is praiseworthy in that respect.
Come now, householder, give a gift to the Saṅgha;
as you give the gift to the Saṅgha, your mind will become serene.
“Thus, with a confident mind, at the breaking up of the body, after death, you will be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
“Venerable sir, from this day forward, I shall give alms to the Saṅgha.
The fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.60 6. Mahāvagga Hatthisāriputtasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Hatthisāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Sāriputta, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has reached assurance, one who stands in the presence of the Deathless, and he is incapable of falling back and is certain of reaching the supreme security from bondage. What are the four? Here, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way;

that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped at, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, Sāriputta, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has reached assurance, one who stands in the presence of the Deathless, and he is incapable of falling back and is certain of reaching the supreme security from bondage. When this was said, the Venerable Hatthisāriputta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way has the Blessed One—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. From today let the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Venerable Hatthisāriputta, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Hatthisāriputta had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to live for a hundred years in a forest dwelling, secluded from people, yet without having developed and cultivated the four establishments of mindfulness, he would be one who has lived in vain, not at all fulfilled in this Dhamma and Discipline. But if a bhikkhu were to live for even a single day endowed with the four establishments of mindfulness, having developed and cultivated them, he would be one who has lived meaningfully, truly fulfilled in this Dhamma and Discipline. What are the four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. If a bhikkhu were to live for even a single day endowed with these four establishments of mindfulness, having developed and cultivated them, he would be one who has lived meaningfully, truly fulfilled in this Dhamma and Discipline. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. And while this discourse was being spoken, the Venerable Hatthisāriputta realized the fruit of stream-entry. Thus there arose in the Venerable Hatthisāriputta the vision of the Dhamma, the realization of the Dhamma, the penetration of the Dhamma, the transcendence of doubt, the absence of perplexity, and the attainment of fearlessness, independent of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction. Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, plunged into the Dhamma, having crossed over uncertainty, having dispelled doubt, attaining fearlessness through independence of others regarding the Teacher’s instruction, the Venerable Hatthisāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the Venerable Hatthisāriputta, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that unsurpassed consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt therein. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Hatthisāriputta became one of the arahants. And the Venerable Hatthisāriputta, having become an arahant, soon thereafter approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Sāriputta, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has reached assurance, one who stands in the presence of the Deathless, and he is incapable of falling back and is certain of reaching the supreme security from bondage. What are the four? Here, Sāriputta, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... in the Dhamma... in the Saṅgha... and he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, Sāriputta, he is one who has reached certainty, one who has reached assurance, one who stands in the presence of the Deathless, and he is incapable of falling back and is certain of reaching the supreme security from bondage. When this was said, the Venerable Hatthisāriputta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned... in the same way has the Blessed One made the Dhamma clear. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. From today let the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Venerable Hatthisāriputta, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Hatthisāriputta had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu were to live for a hundred years in a forest dwelling, secluded from people, yet without having developed and cultivated the four establishments of mindfulness, he would be one who has lived in vain, not at all fulfilled in this Dhamma and Discipline. But if a bhikkhu were to live for even a single day endowed with the four establishments of mindfulness, having developed and cultivated them, he would be one who has lived meaningfully, truly fulfilled in this Dhamma and Discipline. What are the four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body... feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. If a bhikkhu were to live for even a single day endowed with these four establishments of mindfulness, having developed and cultivated them, he would be one who has lived meaningfully, truly fulfilled in this Dhamma and Discipline. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. And while this
(AN 6.60, PTS AN iii 392) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Now at that time, after their meal, on returning from their almsround, a number of elder bhikkhus were sitting together and assembled in the pavilion, discussing the Abhidhamma.
There, while the elder bhikkhus were discussing the Abhidhamma, the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta interrupted their discourse from time to time.
Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said this to the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta:
“Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta has interrupted the Abhidhamma discourse while the elder bhikkhus were speaking; let Venerable Citta wait until the conclusion of the talk.
When this was said, the bhikkhus who were companions of Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta said to Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika:
“Let Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika not disparage Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta; Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta is wise.”
“Is the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta capable of delivering a discourse on the Abhidhamma to the elder bhikkhus?
“Friend, it is difficult for those who do not know the ways of others’ minds to understand them.

For instance, friend, a certain person may be as gentle as ever, as humble as ever, and as tranquil as ever, so long as he dwells in dependence upon the Teacher or some other venerable fellow-celibate.”
But when he is indeed shunned by the Teacher and shunned by his venerable fellow-celibates,
he dwells in association with bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers,
and followers of other sects and their disciples.
As he dwells thus associating, trusting, and being intimate with them, intent on idle chatter, lust invades his mind.
With his mind invaded by lust, he abandons the training and reverts to the low life.
It is just as if, friends, a grain-eating ox were bound by a tether or confined in a pen.
“Friend, if someone were to say: ‘This ox that has eaten grain will not return to eat grain again,’ would he, speaking thus, be speaking rightly?
“No, friend.
“Because, friend, it is possible that this ox which has eaten grain might break its tether or burst through the pen and then return once more to eat grain.”

In the same way, friends, here a certain person is as long as he remains dependent upon the Teacher or some venerable companion in the holy life; for that long he is exceedingly gentle, exceedingly humble, and exceedingly tranquil.
But when he is indeed estranged from the Teacher and estranged from his venerable companions in the holy life, [he becomes otherwise].
He dwells in association with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings,
royal ministers, members of other sects,
and followers of other sects. As he dwells thus associated, confident, open, and intent on conversation, lust invades his mind.
Thus, with a mind not uprooted from passion, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
But here, friends, a certain person, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [as above] ... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
He dwells associated with the thought, "I am an attainer of the first jhāna," and he becomes intimate with the monks... [as above] ...
“Having renounced the training, he returns to the lower life.
Suppose, friend, at a crossroads where four great roads meet, a heavy rain were falling, laying the dust to rest and creating a mire.
Would it be correct, friend, for someone to say: ‘Now, at that crossroads, the dust will never appear again’?”
“No, friend.
“Indeed, friend, it is possible that at that crossroads people might pass by, or cattle and goats might pass by, or wind and sun might dry up the moisture, and then the dust would appear once more.
In the same way, friend, here a certain person, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.”
Thus, thinking "I am not an attainer of the first jhāna," he dwells in association with monks...
[and so on] ...he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
But here, friends, a certain person, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... [and so on] ...enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
Thinking, "I have not attained the second jhāna," he dwells in association with monks...
[and so on] ...he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
It is just as if, friends, there were a large pond not far from a village or town.
"In that case, a rain of large drops has fallen, which could even obliterate the shells of snails and pebbles and gravel.
Now, friend, if someone were to say: 'Never again will shells of snails or pebbles and gravel appear in that pond,' would he, speaking thus, be speaking correctly, friend?
"Certainly not, friend."

“Indeed, friends, it is possible that people might drink from that pond, or cattle and goats might drink from it, or the wind and sun might dry up its moisture, and then again shells, snails, gravel, and pebbles would reappear.

In the same way, friends, here a certain person, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna... [as before]... which is born of concentration and filled with rapture and happiness.”
Thus, thinking, "I am not an attainer of the second jhāna," he dwells in association with monks...
[and so on] ...he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
But here, friends, a certain person, with the fading away of rapture... enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
Thinking, "I am not an attainer of the third jhāna," he dwells in association with the bhikkhus...
[and so on] ...he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
Just as, friends, a man who has eaten a fine meal would have no appetite for food left over from the previous day.
"Friend, if someone were to say: 'That man will not now desire food again,' would he, speaking thus, be speaking rightly?
"Certainly not, friend.
"For it is possible, friend, that after that man has eaten choice food, as long as its nutritive essence remains in his body, he will not desire other food."
"And when that nutritive essence disappears from him, then he will find that food to his liking once again.
In the same way, friends, here a certain person, with the fading away of rapture... enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
He dwells mingled with the bhikkhus, thinking, "I am an attainer of the third jhāna," and so forth.
Having renounced the training, he reverts to the lower life.
But here, friends, a certain person, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain... [as above] ...enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He dwells associated with the monks, thinking: "I am an attainer of the fourth jhāna."... [as above] ...
“Having renounced the training, he returns to the lower life.
Suppose, friend, there were a lake in a mountain cleft, sheltered and free from waves.

Now, friend, would it be correct for someone to say: ‘Now, no more waves will ever appear in that lake’? “No, friend. Why is that? Because the conditions for the arising of waves still exist there; therefore, it would not be correct to say that.”
“No, friend.
“Indeed, friend, it is possible that a violent wind and rain might come from the eastern direction and create waves in that lake.
That which might come from the western direction... [and so on] ...that which might come from the northern direction...”
“Suppose, friend, a violent rainstorm with wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction … or it were to come from the southern direction; would it create waves in that lake?
“In the same way, friend, here a certain person, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He dwells associated [with others], thinking: ‘I am an attainer of the fourth jhāna,’ and he dwells in association with the bhikkhus …” [and so on].
Having renounced the training, he reverts to the lower life.
But here, friends, a certain person, through non-attention to all signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind.

He dwells in association with others, thinking, "I am an attainer of the signless concentration of mind," associating with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, and followers of other sects and their disciples.
As he dwells thus associating, trusting, and being intimate with them, intent on conversation, lust invades his mind.
With his mind invaded by lust, he abandons the training and reverts to the lower life.
It is just as if, friends, a king or a royal minister traveling along a highway with a fourfold army were to take up residence for one night in a certain forest grove.

“In that case, suppose the sound of the *cīrika* were to be eclipsed by the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of infantry, and the resounding noise of kettledrums, tabors, conchs, and tom-toms.
Now, friend, if someone were to say: ‘The sound of the *cīrika* will never again appear in that forest grove,’ would he, friend, be speaking correctly?
“Certainly not, friend.”
“Friend, it is possible that the king or the royal minister might depart from that grove, and then the sound of the drum would appear once again.
In the same way, friend, here some person, through non-attention to all signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind.

Yet, thinking, ‘I am an attainer of the signless concentration of mind,’ he dwells in association with bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, and with members of other sects and their disciples.”
“As he dwells associating with them, trusting them, and being intimate with them, intent on conversation, lust invades his mind.
With his mind invaded by lust, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
Then, at a later time, the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta renounced the training and reverted to the lower life.
Then the monks who were companions of Citta Hatthisāriputta approached the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika. Having approached, they said this to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika:
"Did the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika encompass Citta Hatthisāriputta’s mind with his own mind and know:
‘Citta Hatthisāriputta possesses these and those meditative attainments, yet he will nevertheless renounce the training and return to the lower life’?"
“Or did deities inform you of this matter:
‘Venerable sir, Citta Hatthisāriputta is a recipient of these and those dwellings and attainments, yet he will renounce the training and return to the lower life’?
“I have known it, friend, by encompassing his mind with my own mind.”
‘Citta Hatthisāriputta has attained these and those meditative dwellings and attainments, yet he will nevertheless renounce the training and return to the lower life.
Deities too have informed me of this matter:
‘Venerable sir, Citta Hatthisāriputta has attained these and those meditative dwellings and attainments, yet he will nevertheless renounce the training and return to the lower life.’”
Then the monks who were companions of Citta Hatthisāriputta approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, Citta Hatthisāriputta is a recipient of these and those meditative dwellings and attainments, yet he has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
“Bhikkhus, Citta will not long remember his renunciation,” the Blessed One said.
