Then, before long, Citta Hatthisāriputta shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta, in no long time,

realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which young men of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness; and having attained it, he dwelt therein.
“Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Citta Hatthisāriputta became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the sixth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.61 6. Mahāvagga Majjhesutta “Monks, there are these five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is not well-versed in the Dhamma—the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, which reveals the perfectly complete and pure holy life (brahmacariya). He does not teach the Dhamma to others as he has learned it and mastered it. This is the first thing that leads to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu does not associate with elders, those of long standing, long ordained, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha; he does not attend upon them to inquire about their health or ask after their well-being. This is the second thing that leads to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu does not live in accordance with the training rules, he is not accomplished in virtuous behavior, and he does not train in the training rules of the bhikkhus. This is the third thing that leads to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is not one who delights in meditation, who takes pleasure in meditation, who finds joy in meditation, who is intent on meditation, and who makes meditation his primary concern. This is the fourth thing that leads to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu does not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind (adhicitta) and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the fifth thing that leads to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. There are, monks, these five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is well-versed in the Dhamma—the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, which reveals the perfectly complete and pure holy life. He teaches the Dhamma to others as he has learned it and mastered it. This is the first thing that leads to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu associates with elders, those of long standing, long ordained, fathers and leaders of the Saṅgha; he attends upon them to inquire about their health and ask after their well-being. This is the second thing that leads to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu lives in accordance with the training rules, he is accomplished in virtuous behavior, and he trains in the training rules of the bhikkhus. This is the third thing that leads to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is one who delights in meditation, who takes pleasure in meditation, who finds joy in meditation, who is intent on meditation, and who makes meditation his primary concern. This is the fourth thing that leads to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the fifth thing that leads to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness.”
(AN 6.61, PTS AN iii 399) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Now at that time, after their meal, when they had returned from almsround, a large number of elder bhikkhus were sitting together and assembled in the pavilion, and this discussion arose among them:
"Friends, this was said by the Blessed One in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Metteyya* questions:
'He who, having understood both ends...'"
In the midst of it, the wise one is not defiled;
him I call a great man,
who has sewn up the wound and transcended death.”
“Friends, what is one end? What is the second end? What is the middle? And what is the seamstress?
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to those elder bhikkhus:
“Contact, friends, is one end; the arising of contact is the second end; the cessation of contact is the middle; and craving is the seamstress.”
"For craving indeed sews him on to the production of this or that state of existence.

To this extent, friends, a bhikkhu directly knows what is to be directly known; he fully understands what is to be fully understood. Directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to those elder bhikkhus:
“The past, friend, is one end; the future is the second end; the present is the middle; and craving is the seamstress.
For craving sews one to the production of this or that state of existence.

To this extent, friend, a bhikkhu directly knows what is to be directly known, fully understands what is to be fully understood; and by directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to those elder bhikkhus:
"Friends, pleasant feeling is one extreme, painful feeling is the second extreme, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the middle. Craving is the seamstress;
for craving sews one to the production of this or that state of existence."

"To this extent, friends, a bhikkhu directly knows what is to be directly known, fully understands what is to be fully understood; and by directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to those elder bhikkhus:
"Name, friends, is one extreme; form is the second extreme; consciousness is in between; and craving is the seamstress."
"For craving sews him down to the production of this or that very becoming.

To this extent, friends, a bhikkhu directly knows what is to be directly known; he fully understands what is to be fully understood. Directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to those elder bhikkhus:
“Friend, there are six internal sense bases as one end, and six external sense bases as the second end; consciousness is in the middle, and craving is the seamstress.
For craving sews this [being] together for the production of this or that state of existence.

To this extent, friend, a bhikkhu directly knows what is to be directly known, fully understands what is to be fully understood; and by directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.”
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to those elder bhikkhus:
"Personal existence, friends, is one extreme; the origin of personal existence is the second extreme; the cessation of personal existence is the middle;
and craving is the seamstress, for it is craving that sews one to the production of this or that state of existence."

"To this extent, friends, a bhikkhu directly knows what is to be directly known, fully understands what is to be fully understood; and by directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to those elder bhikkhus:
"Friends, we have all given our explanations according to our own inspiration."
"Come, friends, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we will report this matter to the Blessed One.
We will bear it in mind exactly as the Blessed One explains it.
"So be it, friend," those elder bhikkhus replied to that bhikkhu.
Then the elder bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting there, the elder bhikkhus reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place among them all.
"Venerable sir, who spoke well? they asked.
“Bhikkhus, all that you have spoken is well-spoken from one perspective. However, it was with reference to this that I spoke in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Metteyya* questions:
‘The wise one who, having understood both ends, is not stained by the middle;’”
“Him I call a Great Man, who has transcended the seamstress.
Listen to that; attend closely, and I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those elder bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Contact, bhikkhus, is one end; the arising of contact is the second end; the cessation of contact is the middle; craving is the seamstress.”
For craving sews one on to the production of this or that very becoming.

To this extent, monks, a monk directly knows what is to be directly known; he fully understands what is to be fully understood. Directly knowing what is to be directly known and fully understanding what is to be fully understood, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. Thus ends the seventh [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.62 6. Mahāvagga Purisindriyañāṇasutta: The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Faculties of a Man “Bhikkhus, there are these five faculties. What five? The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

These, bhikkhus, are the five faculties. “Now, bhikkhus, as to how one knows the faculties of a man: Here, bhikkhus, a man possesses the faculty of faith, but he does not possess the faculty of energy; he does not possess the faculty of mindfulness, nor the faculty of concentration, nor the faculty of wisdom. One who knows him thus knows the faculties of that man. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a man possesses the faculty of faith and the faculty of energy, but he does not possess the faculty of mindfulness, nor the faculty of concentration, nor the faculty of wisdom. One who knows him thus knows the faculties of that man. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a man possesses the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, and the faculty of mindfulness, but he does not possess the faculty of concentration, nor the faculty of wisdom. One who knows him thus knows the faculties of that man. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a man possesses the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of concentration, but he does not possess the faculty of wisdom. One who knows him thus knows the faculties of that man. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a man possesses the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. One who knows him thus knows the faculties of that man. These, bhikkhus, are the five faculties. And as to how one knows the faculties of a man, it is by this that one knows them.”
(AN 6.62, PTS AN iii 402) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, arrived at a Kosalan market town named Daṇḍakappaka.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, sat down on a seat prepared at the foot of a certain tree.
Those monks entered Daṇḍakappaka to search for lodgings.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with a number of monks, approached the Aciravatī River to bathe his limbs.
Having bathed his limbs in the river Aciravatī and come out, he stood there, wearing only a single robe, drying his limbs.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:
"Friend Ānanda, did the Blessed One declare concerning Devadatta after having fully considered everything with his mind?"
“Is it said that ‘Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell, staying there for an eon, incurable,’ or is it said so by some particular method?
“It was indeed in this way, friend, that this was declared by the Blessed One.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, I approached the river Aciravatī together with a number of bhikkhus in order to bathe my limbs.
Having bathed my limbs in the river Aciravatī and come back out, I stood wearing a single robe while drying my limbs.
Then, Bhante, a certain bhikkhu approached me; having approached, he said this to me:”
“‘Friend Ānanda, did the Blessed One declare that Devadatta was destined for the states of deprivation,
destined for hell, staying there for an eon, incurable, having fully considered everything with his mind, or was it by some particular method?
When this was said, Bhante, I said this to that bhikkhu:”
“Indeed, friend, it was declared thus by the Blessed One.
“Ānanda, that monk must either be a newcomer who has recently gone forth, or else an elder who is foolish and incompetent.
How can he fall into doubt regarding that which I have declared categorically?”
"Ānanda, I do not see any other single person whom I have so fully considered with my whole mind and declared as I have Devadatta.
And as long as I, Ānanda, saw even a hair-tip’s worth of a white dhamma in Devadatta,
I did not yet declare of Devadatta:"
‘Devadatta is destined for the states of misery, destined for hell, staying there for an eon, incurable.
But, Ānanda, when I did not see even a hair-tip’s worth of a bright quality in Devadatta, only then did I declare of him: [that he was destined for the states of misery...]”
“Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell, staying there for an eon,
incurable. Ānanda, it is just as if there were a cesspit more than a man’s height deep, full of excrement and brimming to the top,
and a man were submerged in it up to his head.
Suppose a certain man were to appear who, desiring his welfare, desiring his benefit, and desiring his security from bondage, wished to pull him out from that cesspit.
As he walked all around that cesspit, he would not see even a spot the size of the tip of a single hair, untouched by filth, where he might take hold of him and pull him out.
In the same way, Ānanda, since I did not see even a spot the size of the tip of a single hair of Devadatta’s that was free of white dhammas (wholesome qualities);
Then, Ānanda, I declared of Devadatta:
“Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation, for hell; he is fixed for an eon and incurable.
If you would listen, Ānanda, I shall analyze the Tathāgata’s knowledges regarding the faculties of men.
“Now is the time for this, Blessed One;
now is the time for this, Sugata, that the Blessed One should analyze the knowledges of the faculties of a person. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will retain it in mind.
“In that case, Ānanda, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, Ānanda, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I understand it thus:”
‘In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states are present.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘In this person, the wholesome states have disappeared and unwholesome states have become manifest.’
‘Indeed, there exists in him a root of the wholesome that is not severed; from that wholesome, further wholesomeness will manifest for him.
Thus this person will, in the future, be of a nature not subject to decline.
It is just as if, Ānanda, there were seeds—unbroken, unrotted, undamaged by wind or sun, fertile, well-preserved—placed in a well-tilled field of excellent soil.
“Ānanda, would you know that these seeds will reach growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Ānanda, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:”
‘In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states are present.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘In this person, wholesome states have disappeared and unwholesome states have become manifest.’
‘Indeed, there is a root of the wholesome in him that is not yet severed; from that wholesome, further wholesomeness will manifest for him.
Thus this person will be of a nature not to decline in the future.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the mind of that person with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the faculties of a person is known by him through encompassing mind with mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s arising of states in the future is known by him through encompassing mind with mind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, here I understand a certain person thus by encompassing mind with mind:
‘Indeed, both wholesome and unwholesome states exist in this person.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘Indeed, the unwholesome states have vanished from this person, and wholesome states have become manifest.’
‘There is, however, a root of unwholesomeness in him that has not been severed; from that unwholesome root, further unwholesomeness will manifest for him.
Thus this person will be subject to decline in the future.
It is just as if, Ānanda, there were seeds—unbroken, undecayed, not damaged by wind or sun, fertile, well-preserved—placed upon a flat stone.
“Ānanda, would you know that these seeds will not reach growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Ānanda, having encompassed the mind with my own mind, I understand of a certain person here:”
‘In this person, both wholesome and unwholesome states are present.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘In this person, unwholesome states have disappeared and wholesome states have become manifest.’
"And yet, there is a root of unwholesomeness in him that has not been severed; from that unwholesome root, further unwholesomeness will manifest for him.
Thus, this person will be subject to decline in the future.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has discerned the mind of that individual with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the faculties of a person is known by him through encompassing mind with mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s arising of phenomena in the future is known by him through encompassing mind with mind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, here I understand a certain person thus by encompassing mind with mind:
‘In this person, indeed, both wholesome states and unwholesome states exist.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘In this person there is not even a speck of white (wholesome) state as small as the tip of a hair; he is possessed of—’
‘This person, because of entirely dark unwholesome states, with the breakup of the body, after death,
will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, downfall, or hell.
It is just as if, Ānanda, seeds that are broken, rotten, and ruined by wind and sun were placed in a fertile field that has been well-prepared.
“Ānanda, would you know that these seeds will not attain growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Ānanda, having encompassed the mind of a certain person here with my own mind, I understand:”
‘In this person, indeed, both wholesome states and unwholesome states exist.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘In this person there is not even a hair-tip’s worth of a bright state; he is possessed of—’
‘This person, because of entirely dark unwholesome states, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of deprivation,
a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the mind of that person by encompassing their mind with his own mind.
“In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the faculties of men has been understood by him through his own mind as he encompassed their minds with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s arising of phenomena in the future has been understood by him through his own mind as he encompassed their minds with his own mind.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Is it possible, Bhante, for three other persons who are counterparts to these three persons to be designated?
“It is possible, Ānanda,” the Blessed One said.
“In this case, Ānanda, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I understand him thus:”
‘In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states are present.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘In this person, wholesome states have disappeared and unwholesome states have become manifest.’
‘There is indeed a root of the wholesome in him that has not been cut off, yet even that will be completely eradicated.
Thus this person will be subject to decline in the future.
It is just as if, Ānanda, embers that are burning, blazing, and glowing were placed upon a large stone.
“Would you know, Ānanda, that these embers will not reach growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, Bhante.
“Or again, Ānanda, as the sun is setting in the evening, would you know, Ānanda, that the light will disappear and darkness will appear?”
“Yes, Bhante.
“Or again, Ānanda, suppose it were at midnight, at the time for a meal after the sun has risen; would you know, Ānanda, that the light has disappeared and darkness has appeared?
“Yes, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Ānanda, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:
‘In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states exist.
Then, at a later time, I encompass his mind with my own mind and understand:”
‘In this person, wholesome states have disappeared and unwholesome states have become manifest.
Although there is still a root of the wholesome that has not been cut off, even that will be completely eradicated.
Thus, this person will be subject to decline in the future.’”
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the mind of a person by encompassing it with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the knowledge of a person’s faculties by encompassing it with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the future arising of phenomena by encompassing it with his own mind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus:
"In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states exist.
Then, at a later time, I understand him by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus: [that he has become established in wholesome states].
‘In this person, unwholesome states have disappeared and wholesome states have become manifest.
Although there is still a root of the unwholesome that has not been severed, even that will be completely eradicated.
Thus, this person will be of a nature not to decline in the future.’”
“Ānanda, suppose embers that are burning, blazing, and glowing were placed upon a heap of dry grass or a heap of wood.
Would you know, Ānanda, that these embers will attain growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Or again, Ānanda, just as at the time of dawn when the sun is rising, would you know, ‘Ānanda, the darkness will vanish and light will appear’?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Or again, Ānanda, just as at midday, at the hour of eating when the sun is overhead, would you know, ‘Ānanda, the darkness has vanished and light has appeared’?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Ānanda, here I encompass the mind of a certain person with my own mind and understand:
‘In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states are present.’”
At a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand of him:
"In this person, unwholesome states have disappeared and wholesome states have become manifest.
Although there is still a root of the unwholesome that has not been severed, even that will be completely eradicated."
"In this way, this person will be of a nature not subject to decline in the future.
In this manner too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the mind of that person by encompassing their mind with his own mind.
In this manner too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the faculties of that person has been understood by him through encompassing their mind with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata’s future arising of states is known by him through having encompassed mind with mind.
Furthermore, Ānanda, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind:
‘In this person, both wholesome states and unwholesome states are present.’”
At a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand of him:
"In this person there is not even a hair’s tip worth of unwholesome state; this person is endowed with entirely bright and blameless states, and he will attain final Nibbāna in this very life.
It is just as if, Ānanda, embers that are cold and extinguished were placed upon a heap of dry grass or a heap of wood.
“Would you know, Ānanda, that these embers will not reach growth, increase, and abundance?
“Yes, Bhante.
“In the same way, Ānanda, having encompassed the mind with my own mind, I understand a certain person here thus:”
‘In this person, both wholesome and unwholesome states exist.
Then, at a later time, having encompassed his mind with my own mind, I understand:

‘In this person there is not even a hair’s tip’s worth of an unwholesome state; this person is endowed with exclusively bright and blameless states, and he will attain final nibbāna in this very life.’
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the mind of a person by encompassing it with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the knowledge of a person’s faculties by encompassing it with his own mind.
In this way too, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has understood the future arising of phenomena by encompassing it with his own mind.

“In this regard, Ānanda, among those three persons mentioned first, one person is of a nature not to fall away, one is of a nature to fall away, and one is destined for states of deprivation, bound for hell.
In this regard, Ānanda, among these latter three persons, one is of a nature to fall away, one is of a nature not to fall away, and one is of a nature to attain final Nibbāna.
Thus was the eighth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63 6.

Mahāvagga Nibbedhikasutta (The Discourse on Penetration) “Bhikkhus, there are these six penetrations. What six? Penetration by means of faith, penetration by means of personal experience, penetration by means of learning, penetration by means of noble silence, penetration by means of view, and penetration by means of liberation. These, bhikkhus, are the six penetrations.”
“Monks, I will teach you a discourse on the Dhamma that is penetrative.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is that penetrative exposition of the Dhamma?

“Bhikkhus, sensual pleasures are to be understood; the source and origin of sensual pleasures is to be understood; the diversity of sensual pleasures is to be understood; the result of sensual pleasures is to be understood; the cessation of sensual pleasures is to be understood; and the practice leading to the cessation of sensual pleasures is to be understood.
“Feeling, bhikkhus, is to be understood; the source and origin of feelings is to be understood; the diversity of feelings is to be understood; the result of feelings is to be understood;
the cessation of feelings is to be understood; and the practice leading to the cessation of feelings is to be understood.”
“Monks, perception is to be understood; the source and origin of perceptions is to be understood; the diversity of perceptions is to be understood; the result of perceptions is to be understood;
the cessation of perceptions is to be understood; and the practice leading to the cessation of perceptions is to be understood.
Monks, the taints are to be understood; the source and origin of the taints is to be understood; the diversity of the taints [is to be understood].”

The taints are to be understood; the ripening of the taints is to be understood; the cessation of the taints is to be understood; the practice leading to the cessation of the taints is to be understood.
Action, monks, is to be understood; the source and origin of actions is to be understood; the diversity of actions is to be understood;
the ripening of actions is to be understood; the cessation of action is to be understood; the practice leading to the cessation of action is to be understood.
“Bhikkhus, suffering is to be understood; the origin and arising of suffering is to be understood; the diversity of suffering is to be understood; the result of suffering is to be understood;
the cessation of suffering is to be understood; and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is to be understood.
‘Sensual pleasures, bhikkhus, are to be understood; the origin and arising of sensual pleasures is to be understood; the diversity of sensual pleasures is to be understood;”

‘Sensual pleasures are to be understood, the result of sensual pleasures is to be understood, the cessation of sensual pleasures is to be understood, and the practice leading to the cessation of sensual pleasures is to be understood’— this is what was said.
With reference to what was this said?
“Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure:
forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear …”
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
Moreover, monks, these are not the sensual pleasures, nor are these the strands of sensual pleasure that are called "sensual pleasures" in the discipline of the Noble One:
"A man's sensual pleasure is lustful intention;
those variegated things in the world are not sensual pleasures."
The desire of a person is the passion of intention;
the various [objects] remain just as they are in the world.
Yet, herein, the wise subdue their longing.
"And what, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of sensual pleasures?
Contact, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of sensual pleasures.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of sensual pleasures?"
“Bhikkhus, the desire for forms is one thing, the desire for sounds is another, the desire for odors is another, the desire for tastes is another, and the desire for tangibles is another.
This, bhikkhus, is called the diversity of desires.
And what, bhikkhus, is the ripening of desires?”
“Bhikkhus, whatever state of selfhood one produces by desiring—whether partaking of merit or partaking of demerit—this, bhikkhus, is called the result of sensual desires.
And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of sensual desires?
The cessation of contact, bhikkhus, is the cessation of sensual desires.”
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of sensual desires; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When, monks, a noble disciple understands sensual desires in this way, and understands the source and origin of sensual desires in this way...

He understands; thus he understands the diversity of sensual pleasures, thus he understands the result of sensual pleasures, thus he understands the cessation of sensual pleasures, and thus he understands the practice leading to the cessation of sensual pleasures. He understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of sensual pleasures.
“Sensual pleasures, bhikkhus, are to be understood … [as before] … the practice leading to the cessation of sensual pleasures is to be understood;
it is with reference to this that it was said.
Feeling, bhikkhus, is to be understood … [as before] … the practice leading to the cessation of feeling is to be understood.”
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
There are these three feelings, monks:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
And what, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of feelings?
Contact, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of feelings.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of feelings?
“Monks, there is pleasant feeling that is worldly; there is pleasant feeling that is unworldly.
There is painful feeling that is worldly; there is painful feeling that is unworldly. There is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is worldly;
there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is unworldly.”
This, monks, is called the diversity of feelings.
And what, monks, is the ripening of feelings?
That which, when one feels it, produces a corresponding personal existence—whether partaking of merit or partaking of demerit.
This, monks, is called the ripening of feelings.
And what, monks, is the cessation of feelings?
The cessation of contact, monks, is the cessation of feelings.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, namely:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, monks, a noble disciple understands feeling in this way, and understands the source and origin of feelings in this way, [he is called a noble disciple].
He understands thus; he understands the diversity of feelings; he understands the result of feelings;
he understands the cessation of feelings; he understands the way leading to the cessation of feelings.
He understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of feelings.
“Feeling, bhikkhus, should be understood... the way leading to the cessation of feeling should be understood.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
“Perception, bhikkhus, should be understood... the way leading to the cessation of perception should be understood.”
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
There are these six perceptions, monks:
the perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of odors, the perception of tastes, the perception of tangibles, and the perception of mental phenomena.
And what, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of perceptions?
Contact, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of perceptions.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of perceptions?

"Bhikkhus, perception of forms is one thing, perception of sounds is another, perception of odors is another, perception of tastes is another, perception of tangibles is another, and perception of mental phenomena is another.
This, bhikkhus, is called the diversity of perceptions.
And what, bhikkhus, is the result of perceptions?"
“Monks, I say that perception ripens into conventional expression.
In whatever way one perceives, in that very way one expresses: ‘I was percipient thus.
This, monks, is called the ripening of perceptions.”
And what, monks, is the cessation of perception?
The cessation of contact, monks, is the cessation of perception.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of perception; that is to say: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view... [right intention] ... right concentration.

When, monks, a noble disciple understands perception in this way, understands the source and origin of perceptions in this way, understands the diversity of perceptions in this way, and understands the result of perceptions in this way—
One understands the cessation of perception; thus one understands the practice leading to the cessation of perception.
One understands this penetrative holy life, which is the cessation of perception.
"Perception, monks, should be understood... the practice leading to the cessation of perception should be understood."
Thus, that which was said—"Monks, the taints are to be known...
the way leading to the cessation of the taints is to be known"—this is said with reference to this.
With reference to what was this said?
“Monks, there are three taints:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.
And what, monks, is the source and origin of the taints?”
Ignorance, monks, is the source and origin of the taints.
And what, monks, is the diversity of the taints?

There are, monks, taints leading to rebirth in hell; there are taints leading to rebirth in the animal realm; there are taints leading to the sphere of hungry ghosts; there are taints leading to the human world; and there are taints leading to the world of the devas.
"This, monks, is called the diversity of the taints.
And what, monks, is the ripening of the taints?
Whatever selfhood one who is immersed in ignorance produces—whether partaking of merit or partaking of demerit—that, monks, is called the ripening of the taints."
And what, monks, is the cessation of the taints?
The cessation of ignorance, monks, is the cessation of the taints.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of the taints; that is to say: [the rest of the eight factors].
Right view ... right concentration.

When, monks, a noble disciple understands the taints in this way, understands the origin and source of the taints in this way, understands the diversity of the taints in this way, and understands the result of the taints in this way—
One understands the cessation of the taints; thus one understands the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.
One understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of the taints.
"The taints, monks, are to be known... the practice leading to the cessation of the taints is to be known."
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
"Action, monks, is to be understood... [and so on] ...the practice leading to the cessation of action is to be understood"—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?
“Bhikkhus, I say that volition is action.
Having willed, one performs an action by way of body, speech, or mind.”
And what, monks, is the source and origin of kamma?
Contact, monks, is the source and origin of kamma.
And what, monks, is the diversity of kamma?
"There is, monks, karma to be experienced in hell; there is karma to be experienced in the animal realm;
there is karma to be experienced in the sphere of hungry ghosts; there is karma to be experienced in the human world; there is karma to be experienced in the world of the devas.
This, monks, is called the diversity of karmas."
"And what, bhikkhus, is the ripening of kamma?
I declare, bhikkhus, that the ripening of kamma is threefold:
either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period."
This, monks, is called the ripening of kamma.
And what, monks, is the cessation of kamma?
The cessation of contact, monks, is the cessation of kamma.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of karma; that is to say:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, monks, a noble disciple understands karma in this way, and understands the source and origin of karma in this way, [he is called a noble disciple].

He understands; thus he understands the diversity of kamma, thus he understands the ripening of kamma, thus he understands the cessation of kamma, and thus he understands the practice leading to the cessation of kamma.
He understands this penetrative holy life as the cessation of kamma.
“Kamma, monks, is to be understood …pe… the practice leading to the cessation of kamma is to be understood.
It is with reference to this that it was said.
“Suffering, monks, is to be understood; the origin and source of suffering is to be understood; the diversity of suffering is to be understood.”
"It should be understood; the result of suffering should be understood; the cessation of suffering should be understood; the practice leading to the cessation of suffering should be understood.
Thus it was said; with reference to what was this said?
Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering;
not to obtain what one desires is suffering; in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
And what, monks, is the origin and source of suffering?
“Craving, bhikkhus, is the source and origin of suffering.
And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of suffering?
There is, bhikkhus, suffering that is excessive, there is that which is slight, there is that which fades away slowly, and there is that which fades away quickly.”
This, monks, is called the diversity of suffering.
And what, monks, is the ripening of suffering?
Here, monks, someone, overcome by a certain suffering and with mind overwhelmed by it, grieves and is exhausted.
One laments, beats one’s breast, and falls into confusion;
or else, overwhelmed by that suffering with a mind consumed by it, one seeks outside for someone who knows even a single word or two regarding the cessation of this suffering: “Who knows [this]?”
"Monks, I say that suffering has either delusion as its result or seeking as its result.
This, monks, is called the result of suffering.
And what, monks, is the cessation of suffering?"
The cessation of craving, monks, is the cessation of suffering.
This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering; that is to say:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
When, monks, a noble disciple thus understands suffering, thus understands the origin and source of suffering,
thus understands the diversity of suffering, thus understands the result of suffering,
thus understands the cessation of suffering, and thus understands the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, he [attains] this penetrative...
One understands the holy life as the cessation of suffering.
Monks, suffering must be understood; the origin and arising of suffering must be understood; the diversity of suffering must be understood; the result of suffering must be understood;
the cessation of suffering must be understood; and the way leading to the cessation of suffering [must be understood].
“The way of practice is to be understood.
Thus, it is with reference to this that it was said.
“This, monks, is that penetrative exposition of the Dhamma.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.64. Chapter Six:
The Great Division (Mahāvagga).
The Lion’s Roar Discourse (Sīhanādasutta). “Monks,
there are these six powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are these six?
Here, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.
And, monks, that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible—[this is the first power].
This too, bhikkhus, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel. Furthermore, bhikkhus,
the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma— past, future, and present— in terms of its basis and its cause.

Furthermore, monks, in that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma— past, future, and present— in terms of its basis and its cause, this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata. Relying on this power,
the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, and roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies.
He sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
Insofar as the Tathāgata [understands this], monks, this too is a power of the Tathāgata.
Relying upon which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births … [and so on] … thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
Furthermore, monks, when the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives— namely, one birth,
two births … [as detailed] … thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and particulars—
this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata, relying upon that power, [utters the bull-like cry].
He claims his place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn... [as they fare] according to their kamma.
And because, monks, the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... [sees beings as they fare according to their kamma].
He understands beings according to their kamma; this too, monks, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata,
by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies,
and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.

Furthermore, monks, with the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata dwells having realized for himself and attained the state of liberation. Monks, that the Tathāgata, with the destruction of the taints...
having realized and attained it, dwells therein—this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata [attains] the preeminent position.
He claims his place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
These, monks, are the six powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
In this regard, monks, if others approach the Tathāgata with questions, asking him as he truly knows through his knowledge what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible:
To whatever extent, monks, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of things as they truly are— knowing what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—

is realized, to that same extent, when questioned about a matter, the Tathāgata answers with that very knowledge of things as they truly are, knowing what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible.
In that regard, monks, if others approach the Tathāgata and ask questions about the ripening of past, future, and present karmic actions as they truly are, according to their basis and cause,

then in whatever way the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the ripening of past, future, and present karmic actions as they truly are, according to their basis and cause, is known, in that very same way the Tathāgata [explains it] to them regarding those past, future, and present...
When asked a question, he answers by means of knowledge regarding the result of the undertaking of kamma according to its basis and its cause as it really is.

Furthermore, monks, if others approach the Tathāgata and ask a question by means of knowledge regarding the defilement, the purification, and the emergence from the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments as they really are—
just as the Tathāgata [knows] the defilement of the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments...
In whatever way the Tathāgata has understood, as they truly are, the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence of those jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments,
he answers questions posed to him with that knowledge of them as they truly are.
In this regard, monks, if others approach the Tathāgata and ask questions concerning the recollection of past lives as they truly are, [he answers them with that knowledge].

To whatever extent, monks, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the recollection of past lives as it really is has been realized, to that same extent, when questioned about the recollection of past lives as it really is, the Tathāgata answers with his knowledge of the recollection of past lives as it really is.

Furthermore, monks, if others approach the Tathāgata and ask a question regarding the passing away and rebirth of beings as they really are, using his knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings as it really is.

"To whatever extent, monks, the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings as they really are has been realized, to that same extent the Tathāgata, when asked a question regarding the passing away and rebirth of beings as they really are, answers with that very knowledge.
In this regard, monks, if others approach the Tathāgata and ask a question concerning his knowledge of the destruction of the taints as it really is..."

“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent the Tathāgata’s knowledge of things as they really are has become manifest through the destruction of the taints—in that same measure, when questioned about those matters, the Tathāgata answers with his knowledge of things as they really are through the destruction of the taints.

In this regard, bhikkhus, I say that even this knowledge of things as they really are—of what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated.”

I say that the knowledge, as it really is, of the result of past, future, and present karmic actions according to their bases and causes, belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.

I say that the knowledge, as it really is, of the defilement, purification, and emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
I say that the knowledge, as it really is, of the recollection of past lives, belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
“Whatever knowledge there is of the passing away and rebirth of beings as they really are, that too, I say, belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
Whatever knowledge there is of the destruction of the taints … [as it really is], that too, I say, belongs to one who is concentrated, not to one who is unconcentrated.
Thus, bhikkhus, concentration is the path; lack of concentration is the wrong path.”
The tenth.
The sixth chapter, the Mahāvagga.
Its summary verse:
Soṇa, Phagguna, Bhīma, Āsava, Dāruka, Hatthi;
with piercing knowledge in their midst.
"The lion’s roar" refers to those ten [qualities].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.65, Chapter 7: The Chapter on Deities.
Anāgāmiphalasutta: “Bhikkhus,
without having abandoned six things, one is incapable of realizing the fruit of non-returning.
Which six? Lack of faith, moral shamelessness, lack of moral dread, laziness, forgetfulness,
and dullness of wisdom— these, monks, are the six things that, if not abandoned, one is incapable of realizing the fruit of non-returning.
“Bhikkhus, having abandoned six things, one is capable of realizing the fruit of non-returning.
Which six?
Lack of faith, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, laziness, muddled mindfulness, and lack of wisdom.”
“Monks, having abandoned these six things, one is capable of realizing the fruit of non-returning.
Thus was the first [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.66

7. Devatāvagga Arahattasutta (AN 6.66, PTS AN iii 421) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is an arahant; the person who is practicing for the realization of arahantship; the person who is a non-returner; and the person who is practicing for the realization of non-returning. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, without having abandoned six things, one is incapable of realizing arahantship.
Which six?
Sloth, torpor, restlessness, remorse, lack of faith, and negligence.”
"Monks, without abandoning these six things, one is incapable of realizing arhatship.
Monks, by abandoning six things, one is capable of realizing arhatship.
Which six?"
“Bhikkhus, having abandoned these six things— sloth, torpor, restlessness, remorse, lack of faith, and negligence— one is capable of realizing arahantship.
This is the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.67 7.

Devatāvagga Mittasutta – The Discourse on Friends “Monks, there are these five kinds of friends. What five? The friend who helps one in times of need; the friend who shares one’s joys and sorrows; the friend who is the same in both prosperity and adversity; the friend who gives what is hard to give; and the friend who acts for one’s benefit even at the cost of their own life. These, monks, are the five kinds of friends.”
“Indeed, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has evil friends, evil companions, and evil associates;
when he frequents, consorts with, and attends upon evil friends, and follows their example in view, he [fails to fulfill] the Dhamma pertaining to proper conduct. (AN 6.67, PTS AN iii 422)

‘One will fulfill the higher training in conduct without having fulfilled the Dhamma of the trainee’—this is impossible. ‘One will fulfill the Dhamma of the trainee without having fulfilled the Dhamma of higher conduct’—this is impossible.
‘One will fulfill the virtues without having fulfilled the Dhamma of the trainee’—this is impossible.
‘Without fulfilling the precepts, one will abandon sensual lust, lust for form, or lust for the formless’—this is impossible.
‘But, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, and good associates;
who, by serving, associating with, and attending upon his good friends, follows their example in matters of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika*)—’

It is possible that he will fulfill the Dhamma pertaining to proper conduct. It is possible that, having fulfilled the Dhamma pertaining to proper conduct, he will fulfill the Dhamma of one in training.
It is possible that, having fulfilled the Dhamma of one in training, he will fulfill the precepts.
“It is possible that, having fulfilled the precepts, one will abandon sensual lust, lust for form, or lust for the formless.
This is the third [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.68

7. Devatāvagga Saṅgaṇikārāmasutta (AN 6.68, PTS AN iii 422) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then a certain deity, in the far extreme of the night, with surpassing radiance, illuminated the entire Jeta’s Grove and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing there, that deity addressed the Blessed One in verse: “Why do they not delight in solitude? Why do they not find joy in seclusion? Why do they not frequent remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves? “They delight in company; they find pleasure in society. They are fond of the bustle of crowds and are attached to gain, honor, and praise. Bound by the fetter of craving, they do not cross over the flood. “But those who are detached from the world, who have abandoned all attachments, who have cut off the stream and crossed over the flood—they delight in solitude and find joy in seclusion. They frequent remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves. Having said this, that deity, having paid homage to the Blessed One, keeping him on the right, vanished right there. Then the venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat at the appropriate time, went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, exactly as it had happened. “Indeed, Ānanda, it is so. It is just as that deity has said. Those who delight in company, who find pleasure in society, who are fond of the bustle of crowds and are attached to gain, honor, and praise—bound by the fetter of craving, they do not cross over the flood. But those who are detached from the world, who have abandoned all attachments, who have cut off the stream and crossed over the flood—they delight in solitude and find joy in seclusion. They frequent remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Then, when the night was far advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she stood to one side.
Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, there are these six qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
What six?
Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, being easy to correct, and having virtuous friends.”
“Venerable sir, these six qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.
This is what that deity said.
The Teacher approved.
Then that deity, thinking, "The Teacher has consented to me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to the right, and vanished right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, during this night, as the night was far advanced, a certain deity of surpassing beauty approached the entire extent of [this assembly]..."
Having illuminated Jeta’s Grove, that deity approached me; having approached, she paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, bhikkhus, that deity said this to me:
“Venerable sir, these six qualities lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.”
“What six?
Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, being easy to correct, and having good friends.
These, venerable sir, are the six qualities that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu.”
“This is what that deity said, monks.
Having said this, she paid homage to me, circumambulated me with her right side toward me, and vanished right there.
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta paid homage to the Blessed One and said this:
“Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of what was stated by the Blessed One in brief as follows:
Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu himself has reverence for the Teacher and speaks in praise of such reverence for the Teacher;
and he encourages other bhikkhus who lack reverence for the Teacher to practice that same reverence for the Teacher.”
And he speaks at the proper time, truthfully and accurately, in praise of those other monks who have reverence for the Teacher.
He himself possesses reverence for the Dhamma … reverence for the Saṅgha …
He has respect for the training;
he is easy to speak to;
he has good friends and speaks in praise of having good friends.
“Those other monks who are not good friends, he encourages them toward having good friends.
And those other monks who are good friends, he speaks in praise of them at the proper time, truthfully and accurately.
This, venerable sir, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.”
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
It is good, Sāriputta, that you understand in such detail the meaning of what I have spoken so briefly.
Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu himself has reverence for the Teacher and speaks in praise of having reverence for the Teacher.”
He encourages those other bhikkhus who lack reverence for the Teacher to practice reverence for the Teacher;
he speaks at the proper time, truthfully and accurately, in praise of those other bhikkhus who do have reverence for the Teacher;
and he himself possesses reverence for the Dhamma. …
He has reverence for the Saṅgha;
he has reverence for the training;
he is easy to admonish.
He is a friend of virtue and speaks in praise of friendship with the virtuous.
Those other monks who are not friends of virtue, he encourages them toward friendship with the virtuous.
And those other monks who are friends of virtue, he speaks their praise at the proper time, truthfully and accurately.
"Sāriputta, this is how the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief should be understood in detail.
The fifth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.70.

Devatāvagga Paṭhamatajjhānasutta (The First Jhāna Discourse) “Bhikkhus, when five factors are abandoned and five factors are present, a bhikkhu is called one who dwells in the first jhāna. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, abandoned ill will, abandoned sloth and torpor, abandoned restlessness and remorse, and abandoned doubt; and he possesses the five factors: rapture, pleasure, tranquility, concentration, and mindfulness and clear comprehension. When these five factors are abandoned and these five factors are present, a bhikkhu is called one who dwells in the first jhāna.”

Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt;

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.74 7. Devatāvagga Second Discourse on the Jhāna “Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters. What five? Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These, bhikkhus, are the five higher fetters.

When a bhikkhu has abandoned these five higher fetters, he is one who attains final knowledge in this very life, or else he becomes one of the non-returners who will attain final nibbāna upon reaching the Brahma-world. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who attains final knowledge in this very life, it is because he has developed and cultivated the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life. What four? Here, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without thought and examination, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous and, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. It is because he has developed and cultivated these four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, that if a bhikkhu is one who attains final knowledge in this very life, he does so. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one of the non-returners who will attain final nibbāna upon reaching the Brahma-world, it is because he has developed and cultivated these same four jhānas. It is because he has developed and cultivated these four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life, that if a bhikkhu is one of the non-returners who will attain final nibbāna upon reaching the Brahma-world, he does so.”
