By which six?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu is skilled in gain, skilled in loss, and skilled in means;
he generates desire for the attainment of wholesome states not yet attained, and [exerts himself] regarding wholesome states already attained.
He guards them; he accomplishes them through constant practice.
Possessing these six qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is capable of attaining wholesome states not yet attained, or of increasing wholesome states already attained.
The fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.80 8. Arahattavagga Mahantattasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five great beings. What five? The great earth, the great ocean, the great Himalaya mountain, the great fire, and the great person. (1) “And how, bhikkhus, is the great earth a great being? This great earth is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great earth is a great being. (2) “And how is the great ocean a great being? This great ocean is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great ocean is a great being. (3) “And how is the great Himalaya mountain a great being? The great Himalaya mountain is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great Himalaya mountain is a great being. (4) “And how is the great fire a great being? The great fire is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great fire is a great being. (5) “And how is the great person a great being? The great person is vast, extensive, and long-lasting;

he endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great person is a great being. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five great beings. What five? The great earth, the great ocean, the great Himalaya mountain, the great fire, and the great person. (1) “And how, bhikkhus, is the great earth a great being? This great earth is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great earth is a great being. (2) “And how is the great ocean a great being? This great ocean is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great ocean is a great being. (3) “And how is the great Himalaya mountain a great being? The great Himalaya mountain is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great Himalaya mountain is a great being. (4) “And how is the great fire a great being? The great fire is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great fire is a great being. (5) “And how is the great person a great being? The great person is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; he endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great person is a great being. “Bhikkhus, just as the great earth is a great being, so too is the great person a great being. Just as the great ocean is a great being, so too is the great person a great being. Just as the great Himalaya mountain is a great being, so too is the great person a great being. Just as the great fire is a great being, so too is the great person a great being. And how, bhikkhus, is the great person a great being? Here, a bhikkhu is endowed with the first jhāna, which is secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, born of solitude, and filled with rapture and pleasure. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, with the subsiding of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in pleasure. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, perceiving space as infinite, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, perceiving consciousness as infinite, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving nothing at all, he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Furthermore, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. And his taints are destroyed by his seeing with wisdom. He dwells having attained this state for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks, for four weeks, for five weeks, for six weeks, or for seven weeks. Because of this, he is called a ‘great person. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling after speaking thus, what did the Blessed One mean? The Venerable Ānanda replied: “Friend, the Blessed One spoke in reference to the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. “This is wonderful, friend Ānanda! This is marvelous, friend Ānanda! How the meaning and the phrasing of the Blessed One’s words have been perfectly explained by the Venerable Ānanda, just as they were spoken by the Blessed One. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five great beings. What five? The great earth, the great ocean, the great Himalaya mountain, the great fire, and the great person. (1) “And how, bhikkhus, is the great earth a great being? This great earth is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great earth is a great being. (2) “And how is the great ocean a great being? This great ocean is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of contraction and expansion. It is because of this that the great ocean is a great being. (3) “And how is the great Himalaya mountain a great being? The great Himalaya mountain is vast, extensive, and long-lasting; it endures through the passing of many aeons of
“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu before long attains greatness and abundance in the teachings. What are the six? [The Buddha said:]”

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is full of light, full of application, full of knowledge, full of non-contentment [with mere good qualities], and does not lay down his burden regarding wholesome states; furthermore, he strives for the higher.
Possessing these six qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu before long attains greatness and abundance in the Dhammas.
The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.81 8. Arahattavagga Paṭhamanirayasutta (The First Discourse on Hell) "Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? "The person who is like a hell-dweller; the person who is like a beast; the person who is like a ghost; the person who is like a deva; and the person who is like a brahmā. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a hell-dweller? Here, bhikkhus, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person like a hell-dweller. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a beast? Here, bhikkhus, someone destroys life... and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness; he is also devoid of faith, shameless, and unafraid of wrongdoing. This is called a person like a beast. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a ghost? Here, bhikkhus, someone destroys life... and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness; he is also devoid of faith, shameless, and unafraid of wrongdoing, yet he possesses some degree of moral dread. This is called a person like a ghost. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a deva? Here, bhikkhus, someone does not destroy life... nor does he indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness; he is endowed with faith, possessed of shame, and afraid of wrongdoing. This is called a person like a deva. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a brahmā? Here, bhikkhus, someone does not destroy life... nor does he indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness; he is endowed with faith, possessed of shame, and afraid of wrongdoing; he is virtuous, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains by undertaking the training rules. This is called a person like a brahmā. "These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with six qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. Which six? [The Buddha said:]”
He is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehood, one of evil desires, and one of wrong view.
Endowed with these six qualities, monks, one is placed in hell as if carried there.
Endowed with six qualities, monks, one is placed in heaven as if carried there.
“By which six?
He abstains from taking life, he abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, he is of few desires, and he holds right view.
It is, monks, by being endowed with these six qualities that one is placed in heaven as if carried there.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.82 8.
Arahattavagga (The Chapter on Arahantship)
The Second Discourse on Hells (Dutiya-niraya-sutta): “Monks,
one who possesses six qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.”
By which six?
He is a destroyer of life, he is a taker of what is not given, he is one who engages in sexual misconduct, he is a speaker of falsehood, he is greedy, and he is shameless.
Endowed with these six qualities, monks, one is placed in hell as if carried there.
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with six qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the six?
He abstains from taking life, he abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, he is not covetous, and he is not frivolous.”
“Monks, one who is endowed with these six qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there.
The eighth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 6.83.

8. Arahattavagga Aggadhammasutta (AN 6.83, PTS AN iii 433) “Bhikkhus, there are these four foremost things. What four? The foremost of all phenomena is the Dhamma; the foremost of all persons is the Tathāgata; the foremost of all conditioned things is dispassion; the foremost of all unconditioned things is Nibbāna. These, bhikkhus, are the four foremost things.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is incapable of realizing the supreme state, arahantship.
With which six?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is faithless, shameless, unafraid of wrongdoing, lazy, muddle-minded, and he is concerned for his body and his life.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities is incapable of realizing the supreme state, arhatship.
Monks, a monk endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the supreme state, arhatship.
With which six?
“Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, he is possessed of a sense of shame, he is possessed of moral dread, he is energetic, he is wise, and he is regardless of both body and life.
Endowed with these six qualities, monks, a monk is capable of realizing the supreme state, arahantship.
Thus was the ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.84 8.

Arahattavagga Rattidivasasutta (The Day and Night) "Bhikkhus, there are these four days and nights that are very fruitful and very beneficial for a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What four? The day and night during which one attains stream-entry; the day and night during which one attains once-returning; the day and night during which one attains non-returning; and the day and night during which one attains arahantship. These, bhikkhus, are the four days and nights that are very fruitful and very beneficial for a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness."

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu possesses six qualities, whether night or day comes, one may expect only decline in wholesome qualities, not growth. What are the six? [The Sutta continues with the list of qualities.]”
"Here, monks, a monk has great desires, is troubled, and is discontented with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive;
he is faithless, immoral, lazy, muddle-minded, and unwise.
For a monk endowed with these six qualities, whether night or day comes, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth."
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu possesses six qualities, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected for him, not decline.
What are the six?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not of great desires, is free from affliction, and is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“He is endowed with faith, he is virtuous, he is energetic, he is mindful, and he is wise.
For a bhikkhu who possesses these six qualities, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
The tenth.
The eighth chapter is the Arahattavagga.
Its summary verse is:
Dukkha, arahatta, and uttara.
And through the attainment of happiness;
the two great things in hell,
and the supreme Dhamma at night.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.85 9.

Sītivagga Sītibhāvasutta – The Cool State “Bhikkhus, there are these four cool states. What four? The cool state of loving-kindness, the cool state of compassion, the cool state of altruistic joy, and the cool state of equanimity. These, bhikkhus, are the four cool states.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing six qualities, a bhikkhu is incapable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness. Which six? [The Buddha said:]”
In this case, monks, when a monk’s mind should be restrained, at that time he does not restrain the mind;
when his mind should be exerted, at that time he does not exert the mind;
when his mind should be gladdened, at that time he does not gladden the mind; when—

At that time, the mind should be looked upon with equanimity; yet at that time, he does not look upon the mind with equanimity, and he is one whose inclination is inferior and who delights in identity-view.
Possessing these six qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is incapable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness.
What are the six?
Here, bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu’s mind should be restrained, at that time he restrains the mind.”
He restrains [the mind]; at the time when the mind should be exerted, he exerts the mind;
at the time when the mind should be gladdened, he gladdens the mind;
at the time when the mind should be looked upon with equanimity, he looks upon the mind with equanimity; and he is one who is intent on the sublime and delights in Nibbāna.
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with these six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 6.86.

9. Sītivagga Āvaraṇasutta (AN 6.86, PTS AN iii 435) “Bhikkhus, there are these five obstructions. What five? The obstruction of sensual desire, the obstruction of ill will, the obstruction of sloth and torpor, the obstruction of restlessness and remorse, and the obstruction of doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five obstructions.”
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses six qualities, even while hearing the true Dhamma, is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.

What are the six? One is possessed of an obstruction due to karma; one is possessed of an obstruction due to defilements; one is possessed of an obstruction due to maturation; one lacks faith; one lacks desire [for the good]; and one is lacking in wisdom.”
“Monks, one who possesses these six qualities, even while hearing the true Dhamma, is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Monks, one who possesses six qualities, while hearing the true Dhamma, is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Which six?”
One does not possess an obstruction of karma, one does not possess an obstruction of defilements, and one does not possess an obstruction of ripening; moreover, one possesses faith, zeal, and wisdom.
Possessing these six qualities, monks, one who hears the true Dhamma is capable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states. Thus it was said.
Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.87 9.

Sītivagga Voropitasutta (The One Who Has Deprived [Life]) “Monks, one who has deprived [a living being] of life, if they are not established in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, at the breaking up of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. But, monks, one who has deprived [a living being] of life, if they are established in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, at the breaking up of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
“Monks, one who possesses six qualities, even while hearing the true Dhamma, is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states. What are the six? [The Sutta continues:]”
One has deprived one’s mother of life; one has deprived one’s father of life; one has deprived an arahant of life;
with a mind of hatred, one has drawn blood from a Tathāgata; one has caused a schism in the Saṅgha; and one is dull-witted, stupid, and mute.
Possessing these six qualities, monks, even while hearing the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses six qualities is capable, while listening to the true Dhamma, of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
What are the six?
One has not deprived one’s mother of life; one has not deprived one’s father of life; one has not deprived an arahant of life...”
"He has not shed the Tathāgata’s blood with a malicious mind, he has not caused a schism in the Saṅgha,
and he is wise, unconfused, and not dull-witted.
Possessing these six qualities, monks, one who hears the true Dhamma is capable of entering into the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states."
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.88 9.
Sītivagga (The Chapter on Cold)
Sussūsatisutta (AN 6.88): “Bhikkhus,
possessing six qualities, even while listening to the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
Which six?

When the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, one does not wish to listen; one does not lend an ear; one does not apply the mind to understanding; one grasps what is meaningless; one discards what is meaningful;

and one possesses a disposition that is contrary [to the teaching]. Possessing these six qualities, monks, even though one hears the true Dhamma, one is incapable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses six qualities, while listening to the true Dhamma, is capable of entering upon the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states.
What are the six?

When the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, he listens with eager intent; he lends an ear; he applies his mind to understanding; he grasps the meaning; he discards what is not the meaning; and he possesses the kind of conviction that conforms to the truth.”
“Monks, one who hears the true Dhamma while endowed with these six qualities is capable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.89

9. Sītivagga: Appahāyasutta (AN 6.89, PTS AN iii 438) “Bhikkhus, as long as these five things have not been abandoned in a bhikkhu, he is incapable of entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, let alone the higher ones. What five? Lustful thought, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. As long as these five things have not been abandoned in a bhikkhu, he is incapable of entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, let alone the higher ones. But when these five things have been abandoned in a bhikkhu, he is capable of entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, let alone the higher ones. What five? Lustful thought, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. When these five things have been abandoned in a bhikkhu, he is capable of entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, let alone the higher ones.”
“Bhikkhus, without having abandoned six things, one is incapable of realizing the perfection of view.
Which six?

The view of a personal body, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust leading to the states of deprivation, hatred leading to the states of deprivation, and delusion leading to the states of deprivation.”
“Monks, without abandoning these six things, one is incapable of realizing the perfection of view.
Monks, by abandoning six things, one is capable of realizing the perfection of view.
Which six?”

“Bhikkhus, by abandoning these six things, one is capable of realizing the perfection of view: personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, greed leading to the states of deprivation, hatred leading to the states of deprivation, and delusion leading to the states of deprivation.
It is by abandoning these six things, bhikkhus, that one is capable of realizing the perfection of view.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.90 9.

Sītivagga Pahīnasutta (The Discourse on What Has Been Abandoned) "Bhikkhus, when these six things are abandoned in a bhikkhu, he is called a bhikkhu who has abandoned what should be abandoned. What six? Greed is abandoned; hatred is abandoned; delusion is abandoned; conceit is abandoned; views are abandoned; and doubt is abandoned. When these six things are abandoned in a bhikkhu, he is called a bhikkhu who has abandoned what should be abandoned."
“Bhikkhus, these six things are abandoned by a person who is accomplished in view. Which six? [The text continues with the list.]”

“Bhikkhus, these six things have been abandoned by a person who is accomplished in view: personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust leading to the states of deprivation, hatred leading to the states of deprivation, and delusion leading to the states of deprivation.
These, bhikkhus, are the six things abandoned by a person accomplished in view.
The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.91 9. Sītivagga Abhabbasutta (The Discourse on the Inability) "Bhikkhus, these five persons are incapable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, let alone the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a person is devoid of faith, devoid of virtuous behavior, devoid of learning, devoid of generosity, and devoid of wisdom. These five persons, bhikkhus, are incapable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, let alone the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. These five persons, bhikkhus, are capable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, let alone the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a person possesses faith, possesses virtuous behavior, possesses learning, possesses generosity, and possesses wisdom. These five persons, bhikkhus, are capable of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, let alone the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna."
“Bhikkhus, a person accomplished in view is incapable of producing six things.
Which six?”

“Bhikkhus, a person endowed with right view is incapable of producing these six things: personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, lust leading to the states of deprivation, hatred leading to the states of deprivation, and delusion leading to the states of deprivation.
These, bhikkhus, are the six things that a person endowed with right view is incapable of producing.
Thus was the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.92 9. Sītivagga First Discourse on the Impossibilities “Monks, these six things are impossible and cannot come to pass for one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment (sammattaniyāma).

What six? It is impossible that one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment could kill his mother; this is impossible. It is impossible that one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment could kill his father; this is impossible. It is impossible that one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment could kill an arahant; this is impossible. It is impossible that one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment could maliciously draw blood from a Tathāgata with a mind of hatred; this is impossible. It is impossible that one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment could split the Saṅgha; this is impossible. It is impossible that one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment could turn back the wheel of the Dhamma set in motion by a Tathāgata, a Perfectly Enlightened One, by means of mere Dhamma; this is impossible. These six things, monks, are impossible and cannot come to pass for one who has entered the fixed course of rightness toward enlightenment.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these six impossible situations.
Which six?
A person endowed with right view is incapable of dwelling without respect or deference toward the Teacher;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of dwelling without respect or deference toward the Dhamma;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of dwelling without respect or deference toward the Saṅgha; a person endowed with right view is incapable of dwelling without respect for the training.
“Lacking respect, a person endowed with right view is incapable of returning to a state from which there is no return;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of producing an eighth existence.
These, monks, are the six states of incapacity.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.93 9.
Sītivagga (The Chapter on Cold)
The Discourse on the Second Set of Impossible Conditions (Dutiya-abhabbaṭṭhāna-sutta):
“Bhikkhus, there are these six impossible conditions. What six? [The text continues with the list of impossible conditions.]”
Which six?
A person endowed with right view is incapable of regarding any conditioned phenomenon as permanent;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of regarding any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant; a person endowed with right view is incapable of regarding any phenomenon...
A person endowed with right view is incapable of regarding [anything] as self; a person endowed with right view is incapable of committing an act of immediate retribution;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of returning to the belief that purification comes through superstitious rites and omens;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of seeking outside this teaching for one worthy of offerings.
“Monks, these indeed are the six situations in which one is incapable.
Thus [ends] the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.94

9. Sītivagga Third Discourse on Impossibilities (Tatiya-abhabbaṭṭhāna-sutta) “Monks, it is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘There is no result or maturation of giving, sacrifice, or offering; there is no fruit or maturation of wholesome and unwholesome deeds. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘There are no beings spontaneously born; there is no world beyond; there are no ascetics or brahmins of right conduct and right practice who, having realized this world and the next by their own super-knowledge, make them known to others. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘A person who acts intentionally, whether for their own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of both, does not perform an action that will lead to long-term harm and suffering. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘When one acts or causes another to act, when one mutilates or causes another to mutilate, when one tortures or causes another to torture, when one inflicts grief or causes another to inflict grief, when one intimidates or causes another to intimidate, when one maims or causes another to maim, when one takes life, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, or indulges in idle chatter—no evil or unwholesome result follows from such actions. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures; there is no danger in sensual pleasures; there is no escape from sensual pleasures. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘There is no fault in killing living beings; there is no fault in taking what is not given; there is no fault in committing sexual misconduct; there is no fault in speaking falsely; there is no fault in speaking divisively; there is no fault in speaking harshly; there is no fault in indulging in idle chatter. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘There is no fault in being stingy; there is no fault in being malicious; there is no fault in being of wrong view. It is impossible for one with right view to hold such a view. It is impossible and inconceivable that one who possesses right view could hold such a view as this: ‘There is no result or maturation of giving, sacrifice, or offering; there is no fruit or maturation of wholesome and unwholesome deeds. “Monks, there are these six impossible situations.
What are the six?
A person endowed with right view is incapable of depriving his mother of life; a person endowed with right view is incapable of [depriving his father of life]...”
A person endowed with right view is incapable of depriving his father of life; a person endowed with right view is incapable of depriving an arahant of life;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of shedding the Tathāgata’s blood with a malicious mind;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of causing a schism in the Saṅgha; a person endowed with right view is incapable of acknowledging another teacher.
“Monks, these indeed are the six impossible situations.
Tenth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.95

9. Sītivagga Catutthaabhabbaṭṭhānasutta (AN 6.95, PTS AN iii 440) The Fourth Discourse on Impossibilities “Monks, these four things are impossible and unattainable for one who has entered the stream, who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, who is firmly established and destined for full enlightenment. What four? (1) ‘May I not be subject to suffering,’ this is impossible; ‘I shall be free from suffering,’ this is possible. (2) ‘May I not be subject to old age,’ this is impossible; ‘I shall be free from old age,’ this is possible. (3) ‘May I not be subject to illness,’ this is impossible; ‘I shall be free from illness,’ this is possible. (4) ‘May I not be subject to death,’ this is impossible; ‘I shall be free from death,’ this is possible. These four things, monks, are impossible and unattainable for one who has entered the stream, who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, who is firmly established and destined for full enlightenment.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these six impossible situations.
What are the six?

A person endowed with right view is incapable of returning to the notion that pleasure and pain are self-made; a person endowed with right view is incapable of [returning to the notion that pleasure and pain are] made by another...”

A person cannot maintain the view that pleasure and pain are created by another; a person endowed with right view is incapable of maintaining the view that pleasure and pain are both self-created and created by another;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of maintaining the view that pleasure and pain arise without cause through chance;
a person endowed with right view is incapable of maintaining the view that pleasure and pain are not created by another.
It is impossible for a person endowed with right view to return to the view that pleasure and pain arise by chance;
it is impossible for such a person to return to the view that pleasure and pain arise neither from one’s own actions nor from the actions of another, but by chance.
For what reason?
For in this way, monks, for a person who has attained right view, the cause is well-seen, as are the phenomena arisen from that cause.
These, monks, are the six impossible situations. Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].
The ninth chapter is the Sītivagga.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is:
"Coolness, obstruction..."
One who has been deprived of [the precepts] desires to hear [the Dharma]; one who has not abandoned [defilements] is incapable of abandoning them—
these four points are likewise.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.96 10.

Ānisaṁsavagga Pātubhāvasutta “Bhikkhus, when six things are manifest, it is possible that a noble disciple will attain final knowledge here and now. What six? The manifestation of the Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; the manifestation of the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata; the manifestation of a person who has gone forth in this Dhamma and Discipline; the manifestation of a person who is a companion in the holy life; the manifestation of the arising of the desire to hear the Dhamma; and the manifestation of the application of the ear. When these six things are manifest, it is possible that a noble disciple will attain final knowledge here and now.”
“Bhikkhus, the manifestation of six things is rare in the world. Which six? [The text continues with the list.]”
The manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, is rare in the world;
a person who teaches the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is rare in the world; rebirth in a noble realm is rare in the world;
the integrity of one’s faculties is rare in the world; and being unconfused and free from dullness is rare in the world.
“Zeal for wholesome states is rare in the world.
Indeed, bhikkhus, the manifestation of these six things is rare in the world.
Thus was the first [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.97 10.

Ānisaṁsavagga Ānisaṁsasutta (The Discourse on Benefits) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for one who is established in virtue, who has entered upon the way. What five? One acquires a good reputation; one is protected by the noble ones; one gains a sense of confidence when entering an assembly; one dies unconfused; and after death, at the breaking-up of the body, one reappears in a happy destination, even in a heavenly world. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for one who is established in virtue, who has entered upon the way.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these six benefits for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. What six? [The text continues as follows:]”

“He is one who is certain of the true Dhamma; he is of a nature not to decline; his suffering has a limit; he is endowed with knowledge that is not shared [with worldlings]; the cause is well-seen by him, as are the phenomena arisen from the cause.
These, monks, are the six benefits for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. This is the second [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.98 10.

Ānisaṁsavagga Aniccasutta (The Discourse on Impermanence) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in contemplating impermanence. What five? One acquires confidence that has not yet been acquired; one consolidates the confidence already acquired; one gains a portion of the Dhamma; one becomes an heir to the Dhamma; and one attains the destruction of the taints. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits in contemplating impermanence.”
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who regards any conditioned phenomenon as permanent could possess the conformity-acceptance;
it is impossible that one who does not possess the conformity-acceptance could enter the fixed course of rightness.”
‘One who does not enter the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship’—this is impossible.
‘That a bhikkhu, by contemplating all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, will come to possess the conformity-acceptance’—this is possible.
‘One who possesses the conformity-acceptance will enter the certainty of rightness’—this is possible.

‘It is possible that one who is entering the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or even arhatship’—this is a possibility. Thus [he spoke].
The third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.99

10. Ānisaṁsavagga Dukkhasutta (AN 6.99) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of suffering. What five? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; and association with what is disliked is suffering—these, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of suffering.”

“Indeed, bhikkhus, it is possible that a bhikkhu who regards any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant … [and so on] … who regards all conditioned phenomena as suffering … [and so on] … this is possible.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.100 10.
Ānisaṁsavagga (Chapter on Benefits)
The Discourse on Not-Self (Anattasutta): “Indeed,
bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu regards any phenomenon as self …” [as in the full sutta].
“While contemplating all phenomena as non-self...
[as before] ...it is possible that this state exists. The fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.101 10. Ānisaṁsavagga Nibbānasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in nibbāna. What five? One does not experience suffering that has arisen; one does not experience the pursuit of what is harmful; one does not experience the pursuit of sensual pleasures; one does not experience the pursuit of unwholesome states; and one does not experience the pursuit of worldly existence. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits in nibbāna.”
“Bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who regards Nibbāna as suffering will possess the conformity-acceptance;
it is impossible that one who does not possess the conformity-acceptance will enter the fixed course of rightness.”
‘That one who has not entered the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arhatship’—this is impossible.
‘That a bhikkhu, perceiving Nibbāna as happiness, will possess the conformable acceptance (anulomikā khanti)’—this is possible.
‘One who possesses the conformable acceptance will enter the certainty of rightness’—this is possible.
“It is possible that one who has entered the certainty of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or even arhatship.
This is the sixth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.102

10. Ānisaṁsavagga Anavatthitasutta (AN 6.102) "Monks, these five things are unstable. What five? Form is unstable; feeling is unstable; perception is unstable; volitional formations are unstable; consciousness is unstable. These five things are unstable."
“Bhikkhus, seeing six advantages, it is enough for a bhikkhu to establish the perception of impermanence without exception regarding all conditioned phenomena.
What six?
‘All conditioned phenomena will appear to me as unstable; my mind will find no delight in the entire world;”
‘My mind will turn away from the entire world; my consciousness will incline toward Nibbāna;
my fetters will come to be abandoned; and I shall be endowed with the supreme state of a recluse.
It is by seeing these six advantages, monks, that it is sufficient for a bhikkhu to establish the perception of impermanence without exception regarding all conditioned phenomena.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.103. 10.
Ānisaṁsavagga (The Chapter on Benefits).
The Discourse on the Raised Sword (Ukkhittāsikasutta):
“Bhikkhus, seeing six advantages, it is sufficient for a bhikkhu to establish the perception of suffering without exception regarding all conditioned phenomena.”
Which six?
"Toward all conditioned phenomena, the perception of disenchantment will be established in me, as if toward an executioner with sword raised.
My mind will withdraw from the entire world, I will be one who sees peace in Nibbāna, and [my] underlying tendencies..."
‘They will go to their eradication; I will have done what was to be done; and the Teacher will have been served by me through the practice of loving-kindness.
It is by seeing these six benefits, monks, that it is sufficient for a bhikkhu to establish the perception of suffering without exception regarding all conditioned formations.
Thus was the eighth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.104 10.

Ānisaṁsavagga Atammayasutta (The Discourse on Not Being Identifying) "Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for one who does not identify with form, who does not identify with feeling, who does not identify with perception, who does not identify with volitional formations, and who does not identify with consciousness. What five? "One gains a firm footing in what is wholesome; one dwells without fear; one does not tremble at the prospect of death; one dies unconfused; and after death, at the breaking up of the body, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for one who does not identify with form... and who does not identify with consciousness."
“Bhikkhus, seeing six advantages, it is enough for a bhikkhu to establish the perception of non-self with regard to all phenomena without exception. What six? [The text continues as follows:]”
"I shall not be attached to anything in the entire world; my 'I-making' (ahaṅkāra) shall cease, and my 'mine-making' (mamaṅkāra) shall cease;
I shall be endowed with uncommon knowledge; and the cause, as well as the phenomena arisen from that cause, shall be clearly seen by me."
“Monks, seeing these six benefits, it is indeed sufficient for a monk to establish the perception of non-self with respect to all phenomena without exception.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.105

10. Ānisaṁsavagga Bhavasutta (AN 6.105) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of existence. What five? Existence in hell, existence as an animal, existence as a ghost, existence as a human, and existence as a deva. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of existence.”
“Bhikkhus, three kinds of existence are to be abandoned, and one should train in the three trainings.
What are the three kinds of existence to be abandoned?
Existence in the sense-sphere realm, existence in the fine-material realm, and existence in the immaterial realm.”
These three states of existence are to be abandoned.
In which three trainings should one train?
In the training of higher virtue, the training of higher mind, and the training of higher wisdom.
"One should train in these three trainings. When, monks,
a monk has abandoned these three states of existence and has trained himself in these three trainings—
he is called, monks, a monk who has cut off craving, stripped away the fetters, and through the right realization of conceit, made an end of suffering."
The Tenth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.106 10.
The Chapter on Benefits (Ānisaṁsavagga)
Taṇhāsutta: “Bhikkhus,
these three kinds of craving are to be abandoned, as are the three kinds of conceit.”
Which three kinds of craving are to be abandoned?
Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—
these three kinds of craving are to be abandoned.
Which three types of conceit are to be abandoned?
Conceit, self-depreciation, and overweening conceit—
these three types of conceit are to be abandoned.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned these three kinds of craving and these three kinds of conceit,
he is called a bhikkhu who has cut off craving, stripped away the fetter, and by the complete penetration of conceit, has made an end of suffering. Thus was the eleventh [sutta].
The tenth chapter: The Chapter on Benefits.
Its summary verse:
Manifestation and benefits.
As impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
Nibbāna is non-abiding,
with the spear thrown away, and free from "that-making."
Existence and craving are one and the same.
The second fiftieth chapter is completed.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.107

11. Tikavagga Rāgasutta (AN 6.107, PTS AN iii 445) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of lust. What three? Lust for sensual pleasures, lust for form, and lust for existence. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of lust.”
“Bhikkhus, there are three things.
Which three?
Lust, hatred, and delusion.”
“Monks, these are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?”

“For the abandoning of lust, the meditation on the foul should be developed; for the abandoning of hatred, loving-kindness should be developed; for the abandoning of delusion, wisdom should be developed.
Indeed, monks, for the abandoning of these three states, these three states should be developed. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.108 11.

Tikavagga Duccaritasutta (The Discourse on Misconduct) “Monks, there are these three kinds of misconduct. What three? Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. These, monks, are the three kinds of misconduct.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things.
Which three?”
Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.
These, monks, are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?

For the abandoning of bodily misconduct, bodily good conduct should be developed; for the abandoning of verbal misconduct, verbal good conduct should be developed; for the abandoning of mental misconduct, mental good conduct should be developed.
It is for the abandoning of these three things, monks, that these three things should be developed.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.109 11.
Tikavagga (The Chapter on Threes)
Vitakkasutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things. [Text: AN 6.109, PTS AN iii 446]”
Which three?
Sensual thought, ill-will thought, and harmful thought.
These, monks, are the three things.
“Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, three things are to be developed.
Which three?

For the abandoning of sensual thought, the thought of renunciation is to be developed; for the abandoning of ill-will thought, the thought of non-ill-will is to be developed; for the abandoning of cruelty thought, the thought of non-cruelty is to be developed.”
“Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, these three things are to be developed.
The third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.110

11. Tikavagga Saññāsutta (AN 6.110, PTS AN iii 446) "Bhikkhus, there are these three perceptions. What three? The perception of unattractiveness, the perception of death, and the perception of the repulsiveness of food. These, bhikkhus, are the three perceptions."
“Bhikkhus, there are three things.
Which three?
Perception of sensual desire, perception of ill will, and perception of cruelty.”
“Monks, these are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?”

“For the abandoning of the perception of sensual desire, the perception of renunciation should be developed; for the abandoning of the perception of ill will, the perception of non-ill will should be developed; for the abandoning of the perception of cruelty, the perception of non-cruelty should be developed.
Indeed, monks, for the abandoning of these three things, these three things should be developed.
This is the fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.111 11. Tikavagga Dhātusutta (The Discourse on Elements) "Bhikkhus, there are these three elements. What three? The element of sensual desire, the element of form, and the element of the formless. These, bhikkhus, are the three elements."
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things. Which three? [The Sutta continues as follows:]”
The realm of sensual desire, the realm of ill will, and the realm of cruelty.
These, monks, are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?

For the abandoning of the element of sensual desire, the element of renunciation should be developed; for the abandoning of the element of ill will, the element of non-ill will should be developed; for the abandoning of the element of cruelty, the element of non-cruelty should be developed.
It is for the abandoning of these three things, monks, that these three things should be developed.”
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.112 11.
Tikavagga (The Chapter on Threes)
The Discourse on Gratification (Assādasutta):
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things. [Text: AN 6.112, PTS AN iii 447]”
Which three?
The view of gratification, the view of self, and wrong view.
These, monks, are the three things.
“Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, three things are to be developed.
Which three?

For the abandoning of the view of gratification, the perception of impermanence is to be developed; for the abandoning of the view of self, the perception of non-self is to be developed; for the abandoning of wrong view, right view is to be developed.”
“Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, these three things are to be developed.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 6.113

11. Tikavagga Aratisutta (AN 6.113, PTS AN iii 448) “Monks, there are these three kinds of discontent. What three? Discontent with regard to gain, discontent with regard to honor, and discontent with regard to fame. These, monks, are the three kinds of discontent.”
“Bhikkhus, there are three things.
Which three?
Discontent, cruelty, and conduct contrary to the Dhamma.”
“Monks, these are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?”

“Displeasure should be developed for the abandoning of discontent; non-cruelty should be developed for the abandoning of cruelty; righteous conduct should be developed for the abandoning of unrighteous conduct.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, these three things should be developed.
This is the seventh [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.114 11.

Tikavagga Santuṭṭhitāsutta: On Contentment “Monks, there are these three kinds of contentment. What three? Contentment with whatever robe one obtains, contentment with whatever almsfood one obtains, and contentment with whatever lodging one obtains. These, monks, are the three kinds of contentment.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things.
Which three?”
Lack of contentment, lack of clear comprehension, and great desire.
These, monks, are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?

For the abandoning of discontent, contentment should be developed; for the abandoning of lack of clear comprehension, clear comprehension should be developed; for the abandoning of great desires, fewness of wishes should be developed.
It is for the abandoning of these three states, monks, that these three states should be developed.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.115 11.
Tikavagga (The Chapter on Threes)
The Discourse on Contumacy (Dovacassatāsutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these three things.”
Which three?
Refractoriness, association with evil friends, and mental distraction.
These, monks, are the three things.
“Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, three things are to be developed.
Which three?

For the abandoning of being difficult to speak with, being easy to speak with is to be developed; for the abandoning of bad friendship, good friendship is to be developed; for the abandoning of mental distraction, mindfulness of breathing is to be developed.”
“Monks, for the abandoning of these three things, these three things are to be developed.
(The ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.116

11. Tikavagga Uddhaccasutta (AN 6.116, PTS AN iii 449) “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is restless, the person who is dull, and the person who is balanced. And how, monks, is one a person who is restless? Here, monks, a certain person is restless in body, restless in speech, and restless in mind. This, monks, is called a person who is restless. And how, monks, is one a person who is dull? Here, monks, a certain person is dull in body, dull in speech, and dull in mind. This, monks, is called a person who is dull. And how, monks, is one a person who is balanced? Here, monks, a certain person is balanced in body, balanced in speech, and balanced in mind. This, monks, is called a person who is balanced. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these three things.
Which three?
Restlessness, lack of restraint, and negligence.”
“Monks, these are the three things.
For the abandoning of these three things, monks, three things are to be developed.
Which three?”

“Bhikkhus, for the abandoning of restlessness, serenity should be developed; for the abandoning of non-restraint, restraint should be developed; for the abandoning of negligence, diligence should be developed.
Indeed, bhikkhus, for the abandoning of these three things, these three things should be developed.
The tenth.
The eleventh chapter: The Group of Triads.
Its summary verse:
Passion, misconduct, and thought;
Perception is called an element;
gratification, danger, and satisfaction,
along with agitation— these two constitute the group.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.117 12.

Sāmaññavagga Kāyānupassīsutta: The Discourse on Contemplation of the Body “Monks, when a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, he may expect one of two results: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning.”
“Bhikkhus, without having abandoned six things, one is incapable of dwelling contemplating the body as the body. What are the six? [The text continues with the list of six things.]”
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, lack of restraint over the sense faculties, and lack of moderation in eating.
Monks, without abandoning these six things, one is incapable of dwelling contemplating the body as the body.
Monks, by abandoning these six things, one is capable of dwelling contemplating the body as the body.
Which six?
Delight in work, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, lack of restraint over the sense faculties, and lack of moderation in eating.
It is by abandoning these six things, monks, that one is capable of dwelling contemplating the body as the body.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.118 12.
Sāmaññavagga (The Chapter on the State of a Recluse)
Dhammānupassīsutta: “Bhikkhus,
without abandoning six things, one is incapable of [establishing] mindfulness of the body internally …” [and so on].
... externally in the body ...
internally and externally in the body ...
internally in feelings ... [and so on].
In external feelings …pe… in internal and external feelings …pe… internally in the mind …pe…
... externally in regard to the mind ...
internally and externally in regard to the mind ...
internally in regard to mental phenomena ... [and so forth].
To dwell contemplating phenomena in external phenomena …pe… and to dwell contemplating phenomena in both internal and external phenomena.
Which six?
“Monks, by abandoning these six things— one being fond of work, fond of talk, fond of sleep, fond of company, lack of restraint over the sense faculties, and lack of moderation in eating—
one is capable of dwelling contemplating phenomena among internal and external phenomena.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.119 12. Sāmaññavagga Tapussasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the wanderer Tapussa approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Tapussa said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the purpose and benefit of the holy life under the ascetic Gotama? “Friend Tapussa, the purpose and benefit of the holy life under the Tathāgata is the complete destruction of suffering. “But, Master Gotama, how does the purpose and benefit of the holy life come about through the complete destruction of suffering? “Here, friend Tapussa, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way;

that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “When a noble disciple possesses these three factors, he has entered the stream of the Dhamma, become one of the noble ones, and is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, certain of rightness, headed for enlightenment. When this was said, the wanderer Tapussa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. Then the wanderer Tapussa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the wanderer Tapussa had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? “The person who is intent on gain, honor, and praise; the person who is intent on harm; the person who is intent on both gain, honor, and praise, and on harm; the person who is intent on neither gain, honor, and praise, nor on harm; and the person who is intent on the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion. These are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Bhante, it is marvelous, Bhante, how well the Blessed One has stated: ‘There are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. “It is because I have seen, Ānanda, that there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world that I have stated: ‘There are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.120–139 12. The Chapter on Asceticism (Sāmaññavagga) The Discourse on the Bhallikas, etc. (Bhallikādisutta) [120] At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these six kinds of persons found existing in the world. What six? The person who is like a stone; the person who is like a water jar; the person who is like a leaking jar; the person who is like a lotus leaf; the person who is like a water lily; and the person who is like a great ocean. And how, monks, is a person like a stone? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is sensual lust in me. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is ill will in me. He dwells with his mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is sloth and torpor in me. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is restlessness and remorse in me. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me.

Just as a stone of one cubit or two cubits, thrown into the water, sinks down and stays at the bottom, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. This, monks, is called a person who is like a stone. And how, monks, is a person like a water jar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, the obsessions subside within him, and he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. Just as a water jar, when filled with water and placed on a stand, might be struck by a stick or a potsherd, and the sound would be loud and long-lasting, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. This, monks, is called a person who is like a water jar. And how, monks, is a person like a leaking jar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. Yet as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions assail him again. Just as a leaking jar, when filled with water and placed on a stand, might leak away its water drop by drop, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. Yet as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions assail him again. This, monks, is called a person who is like a leaking jar. And how, monks, is a person like a lotus leaf? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. And as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions do not assail him. Just as a lotus leaf, though touched by water, is not wetted by it, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. And as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions do not assail him. This, monks, is called a person who is like a lotus leaf. And how, monks, is a person like a water lily? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. And as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions do not assail him. Just as a water lily, though touched by water, is not wetted by it, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. And as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions do not assail him. This, monks, is called a person who is like a water lily. And how, monks, is a person like a great ocean? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. And as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions do not assail him. Just as the great ocean, though touched by rivers, is not filled by them, so too, monks, this person dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust... ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... and doubt, and he does not understand as it really is: ‘There is doubt in me. But when he has gone to the forest... he attains and dwells in the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna. And as soon as he emerges from that attainment, the obsessions do not assail him. This, monks, is called a person who is like a great ocean. These, monks, are the six kinds of persons found existing in the world. The householder Citta of Macchikāsaṇḍa … Hatthaka of Āḷavī … Mahānāma the Sakyan …

13. The Series on Lust (Rāgapeyyāla).
“Bhikkhus, for the direct knowledge of lust, six things are to be developed.”
Which six?
The unsurpassed sight, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.13. Rāgapeyyāla (AN 6.141, AN 6.122, PTS AN iii 452) [The Section on Passion] “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. Rāgapeyyāla* (The Series on Lust)
“Bhikkhus, for the direct knowledge of lust, six things are to be developed. Which six? [The rest of the discourse follows.]”

“Perception of impermanence, perception of suffering in what is impermanent, perception of non-self in what is suffering, perception of abandoning, perception of dispassion, and perception of cessation.
For direct knowledge of lust, bhikkhus, these six things are to be developed.
